Postinfectious Cerebellitis

MONDO:0850107 Pathograph 33 Show in embeddings browser cerebellar disease

An immune-mediated inflammatory syndrome of the cerebellum that follows an infection, or rarely a vaccination, after a latent interval of about a week. It spans a severity spectrum: a benign acute cerebellar ataxia at one end, acute cerebellitis with signal change and swelling in the middle, and a rare fulminant form with cerebellar oedema, hydrocephalus and a risk of herniation at the other. The latent interval is what separates it from an infection of the cerebellum itself. Most children recover completely; a minority are left with ataxia, tremor or cognitive deficits, and death is rare and essentially confined to the fulminant form.

Subtypes

3
Acute cerebellar ataxia (benign post-infectious)
The benign end of the spectrum: acute ataxia with or without nystagmus, and recovery that is usually complete. It is the commonest tier.
Show evidence (1 reference)
PMID:42649322 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical
"Based on neuroimaging findings and the presence of life-threatening features, 34 patients (46.6%) were classified as acute cerebellar ataxia (ACA), 26 (35.6%) as acute cerebellitis (AC), and 13 (17.8%) as acute fulminant cerebellitis (AFC), with complete recovery in 58.8%, 69.2%, and 69.2% of..."
The sentence that defines all three tiers and gives each one's share and outcome in the pooled cohort. Note what it does not show: complete recovery is lowest in the benign tier, at 58.8% against 69.2% in the other two, which is the opposite of what the tier names suggest and is why this entry does not present the tiers as a prognostic ladder.
Acute cerebellitis
The middle tier, distinguished clinically by headache and vomiting accompanying the ataxia and radiologically by cerebellar signal change with swelling. Sequelae are commoner here than the benign tier's reputation suggests.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:32160830 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical
"The diagnosis of acute cerebellitis rather than acute postinfectious cerebellar ataxia should be considered when headache and vomiting accompany ataxia in a child."
The clinical discriminator between this tier and the benign one, stated as a rule for the bedside: headache and vomiting with the ataxia. It is a recommendation rather than a validated rule, which is why it is cited here and not in a definitions block.
PMID:41321459 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical
"AC patients exhibited later onset, longer duration from symptom onset to hospital presentation, and more frequent neurological symptoms (encephalopathy, headache, vomiting) compared to APCA."
The same discriminator from an independent cohort of 257 children, with two more axes: later onset and a longer interval to presentation. Two sources agreeing on headache and vomiting is why the tier is recorded at all.
Acute fulminant cerebellitis
The rare, life-threatening tier: rapid cerebellar oedema with obstructive hydrocephalus and brainstem compression. It may present with depressed consciousness and no cerebellar signs at all, which is what makes it dangerous to recognise late.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:33454719 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical
"The clinical picture started with severe headache, irritability, and acute deterioration of consciousness level with the absence of cerebellar signs. There was radiological evidence of obstructive hydrocephalus and cerebellar tonsillar herniation in the context of the inflamed cerebellum."
The presentation that defines this tier and the reason it is separated from the other two: the cerebellar signs a clinician would look for are absent, and what is present is raised intracranial pressure. Two cases, so it is a description rather than a frequency.
PMID:42699856 SUPPORT DIRECT BACKGROUND Human clinical
"Acute cerebellitis (AC) in children is often benign; however, a fulminant variant featuring rapid cerebellar edema, hydrocephalus, and brainstem compression can be life-threatening."
States the tier against the background of the others, and names the three features that make it fulminant. BACKGROUND because the sentence frames the case series rather than reporting its result.

Discussions and Knowledge Gaps

3
The rodent model of acute cerebellar inflammation produces Purkinje cell hyperexcitability and depression-like behaviour but no ataxia, while the human disease is defined by ataxia. Does the inflammatory mechanism shown in the model explain the human sign, or is a further step missing?
HUMAN MODEL MISMATCH OPEN pic_hyperexcitability_without_ataxia
Attached to
pathophysiology#Purkinje Cell Intrinsic Hyperexcitability pathophysiology#Cerebellar Dysfunction
The microglia-TNF-alpha-Purkinje cell arm of this entry's pathograph rests entirely on rodent work, and the authors of that work say in terms that their animals were not ataxic. Models that are ataxic show the opposite electrophysiology - Purkinje cell loss and hypoexcitability. So the cited mechanism and the cited sign come from different preparations, and the edge from hyperexcitability to cerebellar dysfunction is the entry's weakest. It is drawn because it is what the sources support, and it is marked here rather than left to look settled.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:35326323 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Model organism
"In our animal model of the acute inflammation of the cerebellar cortex, animals did not show any ataxia but hyperexcitability in the cerebellar cortex and depression-like behaviors."
The mismatch stated by the authors of the model itself: inflammation produced hyperexcitability and no ataxia.
PMID:35326323 SUPPORT DIRECT REVIEW SYNTHESIS Model organism
"Therefore, there is a gap in our interpretation between the very early phase of cerebellar inflammation and the emergence of cerebellar ataxia."
The same authors naming the gap as a gap. This is the sentence the discussion exists to carry.
Is the anti-glutamate-receptor-delta2 autoantibody found in some cases a cause of the cerebellar injury or a consequence of it?
CONTROVERSY OPEN pic_glurdelta2_cause_or_consequence
Attached to
pathophysiology#Immune Response Directed at the Cerebellum pathophysiology#Autoantibodies Binding Neural Tissue
Two case reports of the same antibody read it in opposite directions, and neither is in a position to settle the question: one argues the antibody is induced by cerebellar damage because it was absent from the cerebrospinal fluid early on, the other argues it plays a causal role because it was present in both serum and cerebrospinal fluid. Each is a single patient. A review adds that rabbit antibodies against the receptor's putative ligand-binding region caused transient ataxia when injected over the mouse cerebellum, which shows that such an antibody can act, not that the patients' antibodies do. The entry's immune-response node therefore names no effector, and this discussion records why.
Show evidence (3 references)
PMID:17049194 SUPPORT INDIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical
"Thus, we believe that the glutamate receptor delta2 autoantibody may play a role in cerebellar ataxia and consecutive cerebellitis."
One side, stated as a belief by its own authors from one 18-month-old patient in whom the antibody was found in both serum and cerebrospinal fluid.
PMID:17008044 REFUTE INDIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical
"It was suggested that autoantibodies against GluRdelta2 might not have injured the tissue due to the immunological action, but might be induced as a consequence of cerebellar damage."
The other side, from a single 13-year-old in whom the antibody was in serum but not cerebrospinal fluid. REFUTE against the pathogenic reading above, not against the antibody's presence, which both reports agree on.
PMID:26377184 SUPPORT INDIRECT REVIEW SYNTHESIS Model organism
"injection of polyclonal antibodies specific for the putative ligand-binding region of GluRδ2 generated by immunisation of rabbits with a synthetic peptide into the supracerebellar subarachnoid space was shown to cause ... transient ataxia in mice"
Support for the pathogenic reading, as a review reports it: an antibody against the receptor can cause transient ataxia in mice. INDIRECT because the antibodies were raised in rabbits against a synthetic peptide, not taken from patients; the ellipsis skips the culture results in the same sentence.
Do corticosteroids change the outcome of post-infectious cerebellitis, and in which severity tier?
KNOWLEDGE GAP OPEN pic_steroid_effect_untested
Attached to
treatments#Corticosteroid therapy
Three quarters of pooled patients receive corticosteroids and no cited source compares them with no treatment in a controlled design. The nearest thing to a comparison is two children in a fulminant case report, one given immunomodulatory therapy with a better outcome and one not. A multicentre paediatric series of acute cerebellar ataxia and cerebellitis reports that patients with a higher clinical score on admission had a higher probability of receiving intravenous steroids, so an outcome comparison in it would be confounded by indication, and it says randomised controlled trials are needed to confirm its observations. Because most children in the benign tier recover without treatment, a trial would have to be powered on the severe tiers, which are the rare ones - which is a reason the gap has stayed open rather than an argument that it does not matter.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:28606112 SUPPORT DIRECT Human clinical
"Randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm these observations."
The gap, stated by the authors of that multicentre paediatric series. No quote_role is recorded: a call for future work is neither the paper's finding nor somebody else's fact.
PMID:30221603 SUPPORT INDIRECT REVIEW SYNTHESIS Human clinical
"There is no evidence of significant differences in terms of response and prognosis among the various types of immunotherapies."
The adjacent gap for the choice between immunotherapies, from a practical-guidelines review of immune-mediated cerebellar ataxias that treats this disease as one of its members.

Pathophysiology

9
Preceding Infection
An infection, or rarely a vaccination, precedes the cerebellar syndrome by a latent interval of about a week. The interval is what makes the syndrome post-infectious rather than an infection of the cerebellum. No single organism defines it: the commonest trigger differs by era and population, and in a quarter of children none is identified.
Downstream
Immune Response Directed at the Cerebellum The infection raises a response that then acts on the cerebellum. What connects the two is not demonstrated in this disease by any source cited here: none shows a shared epitope in a patient with it, and the two case reports that name a route, molecular mimicry or antibodies that cross-react with cerebellar epitopes, do so in their discussions without testing it.
Show evidence (4 references)
PMID:42649322 SUPPORT DIRECT REVIEW SYNTHESIS Human clinical
"Post-infectious cerebellitis is an immune-mediated cerebellar inflammatory syndrome that follows a preceding infection (or, rarely, vaccination) after a latent interval."
The definitional sentence, and the one that carries the latent interval. It is the interval, not the infection, that places the syndrome after the infection rather than inside it.
PMID:14552515 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical
"Latency from the prodromal illness to the onset of ataxia was 8.8 +/- 7.4 days."
Puts a number on the interval in 39 children: a mean of 8.8 days. The standard deviation of 7.4 is as informative as the mean, since it spans same-week and three-week onsets.
PMID:14552515 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical
"A prodromal febrile illness was noted in 74.4%: varicella, 31%; mumps, 20%; nonspecific viral infection, 15.4%; mycoplasma, 5%; Epstein Barr virus, 3%."
The trigger distribution in that series, and the fact that a quarter of children had no prodromal illness at all.
+ 1 more reference
Immune Response Directed at the Cerebellum
The step that makes this disease immune-mediated rather than infectious. Not every cited source names an immune mechanism: several describe the disease without one, and one of them calls the aetiology usually viral. It places the syndrome in the family of immune-mediated cerebellar ataxias, beside gluten ataxia, the paraneoplastic degenerations and opsoclonus-myoclonus. Which effector does the damage is not settled here: autoantibodies against several cerebellar targets are reported in individual patients, and whether any of them is pathogenic rather than a consequence of damage is an open question recorded in this entry's discussions.
Downstream
Microglial Activation The step from an immune response to a change the cerebellum can register. This arm is shown in a rodent model: no cited source shows it in a patient with this disease.
Cerebellar Swelling and Mass Effect The second arm out of the immune response, and the one that makes the fulminant tier dangerous. A review cited on the swelling node calls swelling the most characteristic MRI finding of acute cerebellitis, and the fulminant tier is defined by its obstructive hydrocephalus and brainstem compression. It is an inflammatory oedema of the cerebellum rather than a functional change in its neurons, and it is what the surgical treatments act on.
Autoantibodies Binding Neural Tissue The humoral arm of the response: some patients have antibodies that bind neural tissue. The edge records that the response produces them. Whether they then injure the cerebellum is not drawn, for the reason the node gives.
Show evidence (3 references)
PMID:30221603 SUPPORT DIRECT REVIEW SYNTHESIS Human clinical
"Immune-mediated cerebellar ataxias (IMCAs), a clinical entity reported for the first time in the 1980s, include gluten ataxia (GA), paraneoplastic cerebellar degenerations (PCDs), antiglutamate decarboxylase 65 (GAD) antibody-associated cerebellar ataxia, post-infectious cerebellitis, and..."
Places this disease in the immune-mediated cerebellar ataxia family, named alongside four others this knowledge base curates or will. REVIEW_SYNTHESIS because the review is classifying rather than reporting its own result.
PMID:17049194 SUPPORT INDIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical
"Cerebro-spinal fluid examination and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrated pleocytosis and meningeal enhancement, respectively. Furthermore, glutamate receptor delta2 autoantibody was detected in serum and cerebro-spinal fluid. Thus, we believe that the glutamate receptor delta2..."
One reported autoantibody, against a receptor the same paper says is predominantly expressed in Purkinje cells, with the authors' own hedge preserved: may play a role. A single case, and the next item is the reason it is not read as cause.
PMID:17008044 REFUTE DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical
"It was suggested that autoantibodies against GluRdelta2 might not have injured the tissue due to the immunological action, but might be induced as a consequence of cerebellar damage."
The counter-reading of the same antibody, from a different case: it may be a consequence of cerebellar damage rather than its cause. REFUTE against the claim that the antibody is pathogenic, which is why this node names no effector.
Autoantibodies Binding Neural Tissue
The humoral arm of the immune response, as far as it can be measured: antibodies in serum or cerebrospinal fluid that bind brain tissue or named neural antigens. The targets differ between patients and studies: glutamate receptor delta 2, a receptor of the Purkinje cell, in single cases; centrosome proteins, pericentrin among them, after varicella; and neuronal, glial and myelin antigens in 10 of 36 children with acute cerebellitis in one multicentre series. No study of this disease cited here found a single neural antigen targeted in most of its patients. Antibodies against centrosome proteins are found after varicella without ataxia as well, though not those against pericentrin. Whether any of them injures the cerebellum, rather than marking an injury already done, is not settled; the node has no edge onward for that reason, and the question is recorded in the discussions.

Show evidence (3 references)
PMID:26377184 SUPPORT DIRECT REVIEW SYNTHESIS Human clinical
"No tumours have been reported so far in patients with anti-GluRδ2-associated cerebellar ataxia. Of note, however, all cases were preceded or accompanied by either infection or vaccination."
A review's tally of the reported cases of cerebellar ataxia with antibodies against glutamate receptor delta 2: every one followed or accompanied an infection or a vaccination, and none had a tumour.
PMID:14503922 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical
"Antibodies to pericentrin were seen in 5/12 children with post-varicella ataxia but not in any of the other sera tested."
The only antibody in the cited sources found in patients with this disease, tested against comparison groups and absent from all of them: five of twelve children after varicella, and none in the comparison groups, which included children with uncomplicated varicella. A single small study.
PMID:38284996 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical
"In 10/36 (28 %) children the following autoantibodies (abs) were found: MOG-abs (n = 5) in serum, GFAPα-abs (n = 1) in CSF, GlyR-abs (n = 1) in CSF, mGluR1-abs (n = 1) in CSF and serum."
How often an antibody is found when serum and cerebrospinal fluid are both tested in a multicentre series of children with acute cerebellitis: 10 of 36, against several different antigens. The biochemical row on this panel records why the figure is not an unselected rate.
Microglial Activation
Microglia in the cerebellar cortex are activated, through toll-like receptor 4, by bacterial endotoxin or by heat-killed bacteria. Shown in rodent cerebellum and established as a step by depleting the cells; not shown in tissue from a patient with this disease by any source cited here.

Animal models
Acute cerebellar inflammation rodent model Mouse and rat recapitulates The node exists because of this model. Activation is established by depleting the cells and by inhibiting their activity, which is a necessity test rather than an observation.
Downstream
TNF-alpha Release Activation through toll-like receptor 4 is what releases the cytokine. The two are separated because the cited study tests them separately: depleting the cells tests the first, inhibiting the cytokine the second.
Show evidence (1 reference)
PMID:31509752 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Model organism
"Region-specific inflammation in the cerebellum in vivo shows depression- and autistic-like behaviors. Furthermore, both TNF-alpha inhibition and microglia depletion revert such behavioral abnormality."
The necessity test for this node: blocking the cytokine or removing the cell reverses the behavioural change. What this model produces is that behavioural change and not ataxia - stated in those terms by a separate review of the same model literature, and recorded as a discussion in this entry.
TNF-alpha Release
Tumour necrosis factor alpha released from activated microglia. Inhibiting it reverses the behavioural change in the rodent model, which is the test that makes this a step rather than a correlate.

GO:0032640 is a biological process from the Gene Ontology.
Downstream
Purkinje Cell Intrinsic Hyperexcitability TNF-alpha acts on its receptor on Bergmann glia, which release glutamate onto metabotropic receptors on the Purkinje cell. Each link in that chain was tested separately, in rat cerebellar slice and, for the glutamate step, in dissociated cortical astrocyte culture.
Show evidence (1 reference)
PMID:31509752 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Model organism
"Activated microglia via exposure to bacterial endotoxin lipopolysaccharide or heat-killed Gram-negative bacteria induce a potentiation of the intrinsic excitability in Purkinje neurons, which is suppressed by microglia-activity inhibitor and microglia depletion."
The whole arm in one sentence, with both tests: a microglial inhibitor and microglial depletion each suppress the effect.
Purkinje Cell Intrinsic Hyperexcitability
The Purkinje cell fires more readily. This is the cellular state the rodent work converges on, and the point at which the model and the human disease part company: the animals became hyperexcitable and did not become ataxic, while the ataxic animal models in the same literature show Purkinje degeneration and hypoexcitability instead.
Purkinje cell CL:0000121 Cell Ontology (CL) Relation: this pathophysiological event involves this cell type This pathophysiological event involves Purkinje cell (CL:0000121). CL:0000121 is a cell type from the Cell Ontology.
Animal models
Acute cerebellar inflammation rodent model Mouse and rat recapitulates The electrophysiological change this entry's chain turns on, measured directly in the model.
Downstream
Cerebellar Dysfunction Recorded as INDIRECT because the step is not demonstrated: the source that describes both ends says there is a gap between them. The edge is drawn so the graph reaches the clinical syndrome, and the gap is a discussion rather than a hidden assumption.
Show evidence (1 reference)
PMID:35326323 SUPPORT DIRECT REVIEW SYNTHESIS Model organism
"In our animal model of the acute inflammation of the cerebellar cortex, animals did not show any ataxia but hyperexcitability in the cerebellar cortex and depression-like behaviors. In contrast, animal models with neurodegeneration of the cerebellar Purkinje cells and hypoexcitability of the..."
The authors state the gap themselves, and this entry does not paper over it: the inflammation model produces hyperexcitability without ataxia, while the models that are ataxic show the opposite cellular state. The chain above is therefore the best-evidenced account of early cerebellar inflammation, not an explanation of the ataxia the patients present with.
Cerebellar Dysfunction
The clinical syndrome: a broad-based ataxic gait with dysmetria, nystagmus, intention tremor and dysarthria in varying combination. It is where the pathograph reaches the phenotypes.

Animal models
Acute cerebellar inflammation rodent model Mouse and rat fails to recapitulate The model does not produce the sign that defines the human disease. Its animals show depression-like and autistic-like behaviour and no ataxia, which is the gap this entry records as a discussion.
Downstream
Ataxic gait The commonest and most characteristic sign.
Dysmetria An appendicular cerebellar sign.
Nystagmus The commonest ocular sign in the paediatric series cited.
Dysarthria Slurred speech, reported among the common symptoms.
Intention tremor A cerebellar sign like the others on this node, and one of the deficits that outlasts the acute phase in the long-term series.
Cognitive and behavioural sequelae Recorded as INDIRECT because the cited series report cognitive deficits at follow-up without establishing the step from the cerebellar lesion to them.
Show evidence (1 reference)
PMID:38008790 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical
"Clinical presentation was divided into two categories: (1) isolated cerebellar signs (CS): ataxic gait, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, intention tremor, dysarthria, and nystagmus; (2) CS-plus symptoms which included CS associated with any of other symptoms such as encephalopathy (GCS < 15),..."
The sign list this node resolves into, and the split the same series shows matters for outcome: isolated cerebellar signs against cerebellar signs plus something else.
Cerebellar Swelling and Mass Effect
The arm that makes the fulminant tier dangerous. Cerebellar oedema in the posterior fossa obstructs cerebrospinal fluid flow and compresses the brainstem, and it is what the surgical treatments act on. A review calls diffuse swelling the most characteristic MRI finding of acute cerebellitis, so it is not confined to the fulminant tier, and mass effect is also reported in children whose reports do not call their disease fulminant: tonsillar descent in 11 of 15 children of an acute cerebellitis series in which no child needed surgical decompression, tonsillar ectopia in 8 of 9 children seen by one neurosurgical service, and herniation with hydrocephalus in two children who both recovered fully.

Downstream
Headache Headache with the ataxia is what marks the tiers in which the cerebellum is swollen. No cited source states the mechanism, so the edge is drawn through unknown intermediates: raised pressure in the posterior fossa is the obvious route and none of these papers measures it.
Vomiting The other half of the pair that marks those tiers, and on the same footing: an association the cited sources report without measuring what lies between.
Obstructive hydrocephalus Swelling in the posterior fossa obstructs cerebrospinal fluid outflow. A review gives hydrocephalus or tonsillar herniation as a frequent complication of the swelling; one series describes triventricular hydrocephalus from extrinsic compression of the aqueduct of Sylvius without saying what compresses it, and one case report's CT shows the swollen hemispheres compressing the fourth ventricle, with obstructive hydrocephalus.
Brainstem Compression and Tonsillar Herniation The swollen cerebellum, confined in the posterior fossa, pushes the tonsils down and can press on the brainstem. A review gives tonsillar herniation as a complication of the swelling, beside hydrocephalus rather than after it, and one case report's CT shows the swollen hemispheres compressing the fourth ventricle and the brainstem.
Increased intracranial pressure The swelling and the hydrocephalus it causes are the evident route to raised pressure, but no cited source says how the pressure rises or measures it: one series names compression of the posterior fossa, acute hydrocephalus and intracranial hypertension together as the causes of death in the fulminant form.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:32160830 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical
"Tonsillar herniation was present in 73.3% and obstructive hydrocephalus in 26.6%."
The frequencies of the two consequences this node drives, in a series of 15 children with acute cerebellitis. Read the denominator: this is an acute cerebellitis series, not an unselected one.
PMID:12879984 SUPPORT DIRECT REVIEW SYNTHESIS Human clinical
"The most characteristic finding by magnetic resonance imaging is diffuse cortical swelling of the cerebellum, often complicated by hydrocephalus or tonsillar herniation."
A review's account of the most characteristic MRI finding of acute cerebellitis: diffuse swelling of the cerebellar cortex.
Brainstem Compression and Tonsillar Herniation
The swollen cerebellum can push the cerebellar tonsils down through the foramen magnum and compress the brainstem. On imaging, tonsillar descent is common where it is reported - in 8 of 9 children seen by one neurosurgical service, in 11 of 15 in an acute cerebellitis series, in both children of one two-child report, in a second two-child report that describes its pair together, and in a boy treated with a shunt - and most of these children survived. Of the three child deaths from cerebellitis that the cited sources report case by case, two are attributed in their cached abstracts to brainstem involvement or brainstem failure; for the third, the 13-year-old who died suddenly, a later case report restates that she had brainstem compression and obstructive hydrocephalus on imaging; and a case report, citing earlier work, describes fatal cerebellitis through tonsillar herniation or hydrocephalus.
brainstem UBERON:0002298 Uberon multi-species anatomy ontology (UBERON) Relation: this pathophysiological event occurs in this anatomical location This pathophysiological event occurs in brainstem (UBERON:0002298). UBERON:0002298 is an anatomical location from the Uberon multi-species anatomy ontology.
Downstream
Sudden death Two of the three child deaths from cerebellitis that the cited sources report case by case are attributed in their cached abstracts to the brainstem: one child died because of brainstem involvement, and in a three-child series the child who died had presented with obstructive hydrocephalus and progressed to brainstem failure; neither abstract says the dead child's brainstem was herniated or compressed, or that the death was sudden. For the 13-year-old who died suddenly, a later case report restates that she had brainstem compression and obstructive hydrocephalus on imaging and deteriorated rapidly to death. Two case reports also say the disease can be fatal through tonsillar herniation, hydrocephalus or brainstem compression, one of them citing earlier work. No cited source says how the compression causes death, so the edge is drawn through unknown intermediates.

PMID:33581790 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical
"Imaging abnormalities included tonsillar ectopia (n = 8, 88.9%), bilateral cerebellar T2 hyperintensity (n = 6, 66.7%), and obstructive hydrocephalus (n = 6, 66.7%)."
Tonsillar descent on imaging in 8 of 9 children referred to one neurosurgical service, with hydrocephalus in 6. Descent on imaging is not by itself a clinical herniation.
PMID:32160830 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical
"Tonsillar herniation was present in 73.3% and obstructive hydrocephalus in 26.6%."
Tonsillar herniation in 11 of 15 children of an acute cerebellitis series, in which no child needed surgical decompression.
PMID:19664537 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical

Both children of a two-child report, who both recovered fully.

The commonest treatment in the pooled literature, at three quarters of patients, given on the reasoning that the disease is immune-mediated. Many of the cited sources never mention a steroid, clinical series among them. No cited source compares it against no treatment in a controlled design; the only treated-against-untreated contrast is two children in a fulminant case report, and it is about immunomodulatory therapy rather than steroids specifically.
Mechanism Target:
Immune Response Directed at the Cerebellum — Suppression of the immune response is what the drug is given for. No cited source demonstrates that it acts on this node in this disease; the target is inferred from the drug class.

Cerebrospinal fluid diversion and posterior fossa decompression
Action: cerebrospinal fluid diversionNCI Thesaurus (NCIT) Relation: this treatment is this clinical intervention This treatment is cerebrospinal fluid diversion (NCIT:C93208). NCIT:C93208 is a clinical intervention from the NCI Thesaurus. Ontology label: Cerebrospinal Fluid Diversion NCIT:C93208
Platform: Surgery
The treatment for the swelling's hydrocephalus and mass effect, needed above all in the fulminant tier, and the one whose timing the cited three-child series turns on. External ventricular drainage or a shunt relieves the hydrocephalus; posterior fossa decompression relieves the mass effect itself. Of nine children seen by one centre's neurosurgical service, four needed external ventricular drainage, for a mean of 11 days, and none needed further surgery; in another series of nine children one needed surgery for triventricular hydrocephalus; a 7-year-old needed emergency drainage for life-threatening hydrocephalus; a 12-year-old boy recovered completely within two weeks of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt and treatment for raised pressure, and his authors call the ventricular decompression life-saving; both children of a two-child report of the fulminant form were given cerebrospinal fluid diversion; in a three-child series one girl recovered fully after emergency posterior fossa decompression when steroids had not stopped her decline; and of two children with herniation and hydrocephalus, one was drained and the other treated without surgery, and both recovered fully.
Mechanism Target:
Cerebellar Swelling and Mass Effect — Both procedures act on the swelling arm directly: one by draining the obstructed cerebrospinal fluid, the other by enlarging the compartment the swollen cerebellum sits in.

Varicella-zoster virus infection
varicella-zoster virus infection ECTO:3000001 Environmental Conditions, Treatments and Exposures Ontology (ECTO) Relation: this environmental factor is this exposure This environmental factor is varicella-zoster virus infection, annotated with exposure to virus (ECTO:3000001). ECTO:3000001 is an exposure from the Environmental Conditions, Treatments and Exposures Ontology.
Bound to the generic virus-exposure term because ECTO has none for this virus. In the ECTO build the term validator uses, `runoak -i sqlite:obo:ecto info` returned nothing for 'l~varicella', 'l~zoster', 'l~chickenpox', 'l~VZV' or 'l~Human alphaherpesvirus 3', and 'l~alphaherpesvirus' returned only the human alphaherpesvirus 1, suid and canid terms. The preferred term names the virus.
Chickenpox, the primary infection with varicella-zoster virus. Before varicella vaccination it was the infection most often identified before the syndrome, in about a quarter of children in large series. The syndrome follows only a small fraction of infections: a Dutch surveillance study put it at 5 cases per 100,000 infections in children up to 5 years.

Epstein-Barr virus infection
Epstein-Barr virus infection ECTO:3000273 Environmental Conditions, Treatments and Exposures Ontology (ECTO) Relation: this environmental factor is this exposure This environmental factor is Epstein-Barr virus infection, annotated with exposure to human gammaherpesvirus 4 (ECTO:3000273). ECTO:3000273 is an exposure from the Environmental Conditions, Treatments and Exposures Ontology.
Graded as a trigger, where the cytomegalovirus and human herpesvirus 6 rows are graded as associations only. For this virus one cited source names it a cause of acute cerebellar ataxia, another reads its case as favouring a syndrome that follows the infection, a pooled review counts it among the identified triggers, and it is reported in children and in adults. Cytomegalovirus rests on one child's work-up and a review's potential association, and the one human herpesvirus 6 case carried a second virus, so it cannot be put on that virus alone.
A recognised but rare cause, less frequent than varicella in children (one of 39 children in a two-centre series) and described as rare in adults. In the two adult reports cited here the infection was shown in the blood while testing of the cerebrospinal fluid for the virus was negative; the authors of one read this as favouring a syndrome that follows the infection rather than an infection of the cerebellum, while noting that serology is a weaker test than PCR. One of the two had no symptoms of the infection before the ataxia.

varicella vaccination ECTO:2000129 Environmental Conditions, Treatments and Exposures Ontology (ECTO) Relation: this environmental factor is this exposure This environmental factor is varicella vaccination, annotated with exposure to vaccination (ECTO:2000129). Protects against the varicella share of the syndrome. In a national Australian surveillance series from a population with high vaccine coverage, none of 20 cases followed varicella. Diagnosis

3
Cerebellar magnetic resonance imaging
The test that separates the tiers. Bilateral symmetrical T2 signal change in the cerebellar cortex with swelling marks the cerebellitis tier; a normal scan does not exclude the benign one. Whether an abnormal scan also carries prognostic weight is unsettled: the two series on the imaging findings point different ways, and they compare different things.
magnetic resonance imaging of the cerebellum NCIT:C16809 NCI Thesaurus (NCIT)
Show evidence (3 references)
PMID:32160830 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical
"Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) generally showed bilateral symmetrical T2 hyperintense changes with moderate swelling in the cerebellar cortex."
The imaging pattern itself, in a series of fifteen children with the cerebellitis tier.
PMID:28606112 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical
"Children with pathological magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or computed tomography (CT) had a higher probability of having clinical sequelae."
The prognostic half of the same test, across 124 children: in that series an abnormal scan at admission went with sequelae, which is the authors' stated reason for imaging every child rather than only the severe ones. A smaller series of acute cerebellitis found MRI results not predictive of outcome; the imaging findings carry both.
PMID:11826604 SUPPORT INDIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical
"Their magnetic resonance imaging showed hyperintense signal of cerebellar gray matter in T2-weighted sequences, which is a strong indication of a diagnosis of acute cerebellitis."
The same pattern read from two cases, with the authors' own statement of how far it takes a diagnosis: a strong indication, not a confirmation. Two patients, so the claim rests on the series above rather than on this.
Cerebrospinal fluid examination
Used to narrow the differential rather than to confirm this diagnosis. A normal result does not exclude it, and in a multicentre paediatric series the cerebrospinal fluid findings did not correlate with symptoms or clinical outcome.
lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid examination NCIT:C15327 NCI Thesaurus (NCIT)
Whether posterior fossa swelling should stop or delay lumbar puncture is not settled by the cited sources: none says when it should, one case report (PMID:28446490) calls the test important when there is no contraindication, without naming one, and in its own case the test was done after a shunt had decompressed the ventricles. Swelling is found in the acute cerebellitis tier, not only the fulminant one, which is defined by rapid swelling with obstructive hydrocephalus and brainstem compression. The entry therefore records the test and not a rule for when to omit it.

"There was no correlation among symptoms, cerebrospinal fluid findings, clinical outcome."
The negative result that sets what this test is for: across 124 children the cerebrospinal fluid findings predicted neither the presentation nor the outcome.

"Diagnosing of acute cerebellitis can sometimes be difficult because the patient may present only mild cerebellar signs and the examination of cerebrospinal fluid may be normal."

The authors' own statement of the division of labour between the two tests in this entry's diagnosis block, from a review of 35 adult cases.
Identification of the antecedent infection
A search that usually fails, and that is a finding rather than a shortfall: no pathogen is identified in a quarter to a third of cases, and the diagnosis does not depend on finding one. 5
Normal neuroimaging in acute cerebellar ataxia
In the mildest cases the scan is normal, and an abnormal scan points instead to acute cerebellitis, though a review of the two notes considerable overlap between them. Whether every child needs imaging is itself unsettled: one series says imaging is needed only for an atypical presentation or a child who has not improved after one to two weeks, while another suggests an instrumental evaluation of every child at admission.

+ 1 more reference
Bilateral T2 hyperintensity and swelling of the cerebellar cortex
The scan of acute cerebellitis: T2 hyperintense signal in the grey matter of the cerebellar cortex, generally bilateral and symmetrical, with swelling. Imaging of the brain is required for the diagnosis, and the same 15-child series that describes the pattern found tonsillar herniation in 11 of its children and obstructive hydrocephalus in 4. Two series point different ways on whether the scan predicts the outcome, and they compare different things: in 124 children, nearly all with acute cerebellar ataxia, an abnormal MRI or CT went with a higher chance of sequelae than a normal one, while among the 15 children with acute cerebellitis, whose scans generally showed the pattern, MRI results did not predict the outcome.

Swelling of one cerebellar hemisphere (hemicerebellitis)
A rare form confined to one cerebellar hemisphere. MRI usually shows a diffusely swollen hemisphere with no well-defined mass, which can be mistaken for a posterior fossa tumour, so recognising it can spare a patient an unnecessary operation. Ipsilateral atrophy of the hemisphere follows in up to half of cases. One review calls it a rare disorder of unknown origin; another describes it as a one-sided presentation of acute cerebellitis. One-sided swelling also appears in a case of acute cerebellitis with antibodies against glutamate receptor delta 2.

Progression

5
Antecedent infection
A febrile illness, usually viral, in roughly three quarters of children. Varicella was historically the commonest and is no longer so where the vaccine is in use.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:14552515 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical
"A prodromal febrile illness was noted in 74.4%: varicella, 31%; mumps, 20%; nonspecific viral infection, 15.4%; mycoplasma, 5%; Epstein Barr virus, 3%."
The frequency and the breakdown, in 39 children seen between 1990 and 2001 - before varicella vaccination, which is why the varicella share here is not the current one.
PMID:35546546 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical
"An acute febrile illness was noted in 55% and none were related to varicella or were temporally related to varicella vaccination or other childhood vaccines."
The same phase counted in a vaccinated population twenty years later: no varicella at all among 20 Australian children. Twenty cases is a small denominator, and the authors present it as a description rather than a rate.
Latent interval
The gap between the infection and the ataxia, of the order of a week. It is the feature that separates this disease from an infection of the cerebellum itself.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:14552515 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical
"Latency from the prodromal illness to the onset of ataxia was 8.8 +/- 7.4 days."
The only series-level figure for this syndrome's interval in any cited source; a case report puts one child's at nine days after a respiratory infection. The standard deviation here is almost as large as the mean, so the figure is a central tendency and not a window.
PMID:42649322 SUPPORT DIRECT BACKGROUND Human clinical
"Post-infectious cerebellitis is an immune-mediated cerebellar inflammatory syndrome that follows a preceding infection (or, rarely, vaccination) after a latent interval."
The latent interval written into the definition of the disease, which is why it is a phase here rather than a detail of the history.
Acute ataxic phase
Ataxia with the cerebellar signs, lasting days to a few weeks in the benign tier. In the fulminant tier this is the phase in which swelling and hydrocephalus develop, and it may begin with headache and depressed consciousness and no cerebellar signs at all.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:14552515 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical
"Full gait recovery took less than 2 weeks on average, and the longest duration of neurologic signs was 24 days (mumps-related)."
The duration of this phase at the benign end: under two weeks on average, 24 days at the longest in a series in which every child recovered completely.
PMID:33454719 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical
"The clinical picture started with severe headache, irritability, and acute deterioration of consciousness level with the absence of cerebellar signs."
The same phase in the fulminant tier, in two children: the cerebellar signs that name the disease were absent, which is the authors' stated reason the diagnosis is missed.
Recovery or residual deficit
Most recover completely. A minority are left with ataxia, tremor or cognitive deficits, and the cognitive ones are the easiest to miss because the motor signs resolve first. Death is rare and reported only in the fulminant tier among the sources cited here.

"Complete recovery occurred in 47/73 patients (64.4%), partial recovery/residual deficit in 15/73 (20.5%), outcome was not stated for 10/73 (13.7%), and one death (1.4%) was recorded (COVID-19-associated necrotizing encephalopathy) - the only fatality, occurring in an adult."
The outcome distribution across 73 pooled patients, with the undetermined fraction left in. A pooled review of case reports is weighted towards the cases worth reporting, so these shares are an upper bound on severity rather than a population figure.

"Ninety-one percent (55/60) of these, including all children with chickenpox, recovered completely from ataxia."

"Acute cerebellitis heals with sequelae in about one-third of cases."
The cerebellitis tier, where the proportion is the other way round from the benign one. This is the authors' summary of their own 15-child series.
Outcome of the severe course
Cited sources describe the fulminant form as carrying a high risk of morbidity and mortality, in the conclusion of a three-child series and a two-case report's introduction, or of death, in the introduction of a paediatric series of nine. The only outcome rate given for the fulminant tier comes from a pooled review of 73 published cases, which counts the cases somebody chose to publish: complete recovery in 69.2% of its 13 fulminant cases, which also held its one death, an adult with a COVID-19-associated necrotising encephalopathy. In a different series, of nine children referred to one centre's neurosurgical service, two recovered completely and six were left functionally dependent, cognitive impairment being the commonest residual deficit, and the authors suggest that hydrocephalus needing surgery may predict a poor outcome.

Epidemiology

2
Age at onset
Mainly a disease of young children, though it occurs at all ages. In two paediatric series the mean age was 4.8 years in 39 children with acute cerebellar ataxia and the median 9.5 years in 15 with acute cerebellitis, and in a third, of children admitted with acute ataxia, onset was later in acute cerebellitis than in acute postinfectious cerebellar ataxia. A systematic review that pooled 73 published patients reports a range of 7 months to 74 years, 40 of them children and 28 adults.

+ 3 more references
Disease in adults
Reported in adults, less often than in children. Orphanet says adult cases mostly follow Epstein-Barr virus or mycoplasma infection. A literature review of acute cerebellitis in adults found 35 patients, including its own case, with a median age of 36 years, and no cause in 34% of them.

Differential Diagnoses

10

Conditions with similar clinical presentations that must be differentiated from Postinfectious Cerebellitis:

Drug or toxin intoxication Not Yet Curated MONDO:0029000
Overlapping Features The second commonest cause of acute ataxia in children after postinfectious cerebellitis in a pooled analysis of 1,167 children from eleven studies, with an expected share of 14.1%; the cause in 24 of 76 children in one series; and in another, which splits the causes by age, 14% of infants and toddlers and of school-age children. One series of acute cerebellar ataxia excludes it by its case definition. No cited source gives a history or examination feature that separates it. One review says every child with acute ataxia should be screened for toxic ingestion, and a systematic review that a toxicology screen should be considered in all of them, and that review reports of its screening tests together, toxicology among them, that in most studies the abnormalities detected were not diagnostic.
Distinguishing Features
  • A toxicology screen. One review says every child with acute ataxia should be screened, and a systematic review that a screen should be considered in all of them. No cited source gives a clinical feature that separates intoxication.

Posterior fossa tumour Not Yet Curated MONDO:0037736
Overlapping Features A neoplasm was the cause in an expected 7.3% of children with acute ataxia in the pooled analysis of 1,167 children, whose cached abstract does not give its site. One review says neuroimaging is needed in acute or subacute ataxia to exclude a focal lesion in the posterior fossa, a tumour among them, and a systematic review that it should be considered in every child with new-onset ataxia. The commonest presenting symptoms overlap: in one series medulloblastoma presented most often with vomiting and headache, then ataxia, and those three were the commonest first symptoms in one paediatric series of acute cerebellitis and the commonest presentation in a review of published adult cases. A tumour's symptoms can run for weeks before diagnosis: in the medulloblastoma series they had lasted a mean of 7.4 weeks in high-stage and 19.5 weeks in low-stage patients before staging. Obstructive hydrocephalus overlaps too: severe acute cerebellitis can present with raised intracranial pressure and hydrocephalus, one paediatric series of acute cerebellitis found obstructive hydrocephalus in 26.6%, and one child whose cerebellitis presented with it was first misdiagnosed as having a posterior fossa neoplasm.
Distinguishing Features
  • A mass in the posterior fossa on neuroimaging, which one review calls necessary in acute or subacute ataxia.
  • A history of weeks to months: in one medulloblastoma series symptoms had lasted a mean of 7.4 weeks in high-stage and 19.5 weeks in low-stage patients before staging.
  • Not headache, vomiting and ataxia alone, which acute cerebellitis also presents with.
  • Not obstructive hydrocephalus alone, which about a quarter of children in one series of acute cerebellitis had.

Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome MONDO:0015247
Overlapping Features Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome usually begins in the second year of life and classically presents with a characteristic eye movement disorder and myoclonus as well as ataxia, irritability and disturbed sleep. It is often first diagnosed as acute cerebellar ataxia, which a review puts down to the gait imbalance children with it often present with: acute cerebellar ataxia was the commonest misdiagnosis in a series of 389 children, and 2 of 15 children later diagnosed with the syndrome in a prospective UK study were first diagnosed with it. In one cohort, provisional diagnoses of acute cerebellar ataxia, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis and acute cerebellitis were common, and opsoclonus was recognised later in the children whose diagnosis was delayed; the authors advise reconsidering the diagnosis when ataxia is prolonged or relapses. The development of opsoclonus or myoclonus declares the diagnosis. In the series of 389 children, no prodromal symptoms were noted in 40%, 60% of patients were irritable, usually crying, before onset, 22% were said to be febrile and fewer than 35% had an overt infection. Unlike acute cerebellar ataxia it rarely resolves without immunotherapy and is paraneoplastic in half of cases, and a systematic review recommends urine catecholamine testing for an occult neuroblastoma in a child with ataxia and opsoclonus-myoclonus.
Distinguishing Features
  • Opsoclonus: chaotic eye movements without an intersaccadic interval, unlike rhythmic nystagmus. Its development, or that of myoclonus, declares the diagnosis.
  • Myoclonus and disturbed sleep with the ataxia, and onset usually in the second year of life.
  • Ataxia that is prolonged or relapses, which one cohort's authors say should prompt reconsidering the diagnosis.
  • A course that rarely resolves without immunotherapy, unlike acute cerebellar ataxia, and often relapses.
  • Urine catecholamine testing for an occult neuroblastoma, which a systematic review recommends in a child with ataxia and opsoclonus-myoclonus; the syndrome is paraneoplastic in half of cases.

Central nervous system infection Not Yet Curated MONDO:0024619
Overlapping Features Infection of the central nervous system is among the causes of acute ataxia in children. In a pooled analysis of 1,167 children from eleven studies, central nervous system infection or inflammation, counted together, was the third commonest group, with an expected share of 8.1%; acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, an inflammatory condition, has its own row. One referral centre lists meningitis among the causes of acute ataxia in its 120 cases; its abstract gives no frequency for it. One review advises that lumbar puncture can usually wait until after admission, suspected meningitis being the major exception. In one series, children with postinfectious ataxia were younger than those with infection or acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, a comparison that pools the two and does not say where the infections were. Cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis is not confined to infection: the referral centre reports it in 40% of its patients with post-infectious cerebellar ataxia, though its abstract does not say how many had a lumbar puncture.

Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis MONDO:0019383
Overlapping Features Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis requires encephalopathy and polyfocal neurological signs by definition, and its lesions are typically bilateral, asymmetrical and large. When its findings are mainly cerebellar it can be confused with acute cerebellitis, though, the review that says so adds, its lesions on neuroimaging are usually widespread. The clinical signs separate them less cleanly, since severe acute cerebellitis can also alter consciousness and cause focal deficits. It was the cause in 8% of infants and toddlers and 14% of preschool children with acute ataxia in a series that splits the causes by age; in another series, children with it or with an infection were older than those with postinfectious acute cerebellar ataxia, and demyelinating diseases, a wider group, accounted for 18.2% of the children with acute ataxia at one centre.
Distinguishing Features
  • Widespread lesions on neuroimaging, which a review sets against acute cerebellitis; another describes them as typically bilateral, asymmetrical and large.
  • Encephalopathy and polyfocal neurological signs, which its definition requires, though severe acute cerebellitis can also alter consciousness and cause focal deficits.

Miller Fisher syndrome Not Yet Curated MONDO:0005851
Overlapping Features A variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome characterised by ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia, whose defining marker is anti-GQ1b antibodies.   • Ophthalmoplegia and areflexia with the ataxia.

Stroke Not Yet Curated MONDO:0005098
Overlapping Features Stroke can present in children with ataxia as its essential, sometimes only, feature, and MRI detects vascular insults in the posterior fossa better than CT. In a Swiss registry of 43 children with posterior-circulation arterial ischaemic stroke, ataxia (58.1%) and one-sided motor or sensory signs (53.5% and 51.2%) were the commonest clinical signs, and most children presented with nonspecific complaints such as headache and nausea or vomiting, which the authors say risk delaying the diagnosis, especially with mild neurological findings. One referral centre lists cerebellar stroke among the causes of acute ataxia in its 120 cases; its abstract gives no frequency for it. After varicella, in one hospital's series, stroke came 2 to 26 weeks after the rash, while the acute complications, acute cerebellar ataxia the commonest of them, began a median of 5 days after it. No cited source, as cached, compares stroke with postinfectious cerebellitis directly or says how often stroke presents as ataxia alone.
Distinguishing Features
  • A vascular lesion in the posterior fossa on MRI, which detects it better than CT.

Inherited episodic ataxia MONDO:0016227
Overlapping Features A familial, dominantly inherited disorder of transient, recurrent attacks of incoordination and truncal instability, often triggered by physical exertion or emotional stress, with normal or near-normal neurological function between attacks, though some have a progressive baseline ataxia. In EA1, EA2 and EA6 onset is mostly before adulthood, and in one type myokymia is evident between attacks. No cited source compares it with postinfectious cerebellitis, and recurrence alone does not separate them: postinfectious acute cerebellar ataxia relapsed more often in children with oligoclonal bands in the spinal fluid in one series, and one boy's ataxia after a respiratory infection worsened again after mumps and varicella. The series that reports those relapses advises genetic and metabolic assessment, among other tests, for recurrent ataxia.
Distinguishing Features
  • Recurrent brief attacks with normal or near-normal function between them.
  • Attacks triggered by physical exertion or emotional stress, in a familial, dominantly inherited disorder.
  • Myokymia between attacks in one type.

Vestibular ataxia Not Yet Curated MONDO:0100312
Overlapping Features Ataxia from a disorder of the vestibular system. Disorders of the inner ear can cause vertigo and imbalance, and vestibular neuritis and viral labyrinthitis provoke severe attacks of vertigo with spontaneous nystagmus, labyrinthitis adding hearing loss to the vestibular loss. Vestibular ataxia was among the causes in one series of 76 children with acute ataxia. Vertigo is the cardinal symptom of vestibular disease and is set apart from gait imbalance, but it can arise in the inner ear or in the central nervous system. Hearing loss does not settle the question either: in a 17-year-old with vertigo and hearing loss whose examination suggested a peripheral cause, the hearing loss raised the suspicion of a central one, and MRI showed demyelinating lesions in a middle cerebellar peduncle from multiple sclerosis.
Distinguishing Features
  • Vertigo, the cardinal symptom of vestibular disease, though it can also arise centrally.
  • Hearing loss with the vestibular loss in labyrinthitis, though in one case it pointed to a central lesion.

Animal Models

1
Acute cerebellar inflammation rodent model
Inflammation induced in the cerebellar cortex of a normal animal, which is the system every mechanistic step in the middle of this entry's chain comes from. It is not a model of this disease's trigger - no antecedent infection, no latent interval, no immune response directed at the cerebellum - and its authors say in a companion review that the animals were not ataxic.
Species
Mouse and rat
Genotype
wild type, with cerebellar inflammation induced by lipopolysaccharide or heat-killed Gram-negative bacteria
Publication
PMID:31509752
Pathograph links
Microglial Activation recapitulates fidelity: moderate observes: cellular The node exists because of this model. Activation is established by depleting the cells and by inhibiting their activity, which is a necessity test rather than an observation.
Limitations: The stimulus is bacterial endotoxin or heat-killed bacteria applied to the cerebellum, not an immune response to an antecedent systemic infection. Nothing in the model represents the latent interval that defines this disease.
Divergences from the human mechanism
proxy quantity qualifying
The model's quantity is microglial activation by a toll-like receptor 4 ligand. The node's quantity is microglial activation downstream of a post-infectious immune response whose effector no cited source identifies.

Cerebellar Dysfunction fails to recapitulate fidelity: low observes: organism The model does not produce the sign that defines the human disease. Its animals show depression-like and autistic-like behaviour and no ataxia, which is the gap this entry records as a discussion.
Limitations: The behavioural readout is not the human one. A model that produces no ataxia cannot show how cerebellar inflammation produces ataxia, which is the step between this entry's mechanism and its phenotypes, and the review of this literature says so in terms.

proxy quantity invalidating
The model's outcome measure is depression-like and autistic-like behaviour. The node's quantity is cerebellar ataxia. They are not the same observation and the model does not produce the second.
