    id: MONDO:0850107
    label: postinfectious cerebellitis
categories:
- Neurological disorder
- Immune-mediated disease
parents:
- cerebellar disease
synonyms:
- acute post-infectious cerebellar ataxia
- acute cerebellar ataxia
- acute cerebellitis
description: >-
  An immune-mediated inflammatory syndrome of the cerebellum that follows an infection, or rarely a
  vaccination, after a latent interval of about a week. It spans a severity spectrum: a benign acute
  cerebellar ataxia at one end, acute cerebellitis with signal change and swelling in the middle, and a
  rare fulminant form with cerebellar oedema, hydrocephalus and a risk of herniation at the other. The
  latent interval is what separates it from an infection of the cerebellum itself. Most children
  recover completely; a minority are left with ataxia, tremor or cognitive deficits, and death is rare
  and essentially confined to the fulminant form.
classifications:
  harrisons_chapter:
  - classification_value: NEUROLOGIC
mappings:
  mondo_mappings:
  - term:
      id: MONDO:0850107
      label: postinfectious cerebellitis
    mapping_predicate: skos:exactMatch
    mapping_source: ORPHA:624244
    mapping_justification: >-
      Orphanet lists MONDO:0850107 as an exact cross-reference for ORPHA:624244, and that is the
      class this entry already binds as its disease_term, so the two sources agree on the concept.
      MONDO's own record maps the class to the same Orphanet term as an exact match.
    consistency:
    - reference: ORPHA:624244
      consistent: CONSISTENT
      notes: "MONDO:0850107 | Exact"
  icd10cm_mappings:
  - term:
      id: ICD10CM:G04.8
      label: Other encephalitis, myelitis and encephalomyelitis
    mapping_predicate: skos:broadMatch
    mapping_source: ORPHA:624244
    mapping_justification: semapv:ManualMappingCuration
    notes: >-
      Taken from the Orphanet cross-reference table for ORPHA:624244, which lists ICD-10 G04.8 with
      the relation Narrower: the disease is narrower than the code, so the match is broad. The code
      is WHO ICD-10's; ICD-10-CM carries the same code and title, as a subcategory whose children
      are G04.81 Other encephalitis and encephalomyelitis, G04.82 Acute flaccid myelitis and G04.89
      Other myelitis. MONDO records no ICD-10-CM cross-reference for this class.
epidemiology:
- name: Age at onset
  description: >-
    Mainly a disease of young children, though it occurs at all ages. In two paediatric series the
    mean age was 4.8 years in 39 children with acute cerebellar ataxia and the median 9.5 years in
    15 with acute cerebellitis, and in a third, of children admitted with acute ataxia, onset was
    later in acute cerebellitis than in acute postinfectious cerebellar ataxia. A systematic review
    that pooled 73 published patients reports a range of 7 months to 74 years, 40 of them children
    and 28 adults.
  evidence:
  - reference: ORPHA:624244
    reference_title: "Postinfectious cerebellitis"
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: >-
      It mainly affects young children following an episode of usually viral infection (notably
      varicella), but sometimes also adults, mostly upon Epstein-Barr virus or mycoplasma infection.
    explanation: >-
      Orphanet's statement that the disease mainly affects young children and sometimes adults.
  - reference: ORPHA:624244
    reference_title: "Postinfectious cerebellitis"
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: >-
      Age of onset: All ages
    explanation: >-
      Orphanet's age of onset for the disease.
  - reference: PMID:14552515
    reference_title: "Post-infectious acute cerebellar ataxia in children."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Thirty-nine children were identified; 54% were male; mean age at presentation was 4.8 +/- 3.8
      years.
    explanation: >-
      The mean age at presentation in a series of 39 children with acute cerebellar ataxia.
  - reference: PMID:32160830
    reference_title: >-
      Acute Cerebellitis or Postinfectious Cerebellar Ataxia? Clinical and Imaging Features in Acute
      Cerebellitis.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      There were 10 boys and 5 girls aged 3-15 years, median 9.5 years.
    explanation: >-
      The age range and median in a series of 15 children with acute cerebellitis.
  - reference: PMID:41321459
    reference_title: "Acute ataxia in children: etiological spectrum and clinical characteristics."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      AC patients exhibited later onset, longer duration from symptom onset to hospital
      presentation, and more frequent neurological symptoms (encephalopathy, headache, vomiting)
      compared to APCA.
    explanation: >-
      Later onset in acute cerebellitis than in acute postinfectious cerebellar ataxia, among
      children admitted with acute ataxia.
  - reference: PMID:42649322
    reference_title: >-
      Post-Infectious Cerebellitis: A Systematic Review of Aetiology, Clinical Presentation,
      Treatment, and Outcomes.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Pooled patients had a mean age of 24.5 years (range 7 months-74 years; 40 pediatric, 28 adult)
    explanation: >-
      The age range of the published patients a systematic review pooled, children and adults
      together.
- name: Disease in adults
  description: >-
    Reported in adults, less often than in children. Orphanet says adult cases mostly follow
    Epstein-Barr virus or mycoplasma infection. A literature review of acute cerebellitis in adults
    found 35 patients, including its own case, with a median age of 36 years, and no cause in 34% of
    them.
  evidence:
  - reference: ORPHA:624244
    reference_title: "Postinfectious cerebellitis"
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: >-
      It mainly affects young children following an episode of usually viral infection (notably
      varicella), but sometimes also adults, mostly upon Epstein-Barr virus or mycoplasma infection.
    explanation: >-
      Orphanet's statement that adult cases mostly follow Epstein-Barr virus or mycoplasma
      infection.
  - reference: PMID:29166939
    reference_title: "Acute cerebellitis in adults: a case report and review of the literature."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Acute cerebellitis is a rare disease with the majority of cases described in children.
    explanation: >-
      That most reported cases of acute cerebellitis are in children, as the adult review's
      background puts it.
  - reference: PMID:29166939
    reference_title: "Acute cerebellitis in adults: a case report and review of the literature."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Including our patient, we identified 35 patients with a median age of 36 years.
    explanation: >-
      The number and median age of the adult patients the review found.
  - reference: PMID:29166939
    reference_title: "Acute cerebellitis in adults: a case report and review of the literature."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The etiology was unknown in 34% of cases.
    explanation: >-
      The share of those adults with no cause identified.
has_subtypes:
- name: ACA
  display_name: Acute cerebellar ataxia (benign post-infectious)
  classification: severity_tier
  description: >-
    The benign end of the spectrum: acute ataxia with or without nystagmus, and recovery that is
    usually complete. It is the commonest tier.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:42649322
    reference_title: "Post-Infectious Cerebellitis: A Systematic Review of Aetiology, Clinical Presentation, Treatment, and Outcomes."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Based on neuroimaging findings and the presence of life-threatening features, 34 patients
      (46.6%) were classified as acute cerebellar ataxia (ACA), 26 (35.6%) as acute cerebellitis
      (AC), and 13 (17.8%) as acute fulminant cerebellitis (AFC), with complete recovery in 58.8%,
      69.2%, and 69.2% of each subtype, respectively, and the cohort's only death occurring in the
      AFC subgroup.
    explanation: >-
      The sentence that defines all three tiers and gives each one's share and outcome in the pooled
      cohort. Note what it does not show: complete recovery is lowest in the benign tier, at 58.8%
      against 69.2% in the other two, which is the opposite of what the tier names suggest and is
      why this entry does not present the tiers as a prognostic ladder.
- name: AC
  display_name: Acute cerebellitis
  classification: severity_tier
  description: >-
    The middle tier, distinguished clinically by headache and vomiting accompanying the ataxia and
    radiologically by cerebellar signal change with swelling. Sequelae are commoner here than the
    benign tier's reputation suggests.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:32160830
    reference_title: >-
      Acute Cerebellitis or Postinfectious Cerebellar Ataxia? Clinical and Imaging Features in Acute
      Cerebellitis.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The diagnosis of acute cerebellitis rather than acute postinfectious cerebellar ataxia should
      be considered when headache and vomiting accompany ataxia in a child.
    explanation: >-
      The clinical discriminator between this tier and the benign one, stated as a rule for the
      bedside: headache and vomiting with the ataxia. It is a recommendation rather than a validated
      rule, which is why it is cited here and not in a definitions block.
  - reference: PMID:41321459
    reference_title: "Acute ataxia in children: etiological spectrum and clinical characteristics."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      AC patients exhibited later onset, longer duration from symptom onset to hospital
      presentation, and more frequent neurological symptoms (encephalopathy, headache, vomiting)
      compared to APCA.
    explanation: >-
      The same discriminator from an independent cohort of 257 children, with two more axes: later
      onset and a longer interval to presentation. Two sources agreeing on headache and vomiting is
      why the tier is recorded at all.
- name: AFC
  display_name: Acute fulminant cerebellitis
  classification: severity_tier
  description: >-
    The rare, life-threatening tier: rapid cerebellar oedema with obstructive hydrocephalus and
    brainstem compression. It may present with depressed consciousness and no cerebellar signs at all,
    which is what makes it dangerous to recognise late.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:33454719
    reference_title: >-
      Pediatric Fulminant Cerebellitis Is Still a Fatal Disease that We Know Little About! Two Case
      Reports and a Literature Review.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The clinical picture started with severe headache, irritability, and acute deterioration of
      consciousness level with the absence of cerebellar signs. There was radiological evidence of
      obstructive hydrocephalus and cerebellar tonsillar herniation in the context of the inflamed
      cerebellum.
    explanation: >-
      The presentation that defines this tier and the reason it is separated from the other two: the
      cerebellar signs a clinician would look for are absent, and what is present is raised
      intracranial pressure. Two cases, so it is a description rather than a frequency.
  - reference: PMID:42699856
    reference_title: "Acute fulminant cerebellitis in children: a case series and literature review on diagnostic challenges and management strategies."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Acute cerebellitis (AC) in children is often benign; however, a fulminant variant featuring
      rapid cerebellar edema, hydrocephalus, and brainstem compression can be life-threatening.
    explanation: >-
      States the tier against the background of the others, and names the three features that make
      it fulminant. BACKGROUND because the sentence frames the case series rather than reporting its
      result.
environmental:
- name: Varicella-zoster virus infection
  description: >-
    Chickenpox, the primary infection with varicella-zoster virus. Before varicella vaccination it was
    the infection most often identified before the syndrome, in about a quarter of children in large
    series. The syndrome follows only a small fraction of infections: a Dutch surveillance study put it
    at 5 cases per 100,000 infections in children up to 5 years.
  exposure_term:
    preferred_term: varicella-zoster virus infection
    term:
      id: ECTO:3000001
      label: exposure to virus
  disease_effect: TRIGGERS
  causal_role: COMPONENT_CAUSE
  notes: >-
    Bound to the generic virus-exposure term because ECTO has none for this virus. In the ECTO build
    the term validator uses, `runoak -i sqlite:obo:ecto info` returned nothing for 'l~varicella',
    'l~zoster', 'l~chickenpox', 'l~VZV' or 'l~Human alphaherpesvirus 3', and 'l~alphaherpesvirus'
    returned only the human alphaherpesvirus 1, suid and canid terms. The preferred term names the
    virus.
  influences_mechanisms:
  - target: Preceding Infection
    environmental_effect: TRIGGERS
    causal_link_type: DIRECT
    description: >-
      Chickenpox is one of the infections that precede the syndrome. Counted from the syndrome's side,
      it came before a third of the cases in the Dutch national surveillance study; counted from the virus's
      side, acute cerebellar ataxia was the commonest neurological complication of the virus in a
      children's hospital series.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:19186201
      reference_title: "Acute cerebellar ataxia in the Netherlands: a study on the association with vaccinations and varicella zoster infection."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: DIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: >-
        45 children with ACA were included (44 and 1 reported by pediatric and AEFI surveillance
        respectively, 30 were hospitalized). Chickenpox preceded ACA in 15 cases, one case followed
        MMR.
      explanation: >-
        Chickenpox before onset in 15 of 45 children found by prospective paediatric surveillance and
        by surveillance of adverse events after immunisation in the Netherlands.
    - reference: PMID:25063723
      reference_title: >-
        Central nervous system complications of varicella-zoster virus.
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: >-
        Clinical syndromes included acute cerebellar ataxia (n = 26), encephalitis (n = 17), isolated
        seizures (n = 16), stroke (n = 10), meningitis (n = 10), Guillain-Barré syndrome (n = 2),
        acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (n = 2), and Ramsay Hunt syndrome (n = 1).
      explanation: >-
        The same association counted from the virus's side: acute cerebellar ataxia was the commonest
        of the neurological syndromes in 84 children admitted to one children's hospital with
        complications of varicella-zoster virus between 1999 and 2012, 26 of them. The abstract does not
        say how many of the 26 had virus in the cerebrospinal fluid, so the count may include some
        infections of the cerebellum itself as well as the syndrome that follows the infection.
        INDIRECT for that reason.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:19186201
    reference_title: "Acute cerebellar ataxia in the Netherlands: a study on the association with vaccinations and varicella zoster infection."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      We found no association with MMR, but chickenpox was clearly related to ACA. According to
      age-specific seroprevalence data the incidence rate of ACA was 5:100,000 VZV infections for
      children up to 5 years, compared to an ACA-reporting rate of 0.15:100,000 doses VZV-vaccine.
    explanation: >-
      The association as the study's conclusion, and its size: about 5 cases for every 100,000
      varicella infections in children up to 5 years, estimated from seroprevalence data.
  - reference: PMID:8210223
    reference_title: >-
      Course and outcome of acute cerebellar ataxia.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Twenty-six percent had chickenpox, 52% had other illnesses that were presumed to be viral, and
      in 3% the ataxia was related to immunization.
    explanation: >-
      A quarter of 73 consecutive children at one hospital over 23 years had chickenpox, in a series
      published in 1994.
  - reference: PMID:35546546
    reference_title: "Postinfectious Acute Cerebellar Syndromes in Children: A Nationally Ascertained Case Series From Australia 2013-2018."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Varicella has historically been the most common cause, associated with up to 25% of cases in
      large cohorts.
    explanation: >-
      The historical position in one sentence. BACKGROUND: it is the introduction of a later series,
      stating what earlier cohorts found.
- name: Epstein-Barr virus infection
  description: >-
    A recognised but rare cause, less frequent than varicella in children (one of 39 children in a
    two-centre series) and described as rare in adults. In the two adult reports cited here the
    infection was shown in the blood while testing of the cerebrospinal fluid for the virus was
    negative; the authors of one read this as favouring a syndrome that follows the infection rather
    than an infection of the cerebellum, while noting that serology is a weaker test than PCR. One of
    the two had no symptoms of the infection before the ataxia.
  exposure_term:
    preferred_term: Epstein-Barr virus infection
    term:
      id: ECTO:3000273
      label: exposure to human gammaherpesvirus 4
  disease_effect: TRIGGERS
  causal_role: COMPONENT_CAUSE
  notes: >-
    Graded as a trigger, where the cytomegalovirus and human herpesvirus 6 rows are graded as
    associations only. For this virus one cited source names it a cause of acute cerebellar ataxia,
    another reads its case as favouring a syndrome that follows the infection, a pooled review counts
    it among the identified triggers, and it is reported in children and in adults. Cytomegalovirus
    rests on one child's work-up and a review's potential association, and the one human herpesvirus
    6 case carried a second virus, so it cannot be put on that virus alone.
  influences_mechanisms:
  - target: Preceding Infection
    environmental_effect: TRIGGERS
    causal_link_type: DIRECT
    description: >-
      Epstein-Barr virus infection is one of the infections that precede the syndrome. In both adult
      reports the virus was found in the blood while testing of the cerebrospinal fluid for it was
      negative; the authors of one favour a post-infectious reading and add that serology is not the
      best test.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:31905189
      reference_title: >-
        Post-Epstein-Barr Virus Acute Cerebellitis in an Adult.
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: DIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: >-
        CSF analysis showed lymphocytosis with negative EBV serology in CSF. However, EBV IgM and IgG
        were positive in serum. This favors the possibility that acute cerebellitis is due to a
        post-infectious phenomenon. However, serology is not an optimal diagnostic method, and PCR is
        superior to serology.
      explanation: >-
        One 23-year-old man with acute cerebellitis: antibodies against the virus in the serum and not
        in the cerebrospinal fluid, read by the authors as favouring a syndrome that follows the
        infection. Their own caveat, that serology is a weaker test than PCR, is kept in the quote.
    - reference: PMID:27558189
      reference_title: "Barr humbug: acute cerebellar ataxia due to Epstein-Barr virus."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: >-
        EBV DNA was detected by real-time PCR in serum, confirming the presence of the virus in
        peripheral blood. EBV DNA was not detected in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) by real-time PCR.
      explanation: >-
        A second adult, a 26-year-old man: the virus's DNA in the blood and not in the cerebrospinal
        fluid. The same report says his presentation was sudden, without viral symptoms beforehand.
        INDIRECT: the quote says where the virus was found, and that the infection came first and set
        off the illness is the reading drawn from it.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:14552515
    reference_title: >-
      Post-infectious acute cerebellar ataxia in children.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      A prodromal febrile illness was noted in 74.4%: varicella, 31%; mumps, 20%; nonspecific viral
      infection, 15.4%; mycoplasma, 5%; Epstein Barr virus, 3%.
    explanation: >-
      Epstein-Barr virus in 3% of 39 children, which is one child, against 31% for varicella in the
      same two-centre series.
  - reference: PMID:42649322
    reference_title: "Post-Infectious Cerebellitis: A Systematic Review of Aetiology, Clinical Presentation, Treatment, and Outcomes."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      SARS-CoV-2 (n = 24, 32.9%) was the most frequently identified trigger, followed by patients
      with no pathogen identified (n = 18, 24.7%), varicella-zoster virus (n = 8, 11.0%),
      Epstein-Barr virus (n = 5, 6.8%), and influenza (n = 5, 6.8%).
    explanation: >-
      Epstein-Barr virus in 5 of 73 patients pooled from published cases, 28 of them adults, against
      8 for varicella-zoster virus.
  - reference: PMID:27558189
    reference_title: "Barr humbug: acute cerebellar ataxia due to Epstein-Barr virus."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a rare cause of acute cerebellar ataxia.
    explanation: >-
      The virus named as a cause, and a rare one. BACKGROUND: one of the report's learning points,
      restating what the literature it cites has established.
  - reference: PMID:31905189
    reference_title: >-
      Post-Epstein-Barr Virus Acute Cerebellitis in an Adult.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Cerebellitis following EBV in adults is rare. The majority of cases that were reported in the
      medical literature included males under the age of 18 years
    explanation: >-
      Why adult reports are single cases: the reported cases are mostly in males under 18.
      BACKGROUND: the report's summary of the literature, not its own finding.
  - reference: PMID:26933545
    reference_title: >-
      Epstein-Barr Virus Neurologic Complications.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Ten children presented with severe, neurologic complications: meningoencephalitis, acute
      encephalitis (5 cases), acute cerebellitis (2), transverse myelitis, and myeloradiculitis.
    explanation: >-
      Counted from the virus's side: 2 of 194 children with Epstein-Barr virus infection in a Polish
      hospital series had acute cerebellitis, as summarised in a commentary on that series. INDIRECT
      because the summary does not say whether the two followed the infection or had virus in the
      cerebellum.
- name: Cytomegalovirus infection
  description: >-
    Found by the work-up for infectious pathogens in one of 15 children with acute cerebellitis seen in
    one department over nine years, and named by a systematic review among the conditions with a
    potential association with the virus. Neither source settles whether the virus acts as a trigger,
    so the row records the association and no more.
  exposure_term:
    preferred_term: cytomegalovirus infection
    term:
      id: ECTO:3000099
      label: exposure to Human betaherpesvirus 5
  causal_role: ASSOCIATED_ONLY
  influences_mechanisms:
  - target: Preceding Infection
    causal_link_type: UNKNOWN
    description: >-
      Drawn without an effect predicate. The work-up of one child found the virus, which places it
      beside the syndrome but does not show that it was the trigger.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:32160830
      reference_title: >-
        Acute Cerebellitis or Postinfectious Cerebellar Ataxia? Clinical and Imaging Features in Acute
        Cerebellitis.
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: >-
        Etiologic workup for infectious pathogens revealed Mycoplasma pneumoniae, influenza A virus,
        cytomegalovirus, and varicella zoster virus in 1 case each.
      explanation: >-
        Cytomegalovirus in one of 15 children. INDIRECT because the abstract does not give the timing
        of the infection or how it was shown.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:38549138
    reference_title: "Association between cytomegalovirus infection and neurological disorders: A systematic review."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Multiple studies suggest a potential association between CMV and ataxia in various conditions,
      including Guillain-Barré syndrome, chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, acute
      cerebellitis, etc.
    explanation: >-
      A systematic review's own hedge, a potential association, with acute cerebellitis among the
      conditions named. INDIRECT because the review does not separate cerebellitis that follows the
      infection from the other settings it lists.
- name: Human herpesvirus 6 infection
  description: >-
    In the one case cited here, a 4-year-old boy who presented about 15 days after a febrile upper
    airway infection, and whose ataxic gait became evident five days after admission, had serological
    evidence of both human herpesvirus 6 and adenovirus, so the case cannot be assigned to either virus
    alone; PCR of his cerebrospinal fluid was negative for both.
  exposure_term:
    preferred_term: human herpesvirus 6 infection
    term:
      id: ECTO:3000100
      label: exposure to Human betaherpesvirus 6
  causal_role: ASSOCIATED_ONLY
  influences_mechanisms:
  - target: Preceding Infection
    causal_link_type: UNKNOWN
    description: >-
      Drawn without an effect predicate. The one case cited carried a second virus at the same time.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:25425177
      reference_title: >-
        Acute post-infectious cerebellar ataxia due to co-infection of human herpesvirus-6 and
        adenovirus mimicking myositis.
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: >-
        Serologic analysis on blood sample resulted positive for adenovirus and HHV6 – DNA (specific
        IgA).
      explanation: >-
        Both viruses positive in the blood of the one child. INDIRECT because the case cannot separate
        the two.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:25425177
    reference_title: >-
      Acute post-infectious cerebellar ataxia due to co-infection of human herpesvirus-6 and
      adenovirus mimicking myositis.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Research by PCR for parvovirus B19, adenovirus, cytomegalovirus (CMV), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV),
      herpes simplex virus 1 and herpes simplex virus 2, HHV-6, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, varicella
      zoster virus (VZV) and enterovirus in CSF were negative.
    explanation: >-
      The same child's cerebrospinal fluid was negative for both viruses, as for the other pathogens
      tested, which is consistent with a syndrome following the infection rather than an infection of
      the nervous system. INDIRECT because one case cannot show that either virus was the trigger.
  - reference: PMID:25425177
    reference_title: >-
      Acute post-infectious cerebellar ataxia due to co-infection of human herpesvirus-6 and
      adenovirus mimicking myositis.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Parents reported a febrile upper airways infection approximately 15 days before, followed by
      skin rash spread.
    explanation: >-
      The timing in the same child: a febrile infection about two weeks before he presented, with the
      ataxia evident five days after admission. INDIRECT because the sentence names no virus.
- name: Varicella vaccination
  description: >-
    Protects against the varicella share of the syndrome. In a national Australian surveillance series
    from a population with high vaccine coverage, none of 20 cases followed varicella. The vaccine itself
    is reported before onset far more rarely than the infection: a Dutch study sets a reporting rate of
    0.15 per 100,000 vaccine doses against 5 cases per 100,000 infections in young children, though its
    abstract does not say where the per-dose figure was measured.
  exposure_term:
    preferred_term: varicella vaccination
    term:
      id: ECTO:2000129
      label: exposure to vaccination
  disease_effect: PROTECTS_AGAINST
  notes: >-
    Bound to the general vaccination-exposure term because ECTO has none for the varicella vaccine:
    `runoak -i sqlite:obo:ecto info` returned no ECTO term for 'l~varicel', and for 'l~vaccin' only two
    ECTO terms, exposure to vaccination and exposure to Orthopoxvirus vaccinia. The preferred term
    names the vaccine.
  influences_mechanisms:
  - target: Preceding Infection
    environmental_effect: PROTECTS_AGAINST
    causal_link_type: DIRECT
    description: >-
      Acts on the varicella share of the preceding infections only; it has no bearing on the other
      triggers. No cited source measures the syndrome's incidence before and after a vaccination
      programme, so the effect rests on a projection from two rates, on a fall in the neurological
      complications of varicella as a whole, and on what is seen in a vaccinated population.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:19186201
      reference_title: "Acute cerebellar ataxia in the Netherlands: a study on the association with vaccinations and varicella zoster infection."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: >-
        According to age-specific seroprevalence data the incidence rate of ACA was 5:100,000 VZV
        infections for children up to 5 years, compared to an ACA-reporting rate of 0.15:100,000 doses
        VZV-vaccine. Therefore, uptake of VZV-vaccine in the immunization programme will diminish the
        incidence rate of ACA.
      explanation: >-
        The authors' projection from two rates: 5 cases per 100,000 infections against 0.15 reports
        per 100,000 vaccine doses. INDIRECT because it is a prediction, and because the vaccine figure
        is a reporting rate whose source the abstract does not give, not a measured incidence.
    - reference: PMID:27749651
      reference_title: "Decline of Neurologic Varicella Complications in Children During the First Seven Years After Introduction of Universal Varicella Vaccination in Germany, 2005-2011."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: >-
        The incidence of varicella-associated neurologic complications in children decreased
        approximately by 60% during the first 7 years following the recommendation for universal
        vaccination.
      explanation: >-
        The fall after a vaccination programme, measured for the neurological complications of
        varicella as a whole in Bavarian children's hospitals. Ataxia was 3.1% of those complications,
        and the abstract puts the marked decline in children up to 7 years down mainly to fewer febrile
        convulsions and cases of encephalitis or meningitis, so it does not show ataxia itself falling.
        INDIRECT for that reason.
    - reference: PMID:35546546
      reference_title: "Postinfectious Acute Cerebellar Syndromes in Children: A Nationally Ascertained Case Series From Australia 2013-2018."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: >-
        The study provides an overall description of this uncommon spectrum of neurologic syndromes
        and shows the infrequency of varicella zoster virus as a cause in a vaccinated population.
      explanation: >-
        What a vaccinated population looks like: varicella almost absent as a cause. INDIRECT because
        the series has no unvaccinated comparison group.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:35546546
    reference_title: "Postinfectious Acute Cerebellar Syndromes in Children: A Nationally Ascertained Case Series From Australia 2013-2018."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      A total of 20 cases (65% were vaccinated for varicella) were included, of which 70% were
      subcategorized as acute cerebellar ataxia (ACA), 20% acute cerebellitis (AC), and 10% acute
      fulminant cerebellitis (AFC). An acute febrile illness was noted in 55% and none were related
      to varicella or were temporally related to varicella vaccination or other childhood vaccines.
    explanation: >-
      In a national series in which 65% of the children had been vaccinated, no case followed
      varicella and none followed the vaccine itself. INDIRECT because the series has no
      unvaccinated comparison group.
pathophysiology:
- name: Preceding Infection
  role: trigger
  biological_scale: ORGANISM
  description: >-
    An infection, or rarely a vaccination, precedes the cerebellar syndrome by a latent interval of
    about a week. The interval is what makes the syndrome post-infectious rather than an infection of
    the cerebellum. No single organism defines it: the commonest trigger differs by era and population,
    and in a quarter of children none is identified.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:42649322
    reference_title: "Post-Infectious Cerebellitis: A Systematic Review of Aetiology, Clinical Presentation, Treatment, and Outcomes."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Post-infectious cerebellitis is an immune-mediated cerebellar inflammatory syndrome that
      follows a preceding infection (or, rarely, vaccination) after a latent interval.
    explanation: >-
      The definitional sentence, and the one that carries the latent interval. It is the interval,
      not the infection, that places the syndrome after the infection rather than inside it.
  - reference: PMID:14552515
    reference_title: >-
      Post-infectious acute cerebellar ataxia in children.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Latency from the prodromal illness to the onset of ataxia was 8.8 +/- 7.4 days.
    explanation: >-
      Puts a number on the interval in 39 children: a mean of 8.8 days. The standard deviation of
      7.4 is as informative as the mean, since it spans same-week and three-week onsets.
  - reference: PMID:14552515
    reference_title: >-
      Post-infectious acute cerebellar ataxia in children.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      A prodromal febrile illness was noted in 74.4%: varicella, 31%; mumps, 20%; nonspecific viral
      infection, 15.4%; mycoplasma, 5%; Epstein Barr virus, 3%.
    explanation: >-
      The trigger distribution in that series, and the fact that a quarter of children had no
      prodromal illness at all.
  - reference: PMID:35546546
    reference_title: "Postinfectious Acute Cerebellar Syndromes in Children: A Nationally Ascertained Case Series From Australia 2013-2018."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      A total of 20 cases (65% were vaccinated for varicella) were included, of which 70% were
      subcategorized as acute cerebellar ataxia (ACA), 20% acute cerebellitis (AC), and 10% acute
      fulminant cerebellitis (AFC). An acute febrile illness was noted in 55% and none were related
      to varicella or were temporally related to varicella vaccination or other childhood vaccines.
    explanation: >-
      Why this node names no organism. Varicella was historically the commonest trigger; in this
      national surveillance series from a population with high varicella vaccine coverage, not one
      of twenty cases was varicella-related. The trigger distribution is a fact about a population
      and an era, not about the disease.
  downstream:
  - target: Immune Response Directed at the Cerebellum
    causal_link_type: DIRECT
    description: >-
      The infection raises a response that then acts on the cerebellum. What connects the two is not
      demonstrated in this disease by any source cited here: none shows a shared epitope in a
      patient with it, and the two case reports that name a route, molecular mimicry or antibodies
      that cross-react with cerebellar epitopes, do so in their discussions without testing it.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:42649322
      reference_title: "Post-Infectious Cerebellitis: A Systematic Review of Aetiology, Clinical Presentation, Treatment, and Outcomes."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: >-
        Post-infectious cerebellitis is a heterogeneous, largely immune-mediated syndrome with a
        generally favorable prognosis after corticosteroid-based immunotherapy, though outcomes
        and evidence quality vary by etiology and severity subgroup.
      explanation: >-
        The review's closing judgement, and the hedge in it is load-bearing: largely
        immune-mediated, not wholly. The edge is drawn because an immune response is what the
        sources attribute the syndrome to, and it is INDIRECT because none of them demonstrates
        the connection in an individual case.
- name: Immune Response Directed at the Cerebellum
  role: central_effector
  biological_scale: ORGANISM
  description: >-
    The step that makes this disease immune-mediated rather than infectious. Not every cited source
    names an immune mechanism: several describe the disease without one, and one of them calls the
    aetiology usually viral. It places the syndrome in the family of immune-mediated cerebellar ataxias, beside
    gluten ataxia, the paraneoplastic degenerations and opsoclonus-myoclonus. Which effector does the
    damage is not settled here: autoantibodies against several cerebellar targets are reported in
    individual patients, and whether any of them is pathogenic rather than a consequence of damage is an
    open question recorded in this entry's discussions.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:30221603
    reference_title: "Immune-mediated Cerebellar Ataxias: Practical Guidelines and Therapeutic Challenges."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Immune-mediated cerebellar ataxias (IMCAs), a clinical entity reported for the first time in
      the 1980s, include gluten ataxia (GA), paraneoplastic cerebellar degenerations (PCDs),
      antiglutamate decarboxylase 65 (GAD) antibody-associated cerebellar ataxia, post-infectious
      cerebellitis, and opsoclonus myoclonus syndrome (OMS).
    explanation: >-
      Places this disease in the immune-mediated cerebellar ataxia family, named alongside four
      others this knowledge base curates or will. REVIEW_SYNTHESIS because the review is classifying
      rather than reporting its own result.
  - reference: PMID:17049194
    reference_title: >-
      Acute cerebellar ataxia and consecutive cerebellitis produced by glutamate receptor delta2
      autoantibody.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Cerebro-spinal fluid examination and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrated
      pleocytosis and meningeal enhancement, respectively. Furthermore, glutamate receptor delta2
      autoantibody was detected in serum and cerebro-spinal fluid. Thus, we believe that the
      glutamate receptor delta2 autoantibody may play a role in cerebellar ataxia and consecutive
      cerebellitis.
    explanation: >-
      One reported autoantibody, against a receptor the same paper says is predominantly expressed
      in Purkinje cells, with the authors' own hedge preserved: may play a role. A single case, and
      the next item is the reason it is not read as cause.
  - reference: PMID:17008044
    reference_title: >-
      A case of acute cerebellitis accompanied by autoantibodies against glutamate receptor delta2.
    supports: REFUTE
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      It was suggested that autoantibodies against GluRdelta2 might not have injured the tissue due
      to the immunological action, but might be induced as a consequence of cerebellar damage.
    explanation: >-
      The counter-reading of the same antibody, from a different case: it may be a consequence of
      cerebellar damage rather than its cause. REFUTE against the claim that the antibody is
      pathogenic, which is why this node names no effector.
  downstream:
  - target: Microglial Activation
    causal_link_type: DIRECT
    description: >-
      The step from an immune response to a change the cerebellum can register. This arm is shown in
      a rodent model: no cited source shows it in a patient with this disease.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:31509752
      reference_title: >-
        Microglia-Triggered Plasticity of Intrinsic Excitability Modulates Psychomotor Behaviors
        in Acute Cerebellar Inflammation.
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: DIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      snippet: >-
        Activated microglia via exposure to bacterial endotoxin lipopolysaccharide or heat-killed
        Gram-negative bacteria induce a potentiation of the intrinsic excitability in Purkinje
        neurons, which is suppressed by microglia-activity inhibitor and microglia depletion. An
        inflammatory cytokine, tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-alpha), released from microglia
        via toll-like receptor 4, triggers this plasticity.
      explanation: >-
        The whole chain in one sentence, in rodent cerebellum: microglial activation through TLR4,
        TNF-alpha release, and a change in Purkinje cell excitability, each step shown by
        suppression or depletion. MODEL_ORGANISM, and the edge is drawn into this entry on the
        understanding that no cited source demonstrates it in a patient with this disease.
  - target: Cerebellar Swelling and Mass Effect
    causal_link_type: DIRECT
    description: >-
      The second arm out of the immune response, and the one that makes the fulminant tier
      dangerous. A review cited on the swelling node calls swelling the most characteristic MRI
      finding of acute cerebellitis, and the fulminant tier is defined by its obstructive
      hydrocephalus and brainstem compression. It is an inflammatory oedema of the cerebellum rather
      than a functional change in its neurons, and it is what the surgical treatments act on.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:42699856
      reference_title: "Acute fulminant cerebellitis in children: a case series and literature review on diagnostic challenges and management strategies."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: DIRECT
      quote_role: BACKGROUND
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: >-
        Acute cerebellitis (AC) in children is often benign; however, a fulminant variant
        featuring rapid cerebellar edema, hydrocephalus, and brainstem compression can be
        life-threatening.
      explanation: >-
        The arm named in one sentence, with its three consequences in order. BACKGROUND: this is
        the framing sentence of a three-case series rather than its finding.
    - reference: PMID:33454719
      reference_title: >-
        Pediatric Fulminant Cerebellitis Is Still a Fatal Disease that We Know Little About! Two
        Case Reports and a Literature Review.
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: >-
        There was radiological evidence of obstructive hydrocephalus and cerebellar tonsillar
        herniation in the context of the inflamed cerebellum.
      explanation: >-
        The inflamed cerebellum and its mechanical consequences observed together in two children,
        which is as close as any cited source comes to showing this edge in a patient.
  - target: Autoantibodies Binding Neural Tissue
    causal_link_type: DIRECT
    description: >-
      The humoral arm of the response: some patients have antibodies that bind neural tissue. The edge
      records that the response produces them. Whether they then injure the cerebellum is not drawn,
      for the reason the node gives.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:11097523
      reference_title: >-
        Autoantibodies in childhood post-varicella acute cerebellar ataxia.
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: >-
        Some children with post-viral ataxia develop antibodies that have strong reactivity with
        cerebral and cerebellar tissue.
      explanation: >-
        The study's conclusion from three of eight children with ataxia after varicella and one after
        Epstein-Barr virus infection. INDIRECT: it shows the antibodies are present, and the same
        high-titre antibodies were found in one child with uncomplicated varicella, so they are not
        confined to the disease.
    - reference: PMID:23892968
      reference_title: "[A case of acute cerebellar ataxia following infectious mononucleosis accompanied by intrathecal anti-glutamate receptor δ2 antibody]."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: >-
        In the present case, secondary immune reactions after EB virus infection may have produced the
        antibody.
      explanation: >-
        The authors' reading of one 18-year-old with ataxia after infectious mononucleosis and the
        antibody in her cerebrospinal fluid: the antibody as a product of the response to the
        infection. INDIRECT because it is a hedged interpretation of a single case.
- name: Autoantibodies Binding Neural Tissue
  biological_scale: MOLECULAR
  description: >-
    The humoral arm of the immune response, as far as it can be measured: antibodies in serum or
    cerebrospinal fluid that bind brain tissue or named neural antigens. The targets differ between
    patients and studies: glutamate receptor delta 2, a receptor of the Purkinje cell, in single
    cases; centrosome proteins, pericentrin among them, after varicella; and neuronal, glial and
    myelin antigens in 10 of 36 children with acute cerebellitis in one multicentre series. No study
    of this disease cited here found a single neural antigen targeted in most of its patients.
    Antibodies against centrosome proteins are found after varicella without ataxia as well, though
    not those against pericentrin. Whether any of them injures the cerebellum, rather than marking
    an injury already done, is not settled; the node has no edge onward for that reason, and the
    question is recorded in the discussions.
  notes: >-
    Antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD65) are not listed here: the immune-mediated
    cerebellar ataxia review cited on the immune response node counts GAD65 antibody-associated
    cerebellar ataxia as a separate disease beside this one.
  biological_processes:
  - preferred_term: autoantibody production
    term:
      id: GO:0002377
      label: immunoglobulin production
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:26377184
    reference_title: "'Medusa head ataxia': the expanding spectrum of Purkinje cell antibodies in autoimmune cerebellar ataxia. Part 2: Anti-PKC-gamma, anti-GluR-delta2, anti-Ca/ARHGAP26 and anti-VGCC."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      No tumours have been reported so far in patients with anti-GluRδ2-associated cerebellar ataxia.
      Of note, however, all cases were preceded or accompanied by either infection or vaccination.
    explanation: >-
      A review's tally of the reported cases of cerebellar ataxia with antibodies against glutamate
      receptor delta 2: every one followed or accompanied an infection or a vaccination, and none had
      a tumour.
  - reference: PMID:14503922
    reference_title: >-
      Spectrum of centrosome autoantibodies in childhood varicella and post-varicella acute cerebellar
      ataxia.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Antibodies to pericentrin were seen in 5/12 children with post-varicella ataxia but not in any of
      the other sera tested.
    explanation: >-
      The only antibody in the cited sources found in patients with this disease, tested against
      comparison groups and absent from all of them: five of twelve children after varicella, and none in the comparison
      groups, which included children with uncomplicated varicella. A single small study.
  - reference: PMID:38284996
    reference_title: "Autoantibody status, neuroradiological and clinical findings in children with acute cerebellitis."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      In 10/36 (28 %) children the following autoantibodies (abs) were found: MOG-abs (n = 5) in serum,
      GFAPα-abs (n = 1) in CSF, GlyR-abs (n = 1) in CSF, mGluR1-abs (n = 1) in CSF and serum.
    explanation: >-
      How often an antibody is found when serum and cerebrospinal fluid are both tested in a
      multicentre series of children with acute cerebellitis: 10 of 36, against several different
      antigens. The biochemical row on this panel records why the figure is not an unselected rate.
- name: Microglial Activation
  role: effector
  biological_scale: CELLULAR
  description: >-
    Microglia in the cerebellar cortex are activated, through toll-like receptor 4, by bacterial
    endotoxin or by heat-killed bacteria. Shown in rodent cerebellum and established as a step by
    depleting the cells; not shown in tissue from a patient with this disease by any source cited
    here.
  cell_types:
  - preferred_term: microglial cell
    term:
      id: CL:0000129
      label: microglial cell
  biological_processes:
  - preferred_term: microglial cell activation
    modifier: INCREASED
    term:
      id: GO:0001774
      label: microglial cell activation
  locations:
  - preferred_term: cerebellum
    term:
      id: UBERON:0002037
      label: cerebellum
  downstream:
  - target: TNF-alpha Release
    causal_link_type: DIRECT
    description: >-
      Activation through toll-like receptor 4 is what releases the cytokine. The two are separated
      because the cited study tests them separately: depleting the cells tests the first, inhibiting
      the cytokine the second.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:31509752
      reference_title: >-
        Microglia-Triggered Plasticity of Intrinsic Excitability Modulates Psychomotor Behaviors
        in Acute Cerebellar Inflammation.
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: DIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      snippet: >-
        An inflammatory cytokine, tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-alpha), released from microglia
        via toll-like receptor 4, triggers this plasticity.
      explanation: >-
        The receptor and the cytokine, named as the route from the activated cell to the next
        node.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:31509752
    reference_title: >-
      Microglia-Triggered Plasticity of Intrinsic Excitability Modulates Psychomotor Behaviors in
      Acute Cerebellar Inflammation.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    snippet: >-
      Region-specific inflammation in the cerebellum in vivo shows depression- and autistic-like
      behaviors. Furthermore, both TNF-alpha inhibition and microglia depletion revert such
      behavioral abnormality.
    explanation: >-
      The necessity test for this node: blocking the cytokine or removing the cell reverses the
      behavioural change. What this model produces is that behavioural change and not ataxia - stated in those terms by a
      separate review of the same model literature, and recorded as a discussion in this entry.
- name: TNF-alpha Release
  role: effector
  biological_scale: MOLECULAR
  description: >-
    Tumour necrosis factor alpha released from activated microglia. Inhibiting it reverses the
    behavioural change in the rodent model, which is the test that makes this a step rather than a
    correlate.
  cell_types:
  - preferred_term: microglial cell
    term:
      id: CL:0000129
      label: microglial cell
  biological_processes:
  - preferred_term: tumor necrosis factor production
    modifier: INCREASED
    term:
      id: GO:0032640
      label: tumor necrosis factor production
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:31509752
    reference_title: >-
      Microglia-Triggered Plasticity of Intrinsic Excitability Modulates Psychomotor Behaviors in
      Acute Cerebellar Inflammation.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    snippet: >-
      Activated microglia via exposure to bacterial endotoxin lipopolysaccharide or heat-killed
      Gram-negative bacteria induce a potentiation of the intrinsic excitability in Purkinje
      neurons, which is suppressed by microglia-activity inhibitor and microglia depletion.
    explanation: >-
      The whole arm in one sentence, with both tests: a microglial inhibitor and microglial
      depletion each suppress the effect.
  downstream:
  - target: Purkinje Cell Intrinsic Hyperexcitability
    causal_link_type: DIRECT
    description: >-
      TNF-alpha acts on its receptor on Bergmann glia, which release glutamate onto metabotropic
      receptors on the Purkinje cell. Each link in that chain was tested separately, in rat cerebellar slice and, for the glutamate step,
      in dissociated cortical astrocyte culture.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:30072733
      reference_title: >-
        TNF-α increases the intrinsic excitability of cerebellar Purkinje cells through elevating
        glutamate release in Bergmann Glia.
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: DIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: IN_VITRO
      snippet: >-
        Interestingly, the effect of TNF-alpha on the intrinsic excitability of PCs was abolished
        under a condition in which the type1 TNF receptor (TNFR1) in Bergmann glia (BG) was
        genetically suppressed by viral delivery of an adeno-associated virus (AAV) containing
        TNFR1-shRNA.
      explanation: >-
        The glial step, tested by knocking the receptor down in Bergmann glia specifically:
        without it the cytokine no longer changes Purkinje excitability. IN_VITRO because the work
        is in slice and culture.
    - reference: PMID:30072733
      reference_title: >-
        TNF-α increases the intrinsic excitability of cerebellar Purkinje cells through elevating
        glutamate release in Bergmann Glia.
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: DIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: IN_VITRO
      snippet: >-
        Taken together, our study reveals that TNF-alpha triggers glutamate release in BG, thereby
        increasing the intrinsic excitability of cerebellar PCs in a mGluR1-dependent manner.
      explanation: >-

- name: Purkinje Cell Intrinsic Hyperexcitability
  role: effector
  biological_scale: CELLULAR
  description: >-
    The Purkinje cell fires more readily. This is the cellular state the rodent work converges on, and
    the point at which the model and the human disease part company: the animals became hyperexcitable
    and did not become ataxic, while the ataxic animal models in the same literature show Purkinje
    degeneration and hypoexcitability instead.
  cell_types:
  - preferred_term: Purkinje cell
    term:
      id: CL:0000121
      label: Purkinje cell
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:35326323
    reference_title: "Acute Cerebellar Inflammation and Related Ataxia: Mechanisms and Pathophysiology."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    snippet: >-
      In our animal model of the acute inflammation of the cerebellar cortex, animals did not show
      any ataxia but hyperexcitability in the cerebellar cortex and depression-like behaviors. In
      contrast, animal models with neurodegeneration of the cerebellar Purkinje cells and
      hypoexcitability of the neurons show cerebellar ataxia. The suppression of the Ca2+-activated
      K+ channels in vivo is associated with a type of ataxia. Therefore, there is a gap in our
      interpretation between the very early phase of cerebellar inflammation and the emergence of
      cerebellar ataxia.
    explanation: >-
      The authors state the gap themselves, and this entry does not paper over it: the inflammation
      model produces hyperexcitability without ataxia, while the models that are ataxic show the
      opposite cellular state. The chain above is therefore the best-evidenced account of early
      cerebellar inflammation, not an explanation of the ataxia the patients present with.

    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES

- name: Cerebellar Swelling and Mass Effect
  role: effector
  biological_scale: TISSUE
  description: >-
    The arm that makes the fulminant tier dangerous. Cerebellar oedema in the posterior fossa
    obstructs cerebrospinal fluid flow and compresses the brainstem, and it is what the surgical
    treatments act on. A review calls diffuse swelling the most characteristic MRI finding of acute
    cerebellitis, so it is not confined to the fulminant tier, and mass effect is also reported in
    children whose reports do not call their disease fulminant: tonsillar descent in 11 of 15
    children of an acute cerebellitis series in which no child needed surgical decompression,
    tonsillar ectopia in 8 of 9 children seen by one neurosurgical service, and herniation with
    hydrocephalus in two children who both recovered fully.

- name: Brainstem Compression and Tonsillar Herniation
  role: effector
  biological_scale: TISSUE
  description: >-
    The swollen cerebellum can push the cerebellar tonsils down through the foramen magnum and
    compress the brainstem. On imaging, tonsillar descent is common where it is reported - in 8 of 9
    children seen by one neurosurgical service, in 11 of 15 in an acute cerebellitis series, in both
    children of one two-child report, in a second two-child report that describes its pair together,
    and in a boy treated with a shunt - and most of these children survived. Of the three child
    deaths from cerebellitis that the cited sources report case by case, two are attributed in their
    cached abstracts to brainstem involvement or brainstem failure; for the third, the 13-year-old
    who died suddenly, a later case report restates that she had brainstem compression and
    obstructive hydrocephalus on imaging; and a case report, citing earlier work, describes fatal
    cerebellitis through tonsillar herniation or hydrocephalus.

  notes: >-
    The sources describe herniation, hydrocephalus and brainstem compression as parallel results of

    survived. Neither of the two deaths attributed to the brainstem is said to have followed
