        Complicated acute cerebellitis with obstructive hydrocephalus and tonsillar herniation in a
        child.
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: BACKGROUND
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: >-
        AC can have a variable course with features of cerebellar dysfunction, raised intracranial
        pressure and neurological deficits, and can sometimes even be potentially fatal due to
        complications such as obstructive hydrocephalus and brainstem compression, warranting
        surgical intervention.
      explanation: >-
        A case report's opening: the disease can be fatal through obstructive hydrocephalus and
        brainstem compression. Indirect for this row: it gives death, as a possibility, not sudden
        death.
    - reference: PMID:28446490
      reference_title: >-
        Complicated acute cerebellitis with obstructive hydrocephalus and tonsillar herniation in a
        child.
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: BACKGROUND
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: >-
        Levy et al reported a case of sudden death from acute fulminant cerebellitis in a
        13-year-old ballet dancer who had a history of influenza-like illness 10 days prior to the
        cerebellitis episode. The patient had brainstem compression and obstructive hydrocephalus on
        imaging, and her condition deteriorated rapidly and progressed to death.
      explanation: >-
        A later case report's account of the 13-year-old who died suddenly, whose own cached
        abstract says only that serial imaging showed rapid progression: brainstem compression and
        obstructive hydrocephalus on imaging, then rapid deterioration to death. Indirect: a
        second-hand account that gives the compression and the death together without saying that
        the one caused the other. It is the same patient as the sudden-death row's first case, not a
        further death.
phenotypes:
- category: Neurological
  name: Ataxic gait
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: broad-based ataxic gait
    term:
      id: HP:0002066
      label: Gait ataxia
  description: >-
    The presenting sign in most children and the most characteristic finding of the disease.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:28606112
    reference_title: "Acute cerebellitis in children: an eleven year retrospective multicentric study in Italy."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The most characteristic finding of AC/ACA was a broad-based gait disturbance. Other common
      symptoms included balance disturbances, slurred speech, vomiting, headache and fever.
    explanation: >-
      Names this as the most characteristic finding across 124 children, and lists the other common
      symptoms, which are the remaining phenotype rows here.
- category: Neurological
  name: Nystagmus
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: nystagmus
    term:
      id: HP:0000639
      label: Nystagmus
  description: >-
    An ocular cerebellar sign, reported with dysmetria as the two commonest associated findings in
    the paediatric series cited.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:14552515
    reference_title: >-
      Post-infectious acute cerebellar ataxia in children.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The most common associated neurologic findings were nystagmus and dysmetria.
    explanation: >-
      Names both this row and the next as the commonest findings accompanying the ataxia in 39
      children.
- category: Neurological
  name: Dysmetria
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: dysmetria
    term:
      id: HP:0001310
      label: Dysmetria
  description: >-
    An appendicular cerebellar sign, and one of the two findings reported as commonest alongside the ataxia.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:14552515
    reference_title: >-
      Post-infectious acute cerebellar ataxia in children.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The most common associated neurologic findings were nystagmus and dysmetria.
    explanation: >-
      Names dysmetria, with nystagmus, as the two commonest findings accompanying the ataxia in 39
      children.
  - reference: PMID:32160830
    reference_title: >-
      Acute Cerebellitis or Postinfectious Cerebellar Ataxia? Clinical and Imaging Features in Acute
      Cerebellitis.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Neurologic examination median 12 months later revealed ataxia and dysmetria in 4 cases (27%),
      accompanied by memory difficulties, dysarthria or tremor.
    explanation: >-
      This sign at follow-up rather than at presentation: it is one of the deficits that persists in
      about a quarter of an acute cerebellitis series at a year.
- category: Neurological
  name: Dysarthria
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: slurred speech
    term:
      id: HP:0001260
      label: Dysarthria
  description: >-
    Cerebellar speech, one of the six signs the cited series counts as isolated cerebellar signs.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:38008790
    reference_title: "\"The Red Flags\" in Clinical Approach to Acute Ataxia-the Experience in Cohort of 76 Children."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Clinical presentation was divided into two categories: (1) isolated cerebellar signs (CS):
      ataxic gait, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, intention tremor, dysarthria, and nystagmus;
    explanation: >-
      The series' own definition of an isolated cerebellar presentation, which names this sign among
      six. It is a case definition rather than a frequency, which is why this row carries no
      frequency band.
- category: Neurological
  name: Intention tremor
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: intention tremor
    term:
      id: HP:0002080
      label: Intention tremor
  description: >-
    A cerebellar sign listed in the series' own definition of isolated cerebellar presentation.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:22936351
    reference_title: >-
      Long-term outcome of children with acute cerebellitis.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Neurological sequelae were reported in five children ranging from ataxia to mild tremor.
      Cognitive deficits were found in six patients.
    explanation: >-
      Tremor among the persisting deficits in a long-term acute cerebellitis follow-up of eleven
      children, beside the cognitive ones.
- category: Clinical
  name: Headache
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: headache
    term:
      id: HP:0002315
      label: Headache
  description: >-
    With vomiting, the pair that distinguishes acute cerebellitis from the benign tier at the bedside, and part of the raised-pressure presentation of the fulminant one.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:29166939
    reference_title: "Acute cerebellitis in adults: a case report and review of the literature."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The most common clinical presentation consisted of headache, nausea/vomiting and ataxia. Six
      patients presented with only headache and nausea and subsequently returned with cerebellar
      signs.
    explanation: >-
      In 35 adults this is the commonest presentation, and six of them presented with headache and
      nausea alone and only later developed cerebellar signs - which is why headache is a phenotype
      row here and not a footnote.
- category: Clinical
  name: Vomiting
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: vomiting
    term:
      id: HP:0002013
      label: Vomiting
  description: >-
    The other half of the pair that marks the cerebellitis tier, and a sign of raised intracranial pressure in the fulminant one.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:32160830
    reference_title: >-
      Acute Cerebellitis or Postinfectious Cerebellar Ataxia? Clinical and Imaging Features in Acute
      Cerebellitis.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The most common first symptoms were ataxia, vomiting, and headache.
    explanation: >-
      The three commonest first symptoms in a series of fifteen children with acute cerebellitis,
      which is the tier this phenotype marks.
- category: Neurological
  name: Encephalopathy
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: encephalopathy
    term:
      id: HP:0001298
      label: Encephalopathy
  description: >-
    Not a cerebellar sign, and that is the point: its presence alongside the cerebellar ones predicts a worse outcome, and in the fulminant tier it may be the presentation with no cerebellar signs at all.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:33581790
    reference_title: >-
      Cerebellitis as a neurosurgical disease in pediatrics.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Common presenting symptoms were headache (n = 6, 66.7%), emesis (n = 5, 55.6%), and altered
      mental status (n = 4, 44.4%).
    explanation: >-
      Altered mental status in 4 of 9 children referred to one neurosurgical service.
  - reference: PMID:28318729
    reference_title: >-
      Acute cerebellitis in paediatric patients: Our experience.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Headache, vomiting, and drowsiness were the most frequent initial symptoms; ataxia,
      dysarthria, and dysmetria were the most common cerebellar signs.
    explanation: >-
      Drowsiness among the commonest first symptoms of a nine-child series. Indirect: drowsiness is
      read here as encephalopathy, which this sentence does not call it.
  - reference: PMID:28318729
    reference_title: >-
      Acute cerebellitis in paediatric patients: Our experience.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      It is a clinical-radiological syndrome characterised by acute or subacute encephalopathy with
      intracranial hypertension and cerebellar syndrome associated with T2-weighted and FLAIR
      hyperintensities in the cerebellar cortex (unilaterally or bilaterally) and possible
      triventricular dilatation.
    explanation: >-
      The same series' definition of the syndrome, which includes an acute or subacute
      encephalopathy.
  - reference: PMID:38008790
    reference_title: "\"The Red Flags\" in Clinical Approach to Acute Ataxia-the Experience in Cohort of 76 Children."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Analysis showed that presence of additional symptoms to ataxia, so called "cerebellar plus
      symptoms" (p = 0.002) and structural abnormalities (p < 0.001), had statistically higher
      frequency of poor outcome.
    explanation: >-
      The outcome consequence, from 76 children and confirmed in that series' multivariate analysis:
      cerebellar-plus symptoms, of which this is one, and structural abnormality on imaging are the
      two factors associated with poor outcome.
- category: Neurological
  name: Obstructive hydrocephalus
  frequency: OCCASIONAL
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: obstructive hydrocephalus
    term:
      id: HP:0000238
      label: Hydrocephalus
  description: >-
    The consequence of posterior fossa swelling, and the reason the fulminant tier may need
    cerebrospinal fluid diversion. Several cited sources call it obstructive hydrocephalus in those words. HPO's nearest narrower term is
    Noncommunicating hydrocephalus, HP:0010953, and the two are not the same concept: asked
    directly, OLS returns no exact synonym for that term at all, and HPO's own definition says the
    most common form of noncommunicating hydrocephalus is obstructive, which makes obstructive a
    subset rather than a synonym. The binding therefore stays at the parent and the preferred term
    carries the sources' word.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:29166939
    reference_title: "Acute cerebellitis in adults: a case report and review of the literature."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      In 9 cases, the cerebellitis was complicated by hydrocephalus.
    explanation: >-
      Nine of 35 adults in this review, which says hydrocephalus without the word obstructive that
      several other cited sources use. The binding stays at the parent term for the reason given in the row's
      description.
- category: Neurological
  name: Cognitive and behavioural sequelae
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: cognitive impairment after recovery
    term:
      id: HP:0100543
      label: Cognitive impairment
  description: >-
    The deficit that outlasts the ataxia, and the one most easily missed because the motor signs resolve. Reported across three independent follow-up series.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:8210223
    reference_title: >-
      Course and outcome of acute cerebellar ataxia.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      One fifth of the children followed for more than 4 months experienced transient behavioral or
      intellectual difficulties, but only 5 of the 60 children demonstrated sustained learning
      problems.
    explanation: >-
      Both halves matter: a fifth had transient difficulties, and five of sixty had sustained
      learning problems. The row records the persisting deficit, and the quote keeps the larger
      transient figure beside it so neither stands alone.
  - reference: PMID:22936351
    reference_title: >-
      Long-term outcome of children with acute cerebellitis.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Neurological and cognitive sequelae are common in children with AC and underline the role of
      the cerebellum in cognition.
    explanation: >-
      The authors' own conclusion from a mean follow-up of four years and four months in children
      with the cerebellitis tier specifically, where cognitive deficits were found in six of eleven.
- category: Neurological
  name: Cerebellar atrophy
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: cerebellar atrophy on follow-up imaging
    term:
      id: HP:0001272
      label: Cerebellar atrophy
  description: >-
    A structural outcome seen on repeat imaging in a majority of one acute cerebellitis series, and a reason to repeat the scan rather than assume resolution.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:32160830
    reference_title: >-
      Acute Cerebellitis or Postinfectious Cerebellar Ataxia? Clinical and Imaging Features in Acute
      Cerebellitis.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Follow-up magnetic resonance imaging (MRI; n = 12) showed diffuse cerebellar cortical
      T2-hyperintense signal changes in 11 cases and cerebellar atrophy in 9.
    explanation: >-
      Nine of twelve re-imaged children in an acute cerebellitis series. The denominator is the
      re-imaged subset of a severe-tier series, not the disease.
- category: Neurological
  name: Increased intracranial pressure
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: increased intracranial pressure
    term:
      id: HP:0002516
      label: Increased intracranial pressure
  description: >-
    Orphanet lists high intracranial pressure among the main presenting features. Raised
    intracranial pressure is part of how one series defines acute cerebellitis, a case report's
    12-year-old boy presented with it, and a review places it, with altered consciousness,
    hydrocephalus and herniation, at the severe end of the spectrum.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:28318729
    reference_title: >-
      Acute cerebellitis in paediatric patients: Our experience.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      It is a clinical-radiological syndrome characterised by acute or subacute encephalopathy with
      intracranial hypertension and cerebellar syndrome associated with T2-weighted and FLAIR
      hyperintensities in the cerebellar cortex (unilaterally or bilaterally) and possible
      triventricular dilatation.
    explanation: >-
      One series' definition of the syndrome, which includes intracranial hypertension.
  - reference: PMID:22805251
    reference_title: >-
      Acute cerebellar ataxia, acute cerebellitis, and opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Severe cases of cerebellitis represent the other end of the spectrum, presenting with acute
      cerebellar signs often overshadowed by alteration of consciousness, focal neurological
      deficits, raised intracranial pressure, hydrocephalus, and even herniation.
    explanation: >-
      A review's account of the severe end of the spectrum.
  - reference: ORPHA:624244
    reference_title: "Postinfectious cerebellitis"
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: >-
      Affected individuals mainly present with acute-onset afebrile gait ataxia, meningeal signs,
      high intracranial pressure with or without extracerebellar manifestations
    explanation: >-
      Orphanet's list of the main presenting features, which includes high intracranial pressure.
  - reference: PMID:28446490
    reference_title: >-
      Complicated acute cerebellitis with obstructive hydrocephalus and tonsillar herniation in a
      child.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      We report a case of a 12-year-old boy who presented with raised intracranial pressure and
      ataxia.
    explanation: >-
      A 12-year-old boy who presented with raised intracranial pressure and ataxia.
- category: Neurological
  name: Papilledema
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: bilateral papilloedema
    term:
      id: HP:0001085
      label: Papilledema
  description: >-
    Bilateral papilloedema on fundus examination is reported in a 12-year-old boy who presented with
    raised intracranial pressure, obstructive hydrocephalus and tonsillar herniation, and recovered
    completely after a shunt. No cited source gives its frequency.
  notes: >-
    Not connected to a mechanism node or to the raised-pressure row: the one cited report gives the
    papilloedema beside the raised intracranial pressure without saying how they are linked.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:28446490
    reference_title: >-
      Complicated acute cerebellitis with obstructive hydrocephalus and tonsillar herniation in a
      child.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Fundus examination revealed bilateral papilloedema.
    explanation: >-
      Bilateral papilloedema in that boy.
- category: Neurological
  name: Sudden death
  subtype: AFC
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: sudden death
    term:
      id: HP:0001699
      label: Sudden death
  description: >-
    Death, sometimes sudden, is the outcome the fulminant form is feared for. Case reports describe
    a 13-year-old who died suddenly and a 9-year-old who died because of brainstem involvement after
    rapid progression, and a three-child series concludes that the fulminant form carries a high
    risk of death.
  notes: >-
    No cited source gives a death rate for the fulminant form in children; the child deaths here are
    single cases. A pooled review of 73 published cases records its one death among its 13 fulminant
    cases, in an adult whose diagnosis was a COVID-19-associated necrotising encephalopathy. The row
    is bound to Sudden death because HPO's Death in childhood (HP:0003819) sits under
    Mortality/Aging, outside the Phenotypic abnormality branch that phenotype rows accept; one cited
    child's death was sudden, and the others are not said to be.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:11490187
    reference_title: >-
      Sudden death from fulminant acute cerebellitis.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      We report a case of sudden death from acute fulminant cerebellitis in a 13-year-old ballet
      dancer.
    explanation: >-
      Sudden death in a 13-year-old.
  - reference: PMID:19664542
    reference_title: >-
      Fulminant cerebellitis: a fatal, clinically isolated syndrome.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      We report a 9-year-old boy in whom death resulted from acute fulminant cerebellitis because of
      brainstem involvement.
    explanation: >-
      A second child's death. Indirect for this row: the abstract does not say the death was sudden.
  - reference: PMID:42699856
    reference_title: >-
      Acute fulminant cerebellitis in children: a case series and literature review on diagnostic
      challenges and management strategies.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Fulminant AC in children, although rare, carries a high risk of morbidity and mortality.
    explanation: >-
      The three-child series' conclusion, drawn with its review of the literature. Indirect for this
      row: it gives a risk of death, not of sudden death.
  - reference: PMID:26961264
    reference_title: >-
      Acute Cerebellitis in Children: A Many-Faceted Disease.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      It may have a benign, self-limiting course or present as a fulminant disease resulting in
      severe cerebellar damage or even sudden death.
    explanation: >-
      Sudden death at the far end of the disease's range, in a series' introduction.
biochemical:
- name: Anti-glutamate receptor delta 2 antibody
  presence: Positive in single cases
  context: Serum and cerebrospinal fluid
  notes: >-
    Reported in single patients rather than measured in a series, in serum, in cerebrospinal fluid or
    in both. What a positive result means is disputed: two case reports read it in opposite
    directions, as the discussions record.
  readouts:
  - target: Autoantibodies Binding Neural Tissue
    relationship: READOUT_OF
    direction: PRESENT_ABSENT
    interpretation: >-
      A positive result shows the humoral arm in that patient. A negative one says little, since no
      cited series has measured how often the antibody is found.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:23892968
      reference_title: "[A case of acute cerebellar ataxia following infectious mononucleosis accompanied by intrathecal anti-glutamate receptor δ2 antibody]."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: DIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: >-
        EB virus DNA and anti-VCA IgM and IgG antibodies were negative and glutamate receptor δ2
        antibody was positive in CSF collected on hospital day 11.
      explanation: >-
        The antibody in the cerebrospinal fluid of an 18-year-old with ataxia after infectious
        mononucleosis, where neither the virus nor antibodies against it were found.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:17049194
    reference_title: >-
      Acute cerebellar ataxia and consecutive cerebellitis produced by glutamate receptor delta2
      autoantibody.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Furthermore, glutamate receptor delta2 autoantibody was detected in serum and cerebro-spinal
      fluid.
    explanation: >-
      Serum and cerebrospinal fluid both positive, in an 18-month-old boy whose ataxia began nine days
      after a respiratory infection.
  - reference: PMID:17008044
    reference_title: >-
      A case of acute cerebellitis accompanied by autoantibodies against glutamate receptor delta2.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      IgG type of autoantibodies against glutamate receptor delta2 (GluRdelta2) were detected in the
      serum, but not in the cerebrospinal fluid in his early clinical course.
    explanation: >-
      Serum positive and cerebrospinal fluid negative early on, in a 13-year-old with acute
      cerebellitis; the same report suggests the antibody might be a consequence of the damage.
  - reference: PMID:26377184
    reference_title: "'Medusa head ataxia': the expanding spectrum of Purkinje cell antibodies in autoimmune cerebellar ataxia. Part 2: Anti-PKC-gamma, anti-GluR-delta2, anti-Ca/ARHGAP26 and anti-VGCC."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      No tumours have been reported so far in patients with anti-GluRδ2-associated cerebellar ataxia.
      Of note, however, all cases were preceded or accompanied by either infection or vaccination.
    explanation: >-
      Across the reported cases, an infection or a vaccination every time, and no tumour.
- name: Anti-centrosome antibodies
  presence: Positive after varicella, with or without ataxia
  context: Serum
  notes: >-
    Not specific to the disease. In the one study that tested recombinant centrosome antigens, most
    children with ataxia after varicella carried antibodies against at least one of them, but so did
    most of their siblings with uncomplicated varicella and both children tested with acute
    disseminated encephalomyelitis. The study's abstract and its results section give slightly
    different counts (11 of 12 and 4 of 5 in the abstract, 10 of 12 and 3 of 5 by immunoblot in the
    results); the entry quotes the abstract.
  readouts:
  - target: Autoantibodies Binding Neural Tissue
    relationship: READOUT_OF
    direction: PRESENT_ABSENT
    interpretation: >-
      A positive result is not specific to the disease: in the one study, such antibodies were also
      found in children with uncomplicated varicella and in both children with acute disseminated
      encephalomyelitis.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:14503922
      reference_title: >-
        Spectrum of centrosome autoantibodies in childhood varicella and post-varicella acute
        cerebellar ataxia.
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: DIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: >-
        Eleven of 12 children with post-varicella ataxia, 4/5 children with uncomplicated varicella
        infections, 1/1 with post-EBV ataxia, 2/2 with ADEM, 1/2 with neuroblastoma and ataxia, and
        2/2 with cerebellitis had antibodies directed against 1 or more recombinant centrosome
        antigens.
      explanation: >-
        Eleven of 12 with the disease after varicella, against 4 of 5 with varicella alone and both
        children with acute disseminated encephalomyelitis.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:11097523
    reference_title: >-
      Autoantibodies in childhood post-varicella acute cerebellar ataxia.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The punctate staining seen on cerebrum and cerebellum sections co-localized with rabbit
      antibodies to the centrosome protein pericentrin.
    explanation: >-
      The earlier study from the same group, which saw a punctate pattern on brain tissue and placed
      it at the centrosome by co-localisation with pericentrin. INDIRECT: co-localisation implies the
      target rather than identifying it.
- name: Anti-pericentrin antibody
  presence: Positive in 5 of 12 children with ataxia after varicella
  context: Serum
  notes: >-
    The only antibody in the cited sources found in patients with this disease, tested against
    comparison groups and absent from all of them, and that study is small: twelve children with
    ataxia after varicella.
  readouts:
  - target: Autoantibodies Binding Neural Tissue
    relationship: READOUT_OF
    direction: PRESENT_ABSENT
    interpretation: >-
      A positive result marks a response to a protein that, in monkey cerebellum, sits in axons and
      centrosomes. It was absent from every comparison group tested, including uncomplicated
      varicella, and no second series in the cited sources has measured it.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:14503922
      reference_title: >-
        Spectrum of centrosome autoantibodies in childhood varicella and post-varicella acute
        cerebellar ataxia.
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: DIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: >-
        Antibodies to pericentrin were seen in 5/12 children with post-varicella ataxia but not in any
        of the other sera tested.
      explanation: >-
        Five of twelve with the disease and none of the others.
    - reference: PMID:14503922
      reference_title: >-
        Spectrum of centrosome autoantibodies in childhood varicella and post-varicella acute
        cerebellar ataxia.
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: IN_VITRO
      snippet: >-
        IIF demonstrated that pericentrin is located in axons and centrosomes of cerebellar cells.
      explanation: >-
        Where the antigen sits, shown by staining monkey cerebellum with rabbit antibodies to
        pericentrin, so a tissue-section result rather than a finding in patients.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:14503922
    reference_title: >-
      Spectrum of centrosome autoantibodies in childhood varicella and post-varicella acute
      cerebellar ataxia.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Our data suggest that children with post-varicella ataxia have unique autoantibody reactivity to
      pericentrin.
    explanation: >-
      The authors' conclusion, stated as a suggestion.
- name: Anti-GQ1b IgG antibody
  presence: Positive in a reported case of an isolated cerebellar syndrome after infection
  context: Serum
  notes: >-
    Reported in one adult whose purely cerebellar syndrome followed an infection; its authors read the
    case as extending the anti-GQ1b antibody syndrome to isolated cerebellar ataxia and recommend the
    test after infection. Whether such a case belongs to this disease or to that syndrome is the
    reader's call. A series of children with acute ataxia of all causes lists GQ1b antibodies among the
    common markers its screening found.
  readouts:
  - target: Autoantibodies Binding Neural Tissue
    relationship: READOUT_OF
    direction: PRESENT_ABSENT
    interpretation: >-
      A positive result in an isolated cerebellar syndrome after infection raises the anti-GQ1b
      antibody syndrome, which the case's authors extend to isolated cerebellar ataxia.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:40787651
      reference_title: "Isolated Pancerebellar Syndrome With anti-GQ1b IgG Positivity: A Case Report."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: DIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: >-
        Serological testing sent during the hospitalization subsequently revealed anti-GQ1b IgG
        positivity.
      explanation: >-
        The measurement, in one 22-year-old woman with no sensory loss, no lost reflexes and no
        ophthalmoplegia.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:40787651
    reference_title: "Isolated Pancerebellar Syndrome With anti-GQ1b IgG Positivity: A Case Report."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      This case expands the spectrum of anti-GQ1b syndrome to include isolated cerebellar ataxia,
      suggesting that ataxia in this syndrome can have cerebellar origin. Clinicians should consider
      anti-GQ1b testing in cases of acute cerebellar ataxia following infection.
    explanation: >-
      The authors' conclusion and their recommendation, from the single case.
  - reference: PMID:41321459
    reference_title: "Acute ataxia in children: etiological spectrum and clinical characteristics."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Autoantibody screening in a subset of 135 patients identified CSF OCB, serum myelin basic
      protein (MBP), myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) immunoglobulin G (IgG), GQ1b, and
      aquaporin-4 (AQP4) antibodies as common markers.
    explanation: >-
      GQ1b antibodies among the common findings when 135 of 257 children with acute ataxia were
      screened. INDIRECT because the series covers every cause of acute ataxia, not this disease alone.
- name: Neural autoantibody panel in serum and cerebrospinal fluid
  biomarker_term:
    preferred_term: neural autoantibody panel
    term:
      id: NCIT:C181397
      label: Autoantibody Measurement
  presence: Positive in 10 of 36 children with acute cerebellitis in one multicentre series
  context: Serum and cerebrospinal fluid
  notes: >-
    The figure is not an unselected rate. The study's case definition allowed an antibody to stand in
    for MRI evidence of cerebellar inflammation, and half of the positive children carried antibodies
    against myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein, which the authors read as widening the spectrum of
    the disease defined by that antibody. The antibody-positive children were also more likely to
    have a better outcome than those without an antibody.
  readouts:
  - target: Autoantibodies Binding Neural Tissue
    relationship: READOUT_OF
    direction: PRESENT_ABSENT
    interpretation: >-
      A positive panel shows the humoral arm and names its target, which differs from child to child.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:38284996
      reference_title: "Autoantibody status, neuroradiological and clinical findings in children with acute cerebellitis."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: DIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: >-
        In 10/36 (28 %) children the following autoantibodies (abs) were found: MOG-abs (n = 5) in
        serum, GFAPα-abs (n = 1) in CSF, GlyR-abs (n = 1) in CSF, mGluR1-abs (n = 1) in CSF and serum.
        In two further children, antibodies were detected only in serum (GlyR-abs, n = 1; GFAPα-abs,
        n = 1).
      explanation: >-
        Ten of 36, against four different antigens, five of them antibodies against myelin
        oligodendrocyte glycoprotein.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:38284996
    reference_title: "Autoantibody status, neuroradiological and clinical findings in children with acute cerebellitis."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      In nearly 30 % of children in our study with AC, a range of abs was found, underscoring that
      autoantibody testing in serum and CSF should be included in the work-up of a child with suspected
      AC. The detection of MOG-abs in AC does expand the MOGAD spectrum.
    explanation: >-
      The authors' conclusion, and their reading of the antibodies against myelin oligodendrocyte
      glycoprotein as part of another disease's spectrum.
  - reference: PMID:38284996
    reference_title: "Autoantibody status, neuroradiological and clinical findings in children with acute cerebellitis."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Children presenting with symptoms suggestive of AC defined as acute/subacute onset of cerebellar
      symptoms and MRI evidence of cerebellar inflammation or additional CSF pleocytosis, positive
      oligoclonal bands (OCBs), and/or presence of autoantibodies in case of negative cerebellar MRI.
    explanation: >-
      The case definition, quoted for the caveat in the notes: an antibody could stand in for MRI
      evidence of inflammation.
  - reference: PMID:38284996
    reference_title: "Autoantibody status, neuroradiological and clinical findings in children with acute cerebellitis."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Antibody (ab)-positive children were significantly more likely to have a better outcome than
      ab-negative children (p = .022).
    explanation: >-
      The outcome difference, as a significance level without an effect size.
animal_models:
- name: Acute cerebellar inflammation rodent model
  species: Mouse and rat
  genotype: wild type, with cerebellar inflammation induced by lipopolysaccharide or heat-killed Gram-negative bacteria
  publication: PMID:31509752
  description: >-
    Inflammation induced in the cerebellar cortex of a normal animal, which is the system every
    mechanistic step in the middle of this entry's chain comes from. It is not a model of this
    disease's trigger - no antecedent infection, no latent interval, no immune response directed at
    the cerebellum - and its authors say in a companion review that the animals were not ataxic.
  notes: >-
    No model-organism gene identifier is bound, because the model carries no engineered allele: the
    intervention is an inflammatory stimulus in a wild-type animal. The species field names both,
    because the cited work spans mouse in vivo behaviour and rat slice and culture electrophysiology.
  modeled_mechanisms:
  - target: Microglial Activation
    relationship: RECAPITULATES
    fidelity: MODERATE
    model_scale: CELLULAR
    description: >-
      The node exists because of this model. Activation is established by depleting the cells and by
      inhibiting their activity, which is a necessity test rather than an observation.
    limitations: >-
      The stimulus is bacterial endotoxin or heat-killed bacteria applied to the cerebellum, not an
      immune response to an antecedent systemic infection. Nothing in the model represents the latent
      interval that defines this disease.
    divergences:
    - divergence_type: PROXY_QUANTITY
      materiality: QUALIFYING
      description: >-
        The model's quantity is microglial activation by a toll-like receptor 4 ligand. The node's
        quantity is microglial activation downstream of a post-infectious immune response whose
        effector no cited source identifies.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:31509752
      reference_title: >-
        Microglia-Triggered Plasticity of Intrinsic Excitability Modulates Psychomotor Behaviors
        in Acute Cerebellar Inflammation.
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: DIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      snippet: >-
        Activated microglia via exposure to bacterial endotoxin lipopolysaccharide or heat-killed
        Gram-negative bacteria induce a potentiation of the intrinsic excitability in Purkinje
        neurons, which is suppressed by microglia-activity inhibitor and microglia depletion.
      explanation: >-
        What the model does and how the step was established.
  - target: Purkinje Cell Intrinsic Hyperexcitability
    relationship: RECAPITULATES
    fidelity: MODERATE
    model_scale: CELLULAR
    description: >-
      The electrophysiological change this entry's chain turns on, measured directly in the model.
    limitations: >-
      Measured in rodent Purkinje cells. No cited source reports Purkinje cell excitability in a
      patient with this disease, so the human end of this node is unmeasured.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:30072733
      reference_title: >-
        TNF-α increases the intrinsic excitability of cerebellar Purkinje cells through elevating
        glutamate release in Bergmann Glia.
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: DIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: IN_VITRO
      snippet: >-
        A bath application of TNF-alpha (100 ng/ml) in acute cerebellar slices elevates spiking
        activity of PCs with no alterations in the regularity of PC firings.
      explanation: >-
        The change measured directly, in rat cerebellar slice.
  - target: Cerebellar Dysfunction
    relationship: FAILS_TO_RECAPITULATE
    fidelity: LOW
    model_scale: ORGANISM
    description: >-
      The model does not produce the sign that defines the human disease. Its animals show
      depression-like and autistic-like behaviour and no ataxia, which is the gap this entry records
      as a discussion.
    limitations: >-
      The behavioural readout is not the human one. A model that produces no ataxia cannot show how
      cerebellar inflammation produces ataxia, which is the step between this entry's mechanism and
      its phenotypes, and the review of this literature says so in terms.
    divergences:
    - divergence_type: PROXY_QUANTITY
      materiality: INVALIDATING
      description: >-
        The model's outcome measure is depression-like and autistic-like behaviour. The node's
        quantity is cerebellar ataxia. They are not the same observation and the model does not
        produce the second.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:35326323
      reference_title: >-
        Acute Cerebellar Inflammation and Related Ataxia: Mechanisms and Pathophysiology.
      supports: REFUTE
      directness: DIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      snippet: >-
        In our animal model of the acute inflammation of the cerebellar cortex, animals did not
        show any ataxia but hyperexcitability in the cerebellar cortex and depression-like
        behaviors.
      explanation: >-
        The failure stated by the authors of the model itself. REFUTE against the claim that this
        model reproduces the human sign.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:35326323
    reference_title: >-
      Acute Cerebellar Inflammation and Related Ataxia: Mechanisms and Pathophysiology.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    snippet: >-
      Therefore, there is a gap in our interpretation between the very early phase of cerebellar
      inflammation and the emergence of cerebellar ataxia.
    explanation: >-
      Why this model is recorded with a failure arm rather than as straightforward support: the
      reviewers of its own literature name the gap.
diagnosis:
- name: Cerebellar magnetic resonance imaging
  diagnosis_term:
    preferred_term: magnetic resonance imaging of the cerebellum
    term:
      id: NCIT:C16809
      label: Magnetic Resonance Imaging
  description: >-
    The test that separates the tiers. Bilateral symmetrical T2 signal change in the cerebellar
    cortex with swelling marks the cerebellitis tier; a normal scan does not exclude the benign one.
    Whether an abnormal scan also carries prognostic weight is unsettled: the two series on the
    imaging findings point different ways, and they compare different things.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:32160830
    reference_title: >-
      Acute Cerebellitis or Postinfectious Cerebellar Ataxia? Clinical and Imaging Features in Acute
      Cerebellitis.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) generally showed bilateral symmetrical T2 hyperintense
      changes with moderate swelling in the cerebellar cortex.
    explanation: >-
      The imaging pattern itself, in a series of fifteen children with the cerebellitis tier.
  - reference: PMID:28606112
    reference_title: "Acute cerebellitis in children: an eleven year retrospective multicentric study in Italy."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Children with pathological magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or computed tomography (CT) had a
      higher probability of having clinical sequelae.
    explanation: >-
      The prognostic half of the same test, across 124 children: in that series an abnormal scan at
      admission went with sequelae, which is the authors' stated reason for imaging every child rather
      than only the severe ones. A smaller series of acute cerebellitis found MRI results not
      predictive of outcome; the imaging findings carry both.
  - reference: PMID:11826604
    reference_title: >-
      Neuroimaging of acute cerebellitis.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Their magnetic resonance imaging showed hyperintense signal of cerebellar gray matter in
      T2-weighted sequences, which is a strong indication of a diagnosis of acute cerebellitis.
    explanation: >-
      The same pattern read from two cases, with the authors' own statement of how far it takes a
      diagnosis: a strong indication, not a confirmation. Two patients, so the claim rests on the
      series above rather than on this.
- name: Cerebrospinal fluid examination
  diagnosis_term:
    preferred_term: lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid examination
    term:
      id: NCIT:C15327
      label: Lumbar Puncture
  description: >-
    Used to narrow the differential rather than to confirm this diagnosis. A normal result does not
    exclude it, and in a multicentre paediatric series the cerebrospinal fluid findings did not
    correlate with symptoms or clinical outcome.
  notes: >-
    Whether posterior fossa swelling should stop or delay lumbar puncture is not settled by the
    cited sources: none says when it should, one case report (PMID:28446490) calls the test
    important when there is no contraindication, without naming one, and in its own case the test
    was done after a shunt had decompressed the ventricles. Swelling is found in the acute
    cerebellitis tier, not only the fulminant one, which is defined by rapid swelling with
    obstructive hydrocephalus and brainstem compression. The entry therefore records the test and
    not a rule for when to omit it.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:28606112
    reference_title: "Acute cerebellitis in children: an eleven year retrospective multicentric study in Italy."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      There was no correlation among symptoms, cerebrospinal fluid findings, clinical outcome.
    explanation: >-
      The negative result that sets what this test is for: across 124 children the cerebrospinal
      fluid findings predicted neither the presentation nor the outcome.
  - reference: PMID:11826604
    reference_title: >-
      Neuroimaging of acute cerebellitis.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Diagnosing of acute cerebellitis can sometimes be difficult because the patient may present
      only mild cerebellar signs and the examination of cerebrospinal fluid may be normal.
    explanation: >-
      States the limitation directly: a normal cerebrospinal fluid does not exclude the diagnosis.
  - reference: PMID:29166939
    reference_title: "Acute cerebellitis in adults: a case report and review of the literature."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      To diagnose cerebellitis, imaging of the brain (preferably MRI) is required and CSF
      examination may be necessary to narrow the differential diagnosis.
    explanation: >-
      The authors' own statement of the division of labour between the two tests in this entry's
      diagnosis block, from a review of 35 adult cases.
- name: Identification of the antecedent infection
  diagnosis_term:
    preferred_term: serological and molecular testing for the preceding pathogen
    term:
      id: NCIT:C217458
      label: Diagnostic Serology Testing
  description: >-
    A search that usually fails, and that is a finding rather than a shortfall: no pathogen is
    identified in a quarter to a third of cases, and the diagnosis does not depend on finding one.
    The row covers molecular testing as well as serology, which the bound term does not: `runoak -i
    sqlite:obo:ncit search 'l~Infectious Disease'` and `'l^Microbiolog'` returned no clinical-action
    term inside the enum that covers both, so the serology term is bound and the preferred term says
    what the row is.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:42649322
    reference_title: "Post-Infectious Cerebellitis: A Systematic Review of Aetiology, Clinical Presentation, Treatment, and Outcomes."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      SARS-CoV-2 (n = 24, 32.9%) was the most frequently identified trigger, followed by patients
      with no pathogen identified (n = 18, 24.7%), varicella-zoster virus (n = 8, 11.0%),
      Epstein-Barr virus (n = 5, 6.8%), and influenza (n = 5, 6.8%).
    explanation: >-
      The yield of the search across 73 pooled patients, with no pathogen found in a quarter. Read
      the denominator with care: this is a pooled review whose publication years are weighted
      towards the pandemic, so the SARS-CoV-2 share is a property of the literature sampled, not of
      the disease.
  - reference: PMID:32160830
    reference_title: >-
      Acute Cerebellitis or Postinfectious Cerebellar Ataxia? Clinical and Imaging Features in Acute
      Cerebellitis.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Etiologic workup for infectious pathogens revealed Mycoplasma pneumoniae, influenza A virus,
      cytomegalovirus, and varicella zoster virus in 1 case each.
    explanation: >-
      The same search in an unpooled series: four pathogens across fifteen children, one case each,
      which is what a low yield looks like at the bedside.
imaging_findings:
- name: Normal neuroimaging in acute cerebellar ataxia
  modality: MRI
  subtype: ACA
  description: >-
    In the mildest cases the scan is normal, and an abnormal scan points instead to acute
    cerebellitis, though a review of the two notes considerable overlap between them. Whether every
    child needs imaging is itself unsettled: one series says imaging is needed only for an atypical
    presentation or a child who has not improved after one to two weeks, while another suggests an
    instrumental evaluation of every child at admission.
  diagnostic: false
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:22805251
    reference_title: >-
      Acute cerebellar ataxia, acute cerebellitis, and opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      It occurs mostly in young children, presents abruptly, and recovers over weeks. Neuroimaging is
      normal.
    explanation: >-
      A review's account of the mildest cases, ending on the normal scan.
  - reference: PMID:22805251
    reference_title: >-
      Acute cerebellar ataxia, acute cerebellitis, and opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      There is considerable overlap between these entities.
    explanation: >-
      The same review on acute cerebellar ataxia and acute cerebellitis, which is why the normal scan
      is tied to the mildest cases rather than to the whole tier. INDIRECT: it is about the entities,
      not the scan.
  - reference: PMID:14552515
    reference_title: >-
      Post-infectious acute cerebellar ataxia in children.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Imaging studies are needed only in atypical presentation or if there is no spontaneous
      improvement after 1 to 2 weeks.
    explanation: >-
      The conclusion of a 39-child series in which every child recovered fully. INDIRECT: it is a
      recommendation on when to image, which implies rather than reports the normal scan.
  - reference: PMID:28606112
    reference_title: >-
      Acute cerebellitis in children: an eleven year retrospective multicentric study in Italy.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      These findings suggest the indication to perform an instrumental evaluation in all patients with
      AC/ACA at admission to identify those at higher risk of neurological outcome.
    explanation: >-
      The opposite view, from the 124-child Italian series, which found an abnormal MRI or CT linked
      to sequelae. INDIRECT: it is a suggestion about whom to evaluate, not a report of the scan.
- name: Bilateral T2 hyperintensity and swelling of the cerebellar cortex
  modality: MRI
  description: >-
    The scan of acute cerebellitis: T2 hyperintense signal in the grey matter of the cerebellar
    cortex, generally bilateral and symmetrical, with swelling. Imaging of the brain is required for
    the diagnosis, and the same 15-child series that describes the pattern found tonsillar herniation
    in 11 of its children and obstructive hydrocephalus in 4. Two series point different ways on
    whether the scan predicts the outcome, and they compare different things: in 124 children, nearly
    all with acute cerebellar ataxia, an abnormal MRI or CT went with a higher chance of sequelae than
    a normal one, while among the 15 children with acute cerebellitis, whose scans generally showed
    the pattern, MRI results did not predict the outcome.
  imaging_finding_term:
    preferred_term: bilateral symmetrical T2 hyperintensity with swelling of the cerebellar cortex
    term:
      id: HP:0030915
      label: Cerebellar edema
  located_in:
    preferred_term: cerebellar cortex
    term:
      id: UBERON:0002129
      label: cerebellar cortex
  laterality: BILATERAL
  diagnostic: true
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:32160830
    reference_title: >-
      Acute Cerebellitis or Postinfectious Cerebellar Ataxia? Clinical and Imaging Features in Acute
      Cerebellitis.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) generally showed bilateral symmetrical T2 hyperintense changes
      with moderate swelling in the cerebellar cortex. Tonsillar herniation was present in 73.3% and
      obstructive hydrocephalus in 26.6%.
    explanation: >-
      The pattern in 15 children with acute cerebellitis: 73.3% is 11 of the 15 and 26.6% is 4.
  - reference: PMID:29166939
    reference_title: "Acute cerebellitis in adults: a case report and review of the literature."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      To diagnose cerebellitis, imaging of the brain (preferably MRI) is required and CSF examination
      may be necessary to narrow the differential diagnosis.
    explanation: >-
      Imaging as a requirement of the diagnosis, from a review of 35 adult cases. With the entry's own
      definition of the acute cerebellitis tier, which rests on imaging, it is why the row is marked
      diagnostic. INDIRECT: the quote requires imaging; it does not make this pattern a criterion.
  - reference: PMID:11826604
    reference_title: >-
      Neuroimaging of acute cerebellitis.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Their magnetic resonance imaging showed hyperintense signal of cerebellar gray matter in
      T2-weighted sequences, which is a strong indication of a diagnosis of acute cerebellitis.
    explanation: >-
      Two patients, and the authors' reading of the grey-matter signal as a strong indication of the
      diagnosis. INDIRECT: a strong indication rather than a criterion.
  - reference: PMID:22805251
    reference_title: >-
      Acute cerebellar ataxia, acute cerebellitis, and opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Neuroimaging is abnormal and the prognosis is less favorable than in acute cerebellar ataxia.
    explanation: >-
      The severe end of the spectrum in the same review that calls the mildest cases' imaging normal.
      INDIRECT: it says the imaging is abnormal, not what it shows. Its second half, a less favourable
      prognosis than in acute cerebellar ataxia, is not borne out on complete recovery by the pooled
      review the entry's notes cite, in which complete recovery was lowest in the benign tier.
  - reference: PMID:28606112

- name: Swelling of one cerebellar hemisphere (hemicerebellitis)
  modality: MRI
  description: >-
    A rare form confined to one cerebellar hemisphere. MRI usually shows a diffusely swollen
    hemisphere with no well-defined mass, which can be mistaken for a posterior fossa tumour, so
    recognising it can spare a patient an unnecessary operation. Ipsilateral atrophy of the hemisphere
    follows in up to half of cases. One review calls it a rare disorder of unknown origin; another
    describes it as a one-sided presentation of acute cerebellitis. One-sided swelling also appears in
    a case of acute cerebellitis with antibodies against glutamate receptor delta 2.
  imaging_finding_term:
    preferred_term: diffuse swelling of one cerebellar hemisphere
    term:
      id: HP:0030915
      label: Cerebellar edema
  located_in:
    preferred_term: one cerebellar hemisphere
    term:
      id: UBERON:0002245
      label: cerebellar hemisphere
  diagnostic: false
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:24423631
    reference_title: >-
      Hemicerebellitis: Report of three paediatric cases and review of the literature.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Acute inflammation of a single cerebellar hemisphere (hemicerebellitis) is a rare disorder of
      unknown origin.
    explanation: >-
      The definition, and one review's view that the cause is unknown.
  - reference: PMID:24423631
    reference_title: >-
      Hemicerebellitis: Report of three paediatric cases and review of the literature.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The neuroimaging of hemicerebellitis raises a challenging differential diagnosis, particularly
      with posterior fossa tumours. Although there is no standard treatment for hemicerebellitis, its
      outcome is usually favourable. However, ipsilateral hemicerebellar atrophy develops in up to half
      of cases, and a minority of children may show persisting fine motor and/or neurocognitive
      sequelae.
    explanation: >-
      The tumour mimic and the later atrophy, from a review of 35 cases including three new ones.
  - reference: PMID:23958482
    reference_title: >-
      Acute pseudotumoral hemicerebellitis: diagnosis and neurosurgical considerations of a rare entity.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Acute pseudotumoral hemicerebellitis is an exceptionally rare unilateral presentation of acute
      cerebellitis mimicking a tumor. It typically has a benign course without specific therapy; thus,
      recognizing this entity is important to avoid needless surgical intervention. MRI provides the
      key for diagnosis and usually reveals a diffusely swollen cerebellar hemisphere with no
      well-defined mass.
    explanation: >-
      The second review's reading, as a one-sided presentation of acute cerebellitis, and the MRI
      appearance it calls the key to the diagnosis. The row is not marked diagnostic because the
      appearance itself can mimic a tumour.
  - reference: PMID:17008044
    reference_title: >-
      A case of acute cerebellitis accompanied by autoantibodies against glutamate receptor delta2.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL

    explanation: >-
      A primary case of one-sided swelling, in a 13-year-old with acute cerebellitis.

- name: Leptomeningeal enhancement

    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL

treatments:
- name: Corticosteroid therapy
  therapeutic_modality: SMALL_MOLECULE
  treatment_term:
    preferred_term: Pharmacotherapy
    term:
      id: NCIT:C15986
      label: Pharmacotherapy
    therapeutic_agent:
    - preferred_term: corticosteroid
      term:
        id: CHEBI:50858
        label: corticosteroid
    - preferred_term: dexamethasone
      term:
        id: CHEBI:41879
        label: dexamethasone
  description: >-
    The commonest treatment in the pooled literature, at three quarters of patients, given on the
    reasoning that the disease is immune-mediated. Many of the cited sources never mention a steroid,
    clinical series among them. No cited source compares it against no treatment
    in a controlled design; the only treated-against-untreated contrast is two children in a
    fulminant case report, and it is about immunomodulatory therapy rather than steroids
    specifically.
  notes: >-
    Antivirals are not recorded as a treatment row, although the pooled review gives them to 47.9% of
    its patients in a sentence this entry already quotes. They treat the trigger rather than the
    post-infectious process, which is what every node in this entry's chain is about, and no cited
    source reports an outcome for them in this disease separable from that of the steroids given with
    them. A row would assert a treatment relationship the sources do not describe.

    No cited source reports a randomised comparison in this disease, and one of them asks for
    exactly that. The paediatric series in which children with a higher clinical score on admission
    were more likely to receive intravenous steroids cannot be read as evidence of effect in either
    direction, and the entry does not read it that way.
  target_mechanisms:
  - target: Immune Response Directed at the Cerebellum
    description: >-
      Suppression of the immune response is what the drug is given for. No cited source demonstrates
      that it acts on this node in this disease; the target is inferred from the drug class.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:42649322
      reference_title: "Post-Infectious Cerebellitis: A Systematic Review of Aetiology, Clinical Presentation, Treatment, and Outcomes."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: >-
        Post-infectious cerebellitis is a heterogeneous, largely immune-mediated syndrome with a
        generally favorable prognosis after corticosteroid-based immunotherapy, though outcomes
        and evidence quality vary by etiology and severity subgroup.
      explanation: >-
        The authors' own summary, and its own caveat about evidence quality. INDIRECT because
        recovery after a drug in an uncontrolled pooled series is one inference step from the drug
        acting on this node.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:42649322
    reference_title: "Post-Infectious Cerebellitis: A Systematic Review of Aetiology, Clinical Presentation, Treatment, and Outcomes."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Corticosteroids were the most common treatment (54/73, 74.0%), followed by antivirals (35/73,
      47.9%) and IVIG (19/73, 26.0%); plasma exchange was given for refractory cases.
    explanation: >-
      The treatment pattern across 73 pooled patients, and the source for the ordering of the rows
      in this block.
  - reference: PMID:28606112
    reference_title: "Acute cerebellitis in children: an eleven year retrospective multicentric study in Italy."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Treatment was decided independently case by case. Patients with a higher clinical score on
      admission had a higher probability of receiving intravenous steroids.
    explanation: >-
      The authors of a multicentre paediatric series report that children with a higher clinical
      score on admission were more likely to receive intravenous steroids, so an outcome comparison
      in it would be confounded by indication. This is why no outcome claim is attached to this row.
  - reference: PMID:28606112
    reference_title: "Acute cerebellitis in children: an eleven year retrospective multicentric study in Italy."
    supports: NO_EVIDENCE
    directness: UNKNOWN
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm these observations.
    explanation: >-
      Kept on this row as NO_EVIDENCE rather than SUPPORT, because a call for trials does not support
      the treatment: it records that the evidence for it has not been gathered. The argument the
      sentence belongs to is in the knowledge-gap discussion, where it is also cited. No quote_role:
      a call for future work is neither this multicentre study's finding nor somebody else's fact.
- name: Intravenous immunoglobulin
  therapeutic_modality: OTHER
  treatment_term:
    preferred_term: Pharmacotherapy
    term:
      id: NCIT:C15986
      label: Pharmacotherapy
    therapeutic_agent:
    - preferred_term: intravenous immunoglobulin
      term:
        id: NCIT:C80829
        label: Human Immunoglobulin G
  description: >-

  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:32160830
    reference_title: >-
      Acute Cerebellitis or Postinfectious Cerebellar Ataxia? Clinical and Imaging Features in Acute

    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-

  - reference: PMID:40787651

- name: Plasma exchange
  therapeutic_modality: OTHER
  treatment_term:
    preferred_term: plasmapheresis
    term:
      id: NCIT:C15304
      label: Plasmapheresis
  description: >-
    Reserved for cases that do not respond to the first two. No cited source reports how many
    received it in this disease, and a review of antibody-positive cerebellar ataxia makes one general
    statement about it, that it had a therapeutic effect in individual patients.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:42649322
    reference_title: "Post-Infectious Cerebellitis: A Systematic Review of Aetiology, Clinical Presentation, Treatment, and Outcomes."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Corticosteroids were the most common treatment (54/73, 74.0%), followed by antivirals (35/73,
      47.9%) and IVIG (19/73, 26.0%); plasma exchange was given for refractory cases.
    explanation: >-
      The only statement in any cited source that counts or indicates this treatment in
      post-infectious cerebellitis specifically, and it gives the indication without a count or an
      outcome. A practical-guidelines review of immune-mediated cerebellar ataxias also lists
      plasmapheresis among the modalities to consider for this disease's class; that is cited on the
      knowledge-gap discussion instead, because it is about the class and not about this treatment's
      use here.
  - reference: PMID:26377184
    reference_title: "'Medusa head ataxia': the expanding spectrum of Purkinje cell antibodies in autoimmune cerebellar ataxia. Part 2: Anti-PKC-gamma, anti-GluR-delta2, anti-Ca/ARHGAP26 and anti-VGCC."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      A potential pathogenic role of anti-GluRδ2 in ACA is conceivable given that GluRδ2 is
      predominantly expressed in PCs, GluRδ2 is present on the cell surface, anti-GluRδ2 was detected in
      the CSF in some cases, GluRδ2 mutations are associated with ataxia (see below), and PEX had a
      therapeutic effect in individual patients.
    explanation: >-
      The review's only general statement of an effect, made in passing within its argument for the
      antibody's pathogenicity and without numbers; one of the patients it describes after plasma
      exchange had limbic encephalitis rather than this disease. INDIRECT for those reasons.
- name: Cerebrospinal fluid diversion and posterior fossa decompression
  therapeutic_modality: SURGERY
  treatment_term:
    preferred_term: cerebrospinal fluid diversion
    term:
      id: NCIT:C93208
      label: Cerebrospinal Fluid Diversion
  description: >-
    The treatment for the swelling's hydrocephalus and mass effect, needed above all in the
    fulminant tier, and the one whose timing the cited three-child series turns on. External
    ventricular drainage or a shunt relieves the hydrocephalus; posterior fossa decompression
    relieves the mass effect itself. Of nine children seen by one centre's neurosurgical service,
    four needed external ventricular drainage, for a mean of 11 days, and none needed further
    surgery; in another series of nine children one needed surgery for triventricular hydrocephalus;
    a 7-year-old needed emergency drainage for life-threatening hydrocephalus; a 12-year-old boy
    recovered completely within two weeks of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt and treatment for raised
    pressure, and his authors call the ventricular decompression life-saving; both children of a
    two-child report of the fulminant form were given cerebrospinal fluid diversion; in a
    three-child series one girl recovered fully after emergency posterior fossa decompression when
    steroids had not stopped her decline; and of two children with herniation and hydrocephalus, one
    was drained and the other treated without surgery, and both recovered fully.
  notes: >-
    The three-child series is the only cited source with drainage at different times and different
    outcomes, a delayed drain in the child who died and an urgent one in a child who recovered, and
    three cases cannot establish that early drainage changes outcome. What it does show is that the
    fatal case was the one in which drainage was delayed, which is a reason to act rather than a
    measured effect. Other cited sources recommend timely or early intervention, and the shunted
    boy's report credits his recovery in part to timely surgery, without setting different timings
    side by side. Besides the three-child series, two of the reports cited here call their
    children's disease fulminant, the shunted boy's and the two-child report of the fulminant form;
    the others do not call their patients' disease fulminant, and one of them calls the condition
    self-limiting.
  target_mechanisms:
  - target: Cerebellar Swelling and Mass Effect
    description: >-
      Both procedures act on the swelling arm directly: one by draining the obstructed cerebrospinal
      fluid, the other by enlarging the compartment the swollen cerebellum sits in.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:42699856
      reference_title: "Acute fulminant cerebellitis in children: a case series and literature review on diagnostic challenges and management strategies."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: >-
        Prompt recognition and aggressive management, including high-dose corticosteroids,
        cerebrospinal fluid diversion, and timely posterior fossa decompression when needed, can
        substantially reduce morbidity and mortality in fulminant cerebellitis.
      explanation: >-
        The authors' own conclusion, naming both procedures. INDIRECT and from three cases: the
        claim that they reduce mortality is the authors' inference from their series, not a
        measured effect.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:33581790
    reference_title: >-
      Cerebellitis as a neurosurgical disease in pediatrics.

    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT

    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-

      external ventricular drain.
    explanation: >-
      Emergency drainage for life-threatening hydrocephalus in a 7-year-old.
  - reference: PMID:28446490
