  - reference: PMID:42699856
    reference_title: "Acute fulminant cerebellitis in children: a case series and literature review on diagnostic challenges and management strategies."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The third patient, a 10-year-old male, was treated with urgent EVD insertion, high-dose
      corticosteroids, and intensive care monitoring, achieving rapid clinical improvement and
      complete recovery.
    explanation: >-
      The contrasting case in the same series: urgent drainage, complete recovery. Two patients
      compared within one report is not a comparison, which is why this row carries no effect claim.
  - reference: PMID:32160830
    reference_title: >-
      Acute Cerebellitis or Postinfectious Cerebellar Ataxia? Clinical and Imaging Features in Acute
      Cerebellitis.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      No patient required surgical decompression.
    explanation: >-
      The counterweight: none of fifteen children in an acute cerebellitis series needed surgical
      decompression, which is why the row is described as needed above all in the fulminant tier.
differential_diagnoses:
- name: Drug or toxin intoxication
  disease_term:
    preferred_term: poisoning
    term:
      id: MONDO:0029000
      label: poisoning
  description: >-
    The second commonest cause of acute ataxia in children after postinfectious cerebellitis in a
    pooled analysis of 1,167 children from eleven studies, with an expected share of 14.1%; the
    cause in 24 of 76 children in one series; and in another, which splits the causes by age, 14% of
    infants and toddlers and of school-age children. One series of acute cerebellar ataxia excludes
    it by its case definition. No cited source gives a history or examination feature that separates
    it. One review says every child with acute ataxia should be screened for toxic ingestion, and a
    systematic review that a toxicology screen should be considered in all of them, and that review
    reports of its screening tests together, toxicology among them, that in most studies the
    abnormalities detected were not diagnostic.
  distinguishing_features:
  - >-
      A toxicology screen. One review says every child with acute ataxia should be screened, and a
      systematic review that a screen should be considered in all of them. No cited source gives a
      clinical feature that separates intoxication.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:41325013
    reference_title: "Etiologies of Acute Ataxia in Children: A Systematic Review of 1167 Subjects."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Eleven studies, consisting of 1167 children, met inclusion criteria of 10 or more patients,
      multiple etiologies of ataxia, and diagnostic data including number of patients with each
      condition.
    explanation: >-
      The pooled analysis's size: eleven studies and 1,167 children. A statement of what the
      analysis included, so no quote role is recorded.
  - reference: PMID:41325013
    reference_title: "Etiologies of Acute Ataxia in Children: A Systematic Review of 1167 Subjects."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Postinfectious cerebellitis (EV, 38.0%; 95% CredI, 35.3-40.8%), drug intoxication/poisoning
      (EV, 14.1%; 95% CredI, 12.1-16.1%), central nervous system infection or inflammation (EV,
      8.1%; 95% CredI, 6.6-9.8%), neoplasm (EV 7.3%; 95% CredI, 5.9-8.8%), and peripheral
      neuropathies including Guillain-Barré syndrome (EV, 6.6%; 95% CredI, 5.3-8.1) occurred most
      commonly and accounted for 74.1% of cases.
    explanation: >-
      Intoxication's expected share among children with acute ataxia, second after postinfectious
      cerebellitis.
  - reference: PMID:38008790
    reference_title: >-
      "The Red Flags" in Clinical Approach to Acute Ataxia-the Experience in Cohort of 76 Children.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The study included 76 children, with a mean age of 5.7 years (IQR 2.1-8.3). The most frequent
      causes of AA were immune-mediated/infective cerebellar ataxia in 27 (35.5%), and intoxication
      in 24 (31.6%) cases, followed by vestibular ataxia, opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome, and
      intracranial expansive process.
    explanation: >-
      Intoxication in 24 of 76 children in one series, the second commonest cause there too.
  - reference: PMID:41321459
    reference_title: "Acute ataxia in children: etiological spectrum and clinical characteristics."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Etiologies varied by age: infants/toddlers (0-3 years) showed acute postinfectious cerebellar
      ataxia (APCA, 66%), drug intoxication (14%), and acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM,
      8%); preschoolers (4-6 years) had APCA (63%), ADEM (14%), and acute cerebellitis (AC, 8%);
      school-aged children (7-14 years) presented APCA (48%), AC (21%), and drug intoxication (14%).
    explanation: >-
      Intoxication in 14% of infants and toddlers and of school-age children, in a series that
      splits the causes by age.
  - reference: PMID:14552515
    reference_title: "Post-infectious acute cerebellar ataxia in children."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The diagnosis of acute cerebellar ataxia was based on the following criteria: acute onset of
      ataxia with or without nystagmus; absence of known genetic predisposing factors, such as
      familial degenerative disorders; and absence of drug intoxication, bacterial meningitis, and
      metabolic disorders.
    explanation: >-
      The series of acute cerebellar ataxia excludes drug intoxication by its own case definition. A
      methods statement, so no quote role is recorded.
  - reference: PMID:27789117
    reference_title: >-
      Acute Ataxia in Children: A Review of the Differential Diagnosis and Evaluation in the
      Emergency Department.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      All patients should be reflexively screened for toxic ingestions.
    explanation: >-
      A review's recommendation that every child with acute ataxia be screened for toxic ingestion.
  - reference: PMID:23683541
    reference_title: "Evaluation of the child with acute ataxia: a systematic review."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      A toxicology screen should be considered in all children presenting with acute ataxia.
    explanation: >-
      A systematic review's advice that a toxicology screen be considered in every child presenting
      with acute ataxia.
  - reference: PMID:23683541
    reference_title: "Evaluation of the child with acute ataxia: a systematic review."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The literature revealed the following frequencies of laboratory screening abnormalities in
      children with acute ataxia: CT (∼2.5%), MRI (∼5%), lumbar puncture (43%), EEG (42%), and
      toxicology (49%). In most studies, abnormalities detected by these screening tests were
      nondiagnostic.
    explanation: >-
      How often screening tests, toxicology among them, were abnormal in the studies the systematic
      review pooled, and that in most studies the abnormalities were not diagnostic.
- name: Posterior fossa tumour
  disease_term:
    preferred_term: posterior fossa tumour
    term:
      id: MONDO:0037736
      label: infratentorial neoplasm
  description: >-
    A neoplasm was the cause in an expected 7.3% of children with acute ataxia in the pooled
    analysis of 1,167 children, whose cached abstract does not give its site. One review says
    neuroimaging is needed in acute or subacute ataxia to exclude a focal lesion in the posterior
    fossa, a tumour among them, and a systematic review that it should be considered in every child
    with new-onset ataxia. The commonest presenting symptoms overlap: in one series medulloblastoma
    presented most often with vomiting and headache, then ataxia, and those three were the commonest
    first symptoms in one paediatric series of acute cerebellitis and the commonest presentation in
    a review of published adult cases. A tumour's symptoms can run for weeks before diagnosis: in
    the medulloblastoma series they had lasted a mean of 7.4 weeks in high-stage and 19.5 weeks in
    low-stage patients before staging. Obstructive hydrocephalus overlaps too: severe acute
    cerebellitis can present with raised intracranial pressure and hydrocephalus, one paediatric
    series of acute cerebellitis found obstructive hydrocephalus in 26.6%, and one child whose
    cerebellitis presented with it was first misdiagnosed as having a posterior fossa neoplasm.
  distinguishing_features:
  - >-
      A mass in the posterior fossa on neuroimaging, which one review calls necessary in acute or
      subacute ataxia.
  - >-
      A history of weeks to months: in one medulloblastoma series symptoms had lasted a mean of 7.4
      weeks in high-stage and 19.5 weeks in low-stage patients before staging.
  - >-
      Not headache, vomiting and ataxia alone, which acute cerebellitis also presents with.
  - >-
      Not obstructive hydrocephalus alone, which about a quarter of children in one series of acute
      cerebellitis had.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:41325013
    reference_title: "Etiologies of Acute Ataxia in Children: A Systematic Review of 1167 Subjects."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Postinfectious cerebellitis (EV, 38.0%; 95% CredI, 35.3-40.8%), drug intoxication/poisoning
      (EV, 14.1%; 95% CredI, 12.1-16.1%), central nervous system infection or inflammation (EV,
      8.1%; 95% CredI, 6.6-9.8%), neoplasm (EV 7.3%; 95% CredI, 5.9-8.8%), and peripheral
      neuropathies including Guillain-Barré syndrome (EV, 6.6%; 95% CredI, 5.3-8.1) occurred most
      commonly and accounted for 74.1% of cases.
    explanation: >-
      A neoplasm's expected share among children with acute ataxia. Indirect: the cached abstract
      does not give the site, so the share may include tumours outside the posterior fossa.
  - reference: PMID:35260471
    reference_title: >-
      Diagnosis and Management of Opsoclonus-Myoclonus-Ataxia Syndrome in Children: An International
      Perspective.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Initially, neuroimaging in children with acute or subacute onset of ataxia, regardless of
      whether they present with opsoclonus, is necessary to exclude focal lesions in the posterior
      fossa, including those due to tumor and other inflammatory or metabolic diseases.
    explanation: >-
      That neuroimaging in acute or subacute ataxia is needed to exclude a focal posterior fossa
      lesion, a tumour among them.
  - reference: PMID:23683541
    reference_title: "Evaluation of the child with acute ataxia: a systematic review."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Neuroimaging should be considered in all children with new onset ataxia.
    explanation: >-
      A systematic review's advice that neuroimaging be considered in every child with new-onset
      ataxia.
  - reference: PMID:8756384
    reference_title: >-
      Is there a correlation between duration of presenting symptoms and stage of medulloblastoma at
      the time of diagnosis?
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The most common presenting symptoms were vomiting (67%), headache (60%), ataxia (40%), and

    explanation: >-
      Ataxia among the presenting symptoms of medulloblastoma, behind vomiting and headache.
  - reference: PMID:8756384
    reference_title: >-

    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Fifty of the 66 patients for whom the duration of symptoms was known (76%) had < or = 3 months

    explanation: >-

  - reference: PMID:32160830
    reference_title: >-
      Acute Cerebellitis or Postinfectious Cerebellar Ataxia? Clinical and Imaging Features in Acute
      Cerebellitis.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The most common first symptoms were ataxia, vomiting, and headache.
    explanation: >-
      The same three symptoms as the commonest first symptoms in one paediatric series of acute

  - reference: PMID:32160830
    reference_title: >-
      Acute Cerebellitis or Postinfectious Cerebellar Ataxia? Clinical and Imaging Features in Acute

    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Tonsillar herniation was present in 73.3% and obstructive hydrocephalus in 26.6%.
    explanation: >-
      Obstructive hydrocephalus in about a quarter of the same paediatric series of acute

  - reference: PMID:29166939
    reference_title: "Acute cerebellitis in adults: a case report and review of the literature."

  - reference: PMID:22805251
    reference_title: >-

    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT

    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL

    explanation: >-
      Severe acute cerebellitis presenting with raised intracranial pressure and hydrocephalus.
  - reference: PMID:42699856
    reference_title: >-
      Acute fulminant cerebellitis in children: a case series and literature review on diagnostic

    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The second patient, a 2-year-old female, presented with obstructive hydrocephalus, initially
      misdiagnosed as a posterior fossa neoplasm; despite high-dose corticosteroids and delayed
      external ventricular drainage (EVD), she progressed to brainstem failure and succumbed.
    explanation: >-
      A child with fulminant cerebellitis who presented with obstructive hydrocephalus and was first

- name: Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome
  disease_term:
    preferred_term: opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome
    term:
      id: MONDO:0015247
      label: opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome
  description: >-
    Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome usually begins in the second year of life and classically presents
    with a characteristic eye movement disorder and myoclonus as well as ataxia, irritability and
    disturbed sleep. It is often first diagnosed as acute cerebellar ataxia, which a review puts
    down to the gait imbalance children with it often present with: acute cerebellar ataxia was the
    commonest misdiagnosis in a series of 389 children, and 2 of 15 children later diagnosed with
    the syndrome in a prospective UK study were first diagnosed with it. In one cohort, provisional
    diagnoses of acute cerebellar ataxia, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis and acute
    cerebellitis were common, and opsoclonus was recognised later in the children whose diagnosis
    was delayed; the authors advise reconsidering the diagnosis when ataxia is prolonged or
    relapses. The development of opsoclonus or myoclonus declares the diagnosis. In the series of
    389 children, no prodromal symptoms were noted in 40%, 60% of patients were irritable, usually
    crying, before onset, 22% were said to be febrile and fewer than 35% had an overt infection.
    Unlike acute cerebellar ataxia it rarely resolves without immunotherapy and is paraneoplastic in
    half of cases, and a systematic review recommends urine catecholamine testing for an occult
    neuroblastoma in a child with ataxia and opsoclonus-myoclonus.
  distinguishing_features:
  - >-
      Opsoclonus: chaotic eye movements without an intersaccadic interval, unlike rhythmic
      nystagmus. Its development, or that of myoclonus, declares the diagnosis.
  - >-
      Myoclonus and disturbed sleep with the ataxia, and onset usually in the second year of life.
  - >-
      Ataxia that is prolonged or relapses, which one cohort's authors say should prompt
      reconsidering the diagnosis.
  - >-
      A course that rarely resolves without immunotherapy, unlike acute cerebellar ataxia, and often
      relapses.
  - >-
      Urine catecholamine testing for an occult neuroblastoma, which a systematic review recommends
      in a child with ataxia and opsoclonus-myoclonus; the syndrome is paraneoplastic in half of
      cases.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:35260471
    reference_title: >-
      Diagnosis and Management of Opsoclonus-Myoclonus-Ataxia Syndrome in Children: An International
      Perspective.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome (OMAS) is a rare disorder of the nervous system with
      onset usually in the second year of life.
    explanation: >-
      The usual age at onset, as a review states it.
  - reference: PMID:35260471
    reference_title: >-
      Diagnosis and Management of Opsoclonus-Myoclonus-Ataxia Syndrome in Children: An International
      Perspective.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      This condition classically presents with a combination of characteristic eye movement disorder
      and myoclonus, in addition to ataxia, irritability, and sleep disturbance.
    explanation: >-
      The presenting combination, of which ataxia is only one part.
  - reference: PMID:35260471
    reference_title: >-
      Diagnosis and Management of Opsoclonus-Myoclonus-Ataxia Syndrome in Children: An International
      Perspective.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Opsoclonus (vimeo.com/208498940), due to saccadic bursts, produces chaotic eye movements,
      without an intersaccadic interval, unlike nystagmus that is rhythmic and has fast or slow
      waves depending on the etiology.
    explanation: >-
      What separates opsoclonus from nystagmus.
  - reference: PMID:35260471
    reference_title: >-
      Diagnosis and Management of Opsoclonus-Myoclonus-Ataxia Syndrome in Children: An International
      Perspective.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Because children with OMAS often present with gait imbalance, initial diagnosis is often acute
      cerebellar ataxia, an infectious or postinfectious illness, which in some cases is associated
      with varicella zoster or Mycoplasma pneumoniae.
    explanation: >-
      That the syndrome is often first diagnosed as acute cerebellar ataxia, because children with
      it often present with gait imbalance.
  - reference: PMID:35260471
    reference_title: >-
      Diagnosis and Management of Opsoclonus-Myoclonus-Ataxia Syndrome in Children: An International
      Perspective.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      In a prospective UK study, 3 of 15 children subsequently diagnosed with OMAS were initially
      misdiagnosed, 2 as acute cerebellar ataxia and 1 as Guillain-Barre syndrome.
    explanation: >-
      How often that happened in one prospective study: 2 of 15 children first diagnosed with acute
      cerebellar ataxia.
  - reference: PMID:28959231
    reference_title: >-
      Demographic, Clinical, and Immunologic Features of 389 Children with Opsoclonus-Myoclonus
      Syndrome: A Cross-sectional Study.
    supports: SUPPORT

    explanation: >-
      Acute cerebellar ataxia as the commonest misdiagnosis among 389 children with the syndrome.
  - reference: PMID:35260471
    reference_title: >-
      Diagnosis and Management of Opsoclonus-Myoclonus-Ataxia Syndrome in Children: An International
      Perspective.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The development of opsoclonus and/or myoclonus declares the OMAS diagnosis.
    explanation: >-
      That opsoclonus or myoclonus is what declares the diagnosis.
  - reference: PMID:41240610
    reference_title: >-
      Diagnostic odyssey of opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome and barriers to early detection.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Provisional diagnoses of acute cerebellar ataxia, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, and
      acute cerebellitis were common.
    explanation: >-
      The provisional diagnoses given before the syndrome was recognised, in one cohort.
  - reference: PMID:41240610
    reference_title: >-
      Diagnostic odyssey of opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome and barriers to early detection.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Analysis of symptoms revealed that nystagmus appeared at the same time in both the early- and
      delayed-diagnosed groups, but opsoclonus was recognized later in the delayed diagnosed group
      (11.5 days versus 96 days, p < 0.01).
    explanation: >-
      Opsoclonus recognised later in the children whose diagnosis was delayed, while nystagmus
      appeared equally early in both groups.
  - reference: PMID:41240610
    reference_title: >-
      Diagnostic odyssey of opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome and barriers to early detection.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Reconsidering the diagnosis in cases of prolonged or relapsing ataxia and recognizing
      opsoclonus early on are vital for the early detection of OMS.
    explanation: >-
      The cohort's authors advise reconsidering the diagnosis when ataxia is prolonged or relapses.
  - reference: PMID:28959231
    reference_title: >-
      Demographic, Clinical, and Immunologic Features of 389 Children with Opsoclonus-Myoclonus
      Syndrome: A Cross-sectional Study.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      In 40%, no prodromal symptoms were noted.
    explanation: >-
      No prodromal symptoms noted in 40% of the 389 children.
  - reference: PMID:28959231
    reference_title: >-
      Demographic, Clinical, and Immunologic Features of 389 Children with Opsoclonus-Myoclonus
      Syndrome: A Cross-sectional Study.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Sixty percent of patients displayed irritability (usually with crying) prior to OMS onset.
      Twenty-two percent of total patients were said to be febrile.
    explanation: >-
      Irritability, usually with crying, before onset in 60% of patients, and fever reported in 22%.
  - reference: PMID:28959231
    reference_title: >-
      Demographic, Clinical, and Immunologic Features of 389 Children with Opsoclonus-Myoclonus
      Syndrome: A Cross-sectional Study.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Irritability/crying dominated prodromal symptomatology (60%); overt infections in <35%.
    explanation: >-
      Overt infection in fewer than 35% of the children.
  - reference: PMID:28959231
    reference_title: >-
      Demographic, Clinical, and Immunologic Features of 389 Children with Opsoclonus-Myoclonus
      Syndrome: A Cross-sectional Study.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      OMS rarely resolves without immunotherapy (acute cerebellar ataxia does) and it is
      paraneoplastic in half of the cases (acute cerebellar ataxia is not)
    explanation: >-
      The two differences from acute cerebellar ataxia as the series' discussion states them: it
      rarely resolves without immunotherapy, and it is paraneoplastic in half of cases.
  - reference: PMID:35260471
    reference_title: >-
      Diagnosis and Management of Opsoclonus-Myoclonus-Ataxia Syndrome in Children: An International
      Perspective.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Although the optimal treatment for OMAS has not been established, the rarity of spontaneous
      remission, the high rate of chronic relapsing course, the risk of permanent neurologic
      sequelae, and evidence supporting an autoimmune cause have led to the widespread use of
      immunotherapy.
    explanation: >-
      The rarity of spontaneous remission and the chronic relapsing course.
  - reference: PMID:23683541
    reference_title: "Evaluation of the child with acute ataxia: a systematic review."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Finally, in a child presenting with ataxia and opsoclonus myoclonus, urine catecholamine
      testing for occult neuroblastoma is recommended.
    explanation: >-
      The recommendation to test urine catecholamines for an occult neuroblastoma.

      id: MONDO:0024619
      label: central nervous system infectious disorder
  description: >-
    Infection of the central nervous system is among the causes of acute ataxia in children. In a
    pooled analysis of 1,167 children from eleven studies, central nervous system infection or
    inflammation, counted together, was the third commonest group, with an expected share of 8.1%;
    acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, an inflammatory condition, has its own row. One referral
    centre lists meningitis among the causes of acute ataxia in its 120 cases; its abstract gives no
    frequency for it. One review advises that lumbar puncture can usually wait until after
    admission, suspected meningitis being the major exception. In one series, children with
    postinfectious ataxia were younger than those with infection or acute disseminated
    encephalomyelitis, a comparison that pools the two and does not say where the infections were.
    Cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis is not confined to infection: the referral centre reports it in
    40% of its patients with post-infectious cerebellar ataxia, though its abstract does not say how
    many had a lumbar puncture.
  distinguishing_features:
  - >-
      Not cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis alone, which one referral centre reports in 40% of its
      patients with post-infectious cerebellar ataxia.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:41325013
    reference_title: >-
      Etiologies of Acute Ataxia in Children: A Systematic Review of 1167 Subjects.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Postinfectious cerebellitis (EV, 38.0%; 95% CredI, 35.3-40.8%), drug intoxication/poisoning
      (EV, 14.1%; 95% CredI, 12.1-16.1%), central nervous system infection or inflammation (EV,
      8.1%; 95% CredI, 6.6-9.8%), neoplasm (EV 7.3%; 95% CredI, 5.9-8.8%), and peripheral
      neuropathies including Guillain-Barré syndrome (EV, 6.6%; 95% CredI, 5.3-8.1) occurred most
      commonly and accounted for 74.1% of cases.
    explanation: >-
      Central nervous system infection or inflammation, an expected 8.1% of children with acute
      ataxia in the pooled analysis of 1,167 children, the third commonest group. Indirect: the
      group counts inflammation together with infection.
  - reference: PMID:27071467
    reference_title: >-
      Acute Ataxia in Childhood: 11-Year Experience at a Major Pediatric Neurology Referral Center.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Of the 120 cases identified over the past 11 years, post-infectious cerebellar ataxia was the
      most commonly diagnosed (59%), followed by drug intoxication, opsoclonus-myoclonus ataxia
      syndrome, episodic ataxia, acute cerebellitis, cerebellar stroke, ADEM, meningitis, cerebral
      vein thrombosis, Leigh's disease, Miller-Fisher syndrome, and concussion.
    explanation: >-
      Meningitis among the causes of acute ataxia in 120 cases at one paediatric neurology referral
      centre, listed after cerebellar stroke and acute disseminated encephalomyelitis; the abstract
      gives no frequency for it.
  - reference: PMID:27789117
    reference_title: >-
      Acute Ataxia in Children: A Review of the Differential Diagnosis and Evaluation in the
      Emergency Department.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Children with stroke, toxic ingestion, infection, and neuro-inflammatory disorders frequently
      exhibit ataxia as an essential-if not the only-presenting feature.
    explanation: >-
      Infection among the conditions in which children frequently show ataxia as an essential,
      sometimes the only, presenting feature. Indirect: the review says infection without saying of
      the central nervous system.
  - reference: PMID:27789117
    reference_title: >-
      Acute Ataxia in Children: A Review of the Differential Diagnosis and Evaluation in the
      Emergency Department.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Lumbar puncture may be deferred until after admission in most instances, with suspicion for
      meningitis being the major exception.
    explanation: >-
      Suspected meningitis as the major exception to deferring lumbar puncture in a child with acute
      ataxia.
  - reference: PMID:31327588
    reference_title: >-
      Acute ataxia in children: Common causes and yield of diagnostic work-up in the era of
      varicella vaccination.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Children diagnosed with post-infectious acute cerebellar ataxia were significantly younger
      (3.48 ± 2.23 vs. 6.5 ± 3.1 years, p = 0.01), as compared with children diagnosed with
      infection and acute disseminated encephalomyelitis.
    explanation: >-
      Children with postinfectious ataxia younger than those with infection or acute disseminated
      encephalomyelitis. Indirect: the comparison group pools the two, and the abstract does not say
      where the infections were.
  - reference: PMID:27071467
    reference_title: >-
      Acute Ataxia in Childhood: 11-Year Experience at a Major Pediatric Neurology Referral Center.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Among the patients with post-infectious cerebellar ataxia, 85% were 1-6 years old and all had
      a history of antecedent viral illness. CSF pleocytosis was present in 40% of patients; all had
      normal brain MRIs.
    explanation: >-
      Pleocytosis in 40% of the same centre's patients with post-infectious cerebellar ataxia, all
      of whom had normal brain MRI.
  notes: >-
    Bound to the general class, central nervous system infectious disorder: the pooled analysis and
    the series name no particular infection, and the review and the referral centre name only
    meningitis.
- name: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis
  disease_term:
    preferred_term: acute disseminated encephalomyelitis
    term:
      id: MONDO:0019383
      label: acute disseminated encephalomyelitis
  description: >-
    Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis requires encephalopathy and polyfocal neurological signs by
    definition, and its lesions are typically bilateral, asymmetrical and large. When its findings
    are mainly cerebellar it can be confused with acute cerebellitis, though, the review that says
    so adds, its lesions on neuroimaging are usually widespread. The clinical signs separate them
    less cleanly, since severe acute cerebellitis can also alter consciousness and cause focal
    deficits. It was the cause in 8% of infants and toddlers and 14% of preschool children with
    acute ataxia in a series that splits the causes by age; in another series, children with it or
    with an infection were older than those with postinfectious acute cerebellar ataxia, and
    demyelinating diseases, a wider group, accounted for 18.2% of the children with acute ataxia at
    one centre.
  distinguishing_features:
  - >-
      Widespread lesions on neuroimaging, which a review sets against acute cerebellitis; another
      describes them as typically bilateral, asymmetrical and large.
  - >-
      Encephalopathy and polyfocal neurological signs, which its definition requires, though severe
      acute cerebellitis can also alter consciousness and cause focal deficits.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:33153097
    reference_title: "Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis: Current Perspectives."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: >-
      By definition, ADEM requires the presence of encephalopathy and polyfocal CNS symptoms.
    explanation: >-
      The definition: encephalopathy and polyfocal signs.

    evidence_source: OTHER

    explanation: >-
      The typical lesions on imaging.

    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis may be confused with acute cerebellitis when the clinical

    explanation: >-
      That it can be confused with acute cerebellitis, and that its lesions on neuroimaging are

  - reference: PMID:22805251
    reference_title: >-
      Acute cerebellar ataxia, acute cerebellitis, and opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome.
    supports: SUPPORT

    explanation: >-
      Severe acute cerebellitis with altered consciousness and focal deficits, which overlap with
      the signs acute disseminated encephalomyelitis requires.

    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL

      Etiologies varied by age: infants/toddlers (0-3 years) showed acute postinfectious cerebellar

    explanation: >-
      Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis in 8% of infants and toddlers and 14% of preschool

    explanation: >-
      Children with postinfectious ataxia younger than those with infection or acute disseminated

  - reference: PMID:38000948

    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL

- name: Miller Fisher syndrome
  disease_term:
    preferred_term: Miller Fisher syndrome
    term:
      id: MONDO:0005851
      label: Miller Fisher syndrome
  description: >-
    A variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome characterised by ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia,
    whose defining marker is anti-GQ1b antibodies. The antibody has also been found in a 22-year-old
    woman with an isolated cerebellar syndrome after an upper respiratory tract infection, with
    normal reflexes and no ophthalmoplegia. That case's authors read it as widening the anti-GQ1b
    syndrome to include isolated cerebellar ataxia, and advise considering anti-GQ1b testing in
    acute cerebellar ataxia following infection. Peripheral neuropathies including Guillain-Barré
    syndrome made up an expected 6.6% of children with acute ataxia in the pooled analysis of 1,167
    children, and Guillain-Barré syndrome was the cause in 9% of children in one paediatric
    emergency-department series, where hyporeflexia or areflexia went with a higher risk of a
    condition needing urgent diagnosis and treatment.
  distinguishing_features:
  - >-
      Ophthalmoplegia and areflexia with the ataxia.
  - >-
      Not anti-GQ1b antibodies alone, which have been found in an isolated cerebellar syndrome after
      infection.
  evidence:
  - reference: DOI:10.1186/s43161-024-00258-8
    reference_title: >-
      Autoimmune mechanisms in Guillain-Barré syndrome subtypes: a systematic review
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      MFS, a variant of GBS, is characterized by ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia, and is
      associated with anti-GQ1b antibodies
    explanation: >-
      The triad and the antibody, as a review's introduction states them.
  - reference: DOI:10.1186/s43161-024-00258-8
    reference_title: >-
      Autoimmune mechanisms in Guillain-Barré syndrome subtypes: a systematic review
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Anti-GQ1b antibodies are the defining marker for MFS, causing cranial nerve dysfunction and

    explanation: >-
      Anti-GQ1b antibodies as the defining marker of Miller Fisher syndrome.

- name: Stroke
  disease_term:
    preferred_term: stroke
    term:
      id: MONDO:0005098
      label: stroke disorder
  description: >-
    Stroke can present in children with ataxia as its essential, sometimes only, feature, and MRI
    detects vascular insults in the posterior fossa better than CT. In a Swiss registry of 43
    children with posterior-circulation arterial ischaemic stroke, ataxia (58.1%) and one-sided
    motor or sensory signs (53.5% and 51.2%) were the commonest clinical signs, and most children
    presented with nonspecific complaints such as headache and nausea or vomiting, which the authors
    say risk delaying the diagnosis, especially with mild neurological findings. One referral centre
    lists cerebellar stroke among the causes of acute ataxia in its 120 cases; its abstract gives no
    frequency for it. After varicella, in one hospital's series, stroke came 2 to 26 weeks after the
    rash, while the acute complications, acute cerebellar ataxia the commonest of them, began a
    median of 5 days after it. No cited source, as cached, compares stroke with postinfectious
    cerebellitis directly or says how often stroke presents as ataxia alone.
  distinguishing_features:
  - >-
      A vascular lesion in the posterior fossa on MRI, which detects it better than CT.
  - >-
      One-sided motor or sensory signs, in about half of the children in a registry of
      posterior-circulation arterial ischaemic stroke.
  - >-
      Timing after varicella: in one hospital's series stroke followed the rash by 2 to 26 weeks,
      while the acute complications, acute cerebellar ataxia the commonest of them, began a median
      of 5 days after it.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:27789117
    reference_title: >-
      Acute Ataxia in Children: A Review of the Differential Diagnosis and Evaluation in the
      Emergency Department.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Children with stroke, toxic ingestion, infection, and neuro-inflammatory disorders frequently
      exhibit ataxia as an essential-if not the only-presenting feature.
    explanation: >-
      That stroke can present with ataxia as its only feature in children.
  - reference: PMID:27789117
    reference_title: >-
      Acute Ataxia in Children: A Review of the Differential Diagnosis and Evaluation in the
      Emergency Department.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      MRI is superior to CT in detecting inflammatory or vascular insults in the posterior fossa,
      though CT may be necessary in emergent situations.
    explanation: >-
      MRI rather than CT for vascular insults in the posterior fossa.

- name: Inherited episodic ataxia
  disease_term:
    preferred_term: hereditary episodic ataxia
    term:
      id: MONDO:0016227
      label: hereditary episodic ataxia
  description: >-
    A familial, dominantly inherited disorder of transient, recurrent attacks of incoordination and
    truncal instability, often triggered by physical exertion or emotional stress, with normal or
    near-normal neurological function between attacks, though some have a progressive baseline
    ataxia. In EA1, EA2 and EA6 onset is mostly before adulthood, and in one type myokymia is
    evident between attacks. No cited source compares it with postinfectious cerebellitis, and
    recurrence alone does not separate them: postinfectious acute cerebellar ataxia relapsed more
    often in children with oligoclonal bands in the spinal fluid in one series, and one boy's ataxia
    after a respiratory infection worsened again after mumps and varicella. The series that reports
    those relapses advises genetic and metabolic assessment, among other tests, for recurrent
    ataxia.
  distinguishing_features:
  - >-
      Recurrent brief attacks with normal or near-normal function between them.
  - >-
      Attacks triggered by physical exertion or emotional stress, in a familial, dominantly
      inherited disorder.
  - >-
      Myokymia between attacks in one type.
  - >-
      Not recurrence alone, since postinfectious ataxia can relapse.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:7842011
    reference_title: >-
      Episodic ataxia/myokymia syndrome is associated with point mutations in the human potassium
      channel gene, KCNA1.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Episodic ataxia (EA) is a rare, familial disorder producing attacks of generalized ataxia,
      with normal or near-normal neurological function between attacks.
    explanation: >-
      The attacks and the normal function between them.
  - reference: PMID:7842011
    reference_title: >-
      Episodic ataxia/myokymia syndrome is associated with point mutations in the human potassium

    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      One type of EA is characterized by brief episodes of ataxia with myokymia (rippling of
      muscles) evident between attacks.
    explanation: >-
      Myokymia between attacks in one type.
  - reference: PMID:29891059
    reference_title: "Episodic ataxias."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Primary episodic ataxias (EAs) are a group of dominantly inherited disorders characterized by
      transient recurrent incoordination and truncal instability, often triggered by physical

    explanation: >-

  - reference: PMID:29891059
    reference_title: "Episodic ataxias."

  - reference: PMID:41321459
    reference_title: "Acute ataxia in children: etiological spectrum and clinical characteristics."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Among APCA cases, CSF oligoclonal band (OCB)-positive patients had later onset, extended
      hospitalization, higher CSF nucleated cell counts, and higher relapse rates.
    explanation: >-
      Higher relapse rates among children with postinfectious acute cerebellar ataxia and

  - reference: PMID:17049194
    reference_title: >-

    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Herein, an 18-month-old boy presented with cerebellar ataxia 9 days following a mild

    explanation: >-
      A child whose ataxia after a respiratory infection worsened again after mumps and varicella
      infections.
  - reference: PMID:41321459
    reference_title: "Acute ataxia in children: etiological spectrum and clinical characteristics."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      For cases suggestive of central nervous system demyelination or recurrent ataxia,
      comprehensive evaluations, including autoantibody testing, tumor screening, and

    explanation: >-
      The series' advice to consider genetic and metabolic assessment, with other tests, for

- name: Vestibular ataxia
  disease_term:
    preferred_term: vestibular ataxia
    term:
      id: MONDO:0100312
      label: vestibular ataxia
  description: >-
    Ataxia from a disorder of the vestibular system. Disorders of the inner ear can cause vertigo
    and imbalance, and vestibular neuritis and viral labyrinthitis provoke severe attacks of vertigo
    with spontaneous nystagmus, labyrinthitis adding hearing loss to the vestibular loss. Vestibular
    ataxia was among the causes in one series of 76 children with acute ataxia. Vertigo is the
    cardinal symptom of vestibular disease and is set apart from gait imbalance, but it can arise in
    the inner ear or in the central nervous system. Hearing loss does not settle the question
    either: in a 17-year-old with vertigo and hearing loss whose examination suggested a peripheral
    cause, the hearing loss raised the suspicion of a central one, and MRI showed demyelinating
    lesions in a middle cerebellar peduncle from multiple sclerosis.
  distinguishing_features:
  - >-
      Vertigo, the cardinal symptom of vestibular disease, though it can also arise centrally.
  - >-
      Hearing loss with the vestibular loss in labyrinthitis, though in one case it pointed to a
      central lesion.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:38008790
    reference_title: >-
      "The Red Flags" in Clinical Approach to Acute Ataxia-the Experience in Cohort of 76 Children.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The study included 76 children, with a mean age of 5.7 years (IQR 2.1-8.3). The most frequent
      causes of AA were immune-mediated/infective cerebellar ataxia in 27 (35.5%), and intoxication
      in 24 (31.6%) cases, followed by vestibular ataxia, opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome, and
      intracranial expansive process.
    explanation: >-
      Vestibular ataxia among the causes of acute ataxia in 76 children, without a count.
  - reference: PMID:23648600
    reference_title: "Inner ear disorders."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Disorders of the inner ear can cause hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo and imbalance.
    explanation: >-
      That inner-ear disorders can cause vertigo and imbalance.
  - reference: PMID:23648600
    reference_title: "Inner ear disorders."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Vertigo is a hallucination of motion, and is the cardinal symptom of vestibular system
      disease. It should be differentiated from other causes of dizziness: gait imbalance,
      disequilibrium, lightheadedness (pre-syncope). Vertigo can be caused by problems in the inner
      ear or central nervous system.
    explanation: >-
      Vertigo as the cardinal symptom of vestibular disease, set apart from gait imbalance, and its
      inner-ear or central origin.
  - reference: PMID:14977076
    reference_title: >-
      Horizontal vestibulo-ocular reflex dynamics in acute vestibular neuritis and viral
      labyrinthitis: evidence of otolith-canal interaction.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      two common labyrinthine diseases that provoke severe attacks of vertigo with spontaneous
      nystagmus: vestibular neuritis (vestibular loss alone) and viral labyrinthitis
      (cochleovestibular loss).
    explanation: >-
      The two labyrinthine diseases, and the hearing loss that separates labyrinthitis from
      vestibular neuritis. An aim statement, so no quote role is recorded.
  - reference: PMID:32353617
    reference_title: >-
      Acute vestibular syndrome and hearing loss mimicking labyrinthitis as initial presentation of
      multiple sclerosis.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The authors present the case of a previously healthy 17-year-old female patient complaining of
      spontaneous vertigo and right-sided hearing loss. Otoneurological examination suggested a
      peripheral vestibular cause and video head impulse test revealed a reduced vestibulo-ocular
      reflex gain.
    explanation: >-
      Vertigo and hearing loss in a 17-year-old, with an examination that suggested a peripheral
      vestibular cause.
  - reference: PMID:32353617
    reference_title: >-
      Acute vestibular syndrome and hearing loss mimicking labyrinthitis as initial presentation of
      multiple sclerosis.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The presence of sensorineural hearing loss raised the suspicion of a central cause and
      prompted imaging evaluation.
    explanation: >-
      The hearing loss raising the suspicion of a central cause.
  - reference: PMID:32353617
    reference_title: >-
      Acute vestibular syndrome and hearing loss mimicking labyrinthitis as initial presentation of
      multiple sclerosis.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      A brain MRI evidenced demyelinating lesions in the right middle cerebellar peduncle and the
      patient was ultimately diagnosed with Multiple Sclerosis.
    explanation: >-
      The central lesion found: demyelination in a middle cerebellar peduncle from multiple
      sclerosis.
- name: Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration
  disease_term:
    preferred_term: paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration
    term:
      id: MONDO:0044877
      label: paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration
  description: >-
    The form with anti-Yo antibodies is its most common variant, and most of what the cited sources
    say is about that form. It presents as a subacute pancerebellar syndrome that reaches a clinical
    plateau within six months, and the vast majority of reported cases are women with pelvic or
    breast tumours. In a systematic review of 379 published patients with anti-Yo antibodies, 96%
    were women, 82% had a gynaecological cancer, 87% of the men had a tumour, mostly
    gastrointestinal, and the median age was 60, so in these sources it is a disease of adults.
    Early MRI is often normal and the spinal fluid often abnormal. A review of immune-mediated
    cerebellar ataxias lists paraneoplastic cerebellar degenerations beside postinfectious
    cerebellitis and makes surgical excision of the primary tumour part of their treatment, though
    in the anti-Yo form a benefit from antitumour therapy has not been consistently observed.
  distinguishing_features:
  - >-
      Subacute onset with a plateau within six months, rather than an acute onset, in the anti-Yo
      form.
  - >-
      An underlying tumour: with anti-Yo antibodies, most often pelvic or breast in an adult woman,
      and gastrointestinal in the few men.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:27606347
    reference_title: "Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration with anti-Yo antibodies - a review."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The ataxic syndrome associated with Anti-Yo antibody, or Purkinje cell cytoplasmic antibody
      type 1 (PCA1), is the most common variant of paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration (PCD).
    explanation: >-
      The anti-Yo form as the most common variant, which is what this review describes.
  - reference: PMID:27606347
    reference_title: "Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration with anti-Yo antibodies - a review."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The typical presentation involves the subacute development of pancerebellar deficits with a
      clinical plateau within 6 months.
    explanation: >-
      The subacute course and its plateau, in the anti-Yo form.
  - reference: PMID:27606347
    reference_title: "Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration with anti-Yo antibodies - a review."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The vast majority of cases have been reported in women with pelvic or breast tumors.
    explanation: >-
      Reported anti-Yo cases mostly in women with pelvic or breast tumours.
  - reference: PMID:36334195
    reference_title: >-
      A Systematic Review on Anti-Yo/PCA-1 Antibody: Beyond Cerebellar Ataxia in Middle-Aged Women
      with Gynecologic Cancer.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Of 379 included patients, 96% were female with gynecologic cancer (82%).
    explanation: >-
      Mostly women with a gynaecological cancer, in a systematic review of 379 published patients
      with anti-Yo antibodies.
  - reference: PMID:36334195
    reference_title: >-
      A Systematic Review on Anti-Yo/PCA-1 Antibody: Beyond Cerebellar Ataxia in Middle-Aged Women
      with Gynecologic Cancer.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Among men, 87% had an associated tumor, mainly of gastrointestinal origin.
    explanation: >-
      A tumour, mostly gastrointestinal, in most of the men in the same review.
  - reference: PMID:36334195
    reference_title: >-
      A Systematic Review on Anti-Yo/PCA-1 Antibody: Beyond Cerebellar Ataxia in Middle-Aged Women
      with Gynecologic Cancer.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The median age was 60 years old.
    explanation: >-
      The median age in the same review.
  - reference: PMID:27606347
    reference_title: "Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration with anti-Yo antibodies - a review."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain is often normal in the early stages, with cerebellar
      atrophy seen later.
    explanation: >-
      Normal MRI early, atrophy later, in the anti-Yo form.
  - reference: PMID:27606347
    reference_title: "Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration with anti-Yo antibodies - a review."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Cerebrospinal fluid abnormalities, primarily elevated protein, lymphocytic pleocytosis, and
      oligoclonal bands, are common in the early stages.
    explanation: >-
      Abnormal spinal fluid early, in the anti-Yo form.
  - reference: PMID:30221603
    reference_title: >-
      Immune-mediated Cerebellar Ataxias: Practical Guidelines and Therapeutic Challenges.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Immune-mediated cerebellar ataxias (IMCAs), a clinical entity reported for the first time in
      the 1980s, include gluten ataxia (GA), paraneoplastic cerebellar degenerations (PCDs),
      antiglutamate decarboxylase 65 (GAD) antibody-associated cerebellar ataxia, post-infectious
      cerebellitis, and opsoclonus myoclonus syndrome (OMS).
    explanation: >-
      Both listed among the immune-mediated cerebellar ataxias.
  - reference: PMID:30221603
    reference_title: >-
      Immune-mediated Cerebellar Ataxias: Practical Guidelines and Therapeutic Challenges.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      When certain factors trigger immune processes, elimination of the antigen( s) becomes a
      priority: e.g., gluten-free diet in GA and surgical excision of the primary tumor in PCDs.
    explanation: >-
      Removing the tumour as part of treatment.
  - reference: PMID:27606347
    reference_title: "Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration with anti-Yo antibodies - a review."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Although some reports indicate benefit from antitumor therapies like surgery and chemotherapy,
      this has not been consistently observed.
    explanation: >-
      That in the anti-Yo form a benefit from antitumour therapy has not been consistently observed.
progression:
- phase: Antecedent infection
  notes: >-
    A febrile illness, usually viral, in roughly three quarters of children. Varicella was
    historically the commonest and is no longer so where the vaccine is in use.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:14552515
    reference_title: >-
      Post-infectious acute cerebellar ataxia in children.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      A prodromal febrile illness was noted in 74.4%: varicella, 31%; mumps, 20%; nonspecific viral
      infection, 15.4%; mycoplasma, 5%; Epstein Barr virus, 3%.
    explanation: >-
      The frequency and the breakdown, in 39 children seen between 1990 and 2001 - before varicella
      vaccination, which is why the varicella share here is not the current one.
  - reference: PMID:35546546
    reference_title: "Postinfectious Acute Cerebellar Syndromes in Children: A Nationally Ascertained Case Series From Australia 2013-2018."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      An acute febrile illness was noted in 55% and none were related to varicella or were
      temporally related to varicella vaccination or other childhood vaccines.
    explanation: >-
      The same phase counted in a vaccinated population twenty years later: no varicella at all
      among 20 Australian children. Twenty cases is a small denominator, and the authors present it
      as a description rather than a rate.
- phase: Latent interval
  notes: >-
    The gap between the infection and the ataxia, of the order of a week. It is the feature that
    separates this disease from an infection of the cerebellum itself.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:14552515
    reference_title: >-
      Post-infectious acute cerebellar ataxia in children.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Latency from the prodromal illness to the onset of ataxia was 8.8 +/- 7.4 days.
    explanation: >-
      The only series-level figure for this syndrome's interval in any cited source; a case report puts
      one child's at nine days after a respiratory infection. The standard deviation here is almost
      as large as the mean, so the figure is a central tendency and not a window.
  - reference: PMID:42649322
    reference_title: "Post-Infectious Cerebellitis: A Systematic Review of Aetiology, Clinical Presentation, Treatment, and Outcomes."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Post-infectious cerebellitis is an immune-mediated cerebellar inflammatory syndrome that
      follows a preceding infection (or, rarely, vaccination) after a latent interval.
    explanation: >-
      The latent interval written into the definition of the disease, which is why it is a phase
      here rather than a detail of the history.
- phase: Acute ataxic phase
  notes: >-
    Ataxia with the cerebellar signs, lasting days to a few weeks in the benign tier. In the
    fulminant tier this is the phase in which swelling and hydrocephalus develop, and it may begin
    with headache and depressed consciousness and no cerebellar signs at all.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:14552515
    reference_title: >-
      Post-infectious acute cerebellar ataxia in children.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Full gait recovery took less than 2 weeks on average, and the longest duration of neurologic
      signs was 24 days (mumps-related).
    explanation: >-
      The duration of this phase at the benign end: under two weeks on average, 24 days at the
      longest in a series in which every child recovered completely.
  - reference: PMID:33454719
    reference_title: >-
      Pediatric Fulminant Cerebellitis Is Still a Fatal Disease that We Know Little About! Two Case
      Reports and a Literature Review.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      The clinical picture started with severe headache, irritability, and acute deterioration of
      consciousness level with the absence of cerebellar signs.
    explanation: >-
      The same phase in the fulminant tier, in two children: the cerebellar signs that name the
      disease were absent, which is the authors' stated reason the diagnosis is missed.
- phase: Recovery or residual deficit
  notes: >-
    Most recover completely. A minority are left with ataxia, tremor or cognitive deficits, and the
    cognitive ones are the easiest to miss because the motor signs resolve first. Death is rare and
    reported only in the fulminant tier among the sources cited here.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:42649322
    reference_title: "Post-Infectious Cerebellitis: A Systematic Review of Aetiology, Clinical Presentation, Treatment, and Outcomes."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Complete recovery occurred in 47/73 patients (64.4%), partial recovery/residual deficit in
      15/73 (20.5%), outcome was not stated for 10/73 (13.7%), and one death (1.4%) was recorded
      (COVID-19-associated necrotizing encephalopathy) - the only fatality, occurring in an adult.
    explanation: >-
      The outcome distribution across 73 pooled patients, with the undetermined fraction left in. A
      pooled review of case reports is weighted towards the cases worth reporting, so these shares
      are an upper bound on severity rather than a population figure.
  - reference: PMID:8210223
    reference_title: >-
      Course and outcome of acute cerebellar ataxia.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Ninety-one percent (55/60) of these, including all children with chickenpox, recovered
      completely from ataxia.
    explanation: >-
      The benign end measured without the publication bias of a pooled case review: 55 of the 60 followed
      for four months or more, out of 73 consecutive children at one hospital over 23 years.
  - reference: PMID:32160830
    reference_title: >-
      Acute Cerebellitis or Postinfectious Cerebellar Ataxia? Clinical and Imaging Features in Acute
      Cerebellitis.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Acute cerebellitis heals with sequelae in about one-third of cases.
    explanation: >-
      The cerebellitis tier, where the proportion is the other way round from the benign one. This
      is the authors' summary of their own 15-child series.
- phase: Outcome of the severe course
  notes: >-
    Cited sources describe the fulminant form as carrying a high risk of morbidity and mortality, in
    the conclusion of a three-child series and a two-case report's introduction, or of death, in the
    introduction of a paediatric series of nine. The only outcome rate given for the fulminant tier
    comes from a pooled review of 73 published cases, which counts the cases somebody chose to
    publish: complete recovery in 69.2% of its 13 fulminant cases, which also held its one death, an
    adult with a COVID-19-associated necrotising encephalopathy. In a different series, of nine
    children referred to one centre's neurosurgical service, two recovered completely and six were
    left functionally dependent, cognitive impairment being the commonest residual deficit, and the
    authors suggest that hydrocephalus needing surgery may predict a poor outcome.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:42699856
    reference_title: >-
      Acute fulminant cerebellitis in children: a case series and literature review on diagnostic
      challenges and management strategies.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Fulminant AC in children, although rare, carries a high risk of morbidity and mortality.
    explanation: >-
      The series' conclusion on the fulminant form, drawn with its review of the literature.
  - reference: PMID:33454719
    reference_title: >-
      Pediatric Fulminant Cerebellitis Is Still a Fatal Disease that We Know Little About! Two Case
      Reports and a Literature Review.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Acute cerebellitis is a rare inflammatory disease with a variable clinical course that ranges
      from self-limiting illness with a benign outcome to a fulminant process (known as fulminant
      cerebellitis) associated with high risk of morbidity and mortality.
    explanation: >-
      The same risk, in a two-case report's background.
  - reference: PMID:28318729
    reference_title: >-
      Acute cerebellitis in paediatric patients: Our experience.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Acute cerebellitis is a rare inflammatory disease with a highly variable clinical course that
      ranges from benign self-limiting symptoms to a fulminant presentation associated with a high
      risk of death due to compression of the posterior fossa, acute hydrocephalus, and intracranial
      hypertension.
    explanation: >-
      A nine-child series' introduction: the fulminant presentation carries a high risk of death.
  - reference: PMID:42649322
    reference_title: >-
      Post-Infectious Cerebellitis: A Systematic Review of Aetiology, Clinical Presentation,
      Treatment, and Outcomes.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Based on neuroimaging findings and the presence of life-threatening features, 34 patients
      (46.6%) were classified as acute cerebellar ataxia (ACA), 26 (35.6%) as acute cerebellitis
      (AC), and 13 (17.8%) as acute fulminant cerebellitis (AFC), with complete recovery in 58.8%,
      69.2%, and 69.2% of each subtype, respectively, and the cohort's only death occurring in the
      AFC subgroup.
    explanation: >-
      Complete recovery in 69.2% of the 13 fulminant cases of a pooled review, which also held its
      only death.
  - reference: PMID:42649322
    reference_title: >-
      Post-Infectious Cerebellitis: A Systematic Review of Aetiology, Clinical Presentation,
      Treatment, and Outcomes.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT

discussions:
- discussion_id: pic_hyperexcitability_without_ataxia
  kind: HUMAN_MODEL_MISMATCH
  status: OPEN
  prompt: >-
    The rodent model of acute cerebellar inflammation produces Purkinje cell hyperexcitability and
    depression-like behaviour but no ataxia, while the human disease is defined by ataxia. Does the
    inflammatory mechanism shown in the model explain the human sign, or is a further step missing?
  attaches_to:
  - pathophysiology#Purkinje Cell Intrinsic Hyperexcitability
  - pathophysiology#Cerebellar Dysfunction
  rationale: >-
    The microglia-TNF-alpha-Purkinje cell arm of this entry's pathograph rests entirely on rodent
    work, and the authors of that work say in terms that their animals were not ataxic. Models that
    are ataxic show the opposite electrophysiology - Purkinje cell loss and hypoexcitability. So the
    cited mechanism and the cited sign come from different preparations, and the edge from
    hyperexcitability to cerebellar dysfunction is the entry's weakest. It is drawn because it is
    what the sources support, and it is marked here rather than left to look settled.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:35326323
    reference_title: "Acute Cerebellar Inflammation and Related Ataxia: Mechanisms and Pathophysiology."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    snippet: >-
      In our animal model of the acute inflammation of the cerebellar cortex, animals did not show
      any ataxia but hyperexcitability in the cerebellar cortex and depression-like behaviors.
    explanation: >-
      The mismatch stated by the authors of the model itself: inflammation produced
      hyperexcitability and no ataxia.
  - reference: PMID:35326323
    reference_title: "Acute Cerebellar Inflammation and Related Ataxia: Mechanisms and Pathophysiology."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    snippet: >-
      Therefore, there is a gap in our interpretation between the very early phase of cerebellar
      inflammation and the emergence of cerebellar ataxia.
    explanation: >-
      The same authors naming the gap as a gap. This is the sentence the discussion exists to carry.
- discussion_id: pic_glurdelta2_cause_or_consequence
  kind: CONTROVERSY
  status: OPEN
  prompt: >-
    Is the anti-glutamate-receptor-delta2 autoantibody found in some cases a cause of the cerebellar
    injury or a consequence of it?
  attaches_to:
  - pathophysiology#Immune Response Directed at the Cerebellum
  - pathophysiology#Autoantibodies Binding Neural Tissue
  rationale: >-
    Two case reports of the same antibody read it in opposite directions, and neither is in a
    position to settle the question: one argues the antibody is induced by cerebellar damage because
    it was absent from the cerebrospinal fluid early on, the other argues it plays a causal role
    because it was present in both serum and cerebrospinal fluid. Each is a single patient. A review
    adds that rabbit antibodies against the receptor's putative ligand-binding region caused transient
    ataxia when injected over the mouse cerebellum, which shows that such an antibody can act, not that the
    patients' antibodies do. The entry's immune-response node therefore names no effector, and this
    discussion records why.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:17049194
    reference_title: >-
      Acute cerebellar ataxia and consecutive cerebellitis produced by glutamate receptor delta2
      autoantibody.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Thus, we believe that the glutamate receptor delta2 autoantibody may play a role in cerebellar
      ataxia and consecutive cerebellitis.
    explanation: >-
      One side, stated as a belief by its own authors from one 18-month-old patient in whom the
      antibody was found in both serum and cerebrospinal fluid.
  - reference: PMID:17008044
    reference_title: >-
      A case of acute cerebellitis accompanied by autoantibodies against glutamate receptor delta2.
    supports: REFUTE
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      It was suggested that autoantibodies against GluRdelta2 might not have injured the tissue due
      to the immunological action, but might be induced as a consequence of cerebellar damage.
    explanation: >-
      The other side, from a single 13-year-old in whom the antibody was in serum but not
      cerebrospinal fluid. REFUTE against the pathogenic reading above, not against the antibody's
      presence, which both reports agree on.
  - reference: PMID:26377184
    reference_title: "'Medusa head ataxia': the expanding spectrum of Purkinje cell antibodies in autoimmune cerebellar ataxia. Part 2: Anti-PKC-gamma, anti-GluR-delta2, anti-Ca/ARHGAP26 and anti-VGCC."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    snippet: >-
      injection of polyclonal antibodies specific for the putative ligand-binding region of GluRδ2
      generated by immunisation of rabbits with a synthetic peptide into the supracerebellar
      subarachnoid space was shown to cause ... transient ataxia in mice
    explanation: >-
      Support for the pathogenic reading, as a review reports it: an antibody against the receptor can
      cause transient ataxia in mice. INDIRECT because the antibodies were raised in rabbits against a
      synthetic peptide, not taken from patients; the ellipsis skips the culture results in the same

- discussion_id: pic_steroid_effect_untested
  kind: KNOWLEDGE_GAP
  status: OPEN
  prompt: >-
    Do corticosteroids change the outcome of post-infectious cerebellitis, and in which severity
    tier?
  attaches_to:
  - treatments#Corticosteroid therapy
  rationale: >-
    Three quarters of pooled patients receive corticosteroids and no cited source compares them with
    no treatment in a controlled design. The nearest thing to a comparison is two children in a
    fulminant case report, one given immunomodulatory therapy with a better outcome and one not. A
    multicentre paediatric series of acute cerebellar ataxia and cerebellitis reports that patients
    with a higher clinical score on admission had a higher probability of receiving intravenous
    steroids, so an outcome comparison in it would be confounded by indication, and it says
    randomised controlled trials are needed to confirm its observations. Because most children in
    the benign tier recover without treatment, a trial would have to be powered on the severe tiers,
    which are the rare ones - which is a reason the gap has stayed open rather than an argument that
    it does not matter.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:28606112
    reference_title: "Acute cerebellitis in children: an eleven year retrospective multicentric study in Italy."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm these observations.
    explanation: >-
      The gap, stated by the authors of that multicentre paediatric series. No quote_role is
      recorded: a call for future work is neither the paper's finding nor somebody else's fact.
  - reference: PMID:30221603
    reference_title: "Immune-mediated Cerebellar Ataxias: Practical Guidelines and Therapeutic Challenges."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      There is no evidence of significant differences in terms of response and prognosis among the
      various types of immunotherapies.
    explanation: >-
      The adjacent gap for the choice between immunotherapies, from a practical-guidelines review of
